details: Single-language Go module (Go 1.25). Sibling Python and Java ports exist as independent codebases but adk-go is not a wrapper. No secondary language in this repo.

Python-only (>=3.10, <3.14). No TypeScript/Go/Rust SDKs. Multiple PyPI packages (crewai, crewai-core, crewai-cli, crewai-tools, crewai-files).

Python primary (3.10+). TypeScript sibling repo (openai-agents-js) is maintained separately as a parallel implementation, not a dependency.
TypeScript single-language project (Node 22+, Deno, Bun; experimental Cloudflare Workers). The Python sibling repo is a parallel implementation.
Python 3.10-3.14 single-language project. No second runtime.

Python >=3.10 library. Companion strands-agents-tools package is also Python. No second-language runtime required.

TypeScript (ESM-first). Consumed via npm/yarn/pnpm; runs in Node.js or compatible JS runtimes (Edge, Bun, Deno where supported).

Heavy Go framework with bundled run loop, REST/A2A servers, web UI, OTel, session/memory/artifact stores, plugin and skill systems. Not a thin SDK — comparable scope to Mastra.
Heavy Python platform — FastAPI-based AgentOS with 50+ routers (auth, scheduler, tracing, evals, approvals, MCP) plus an Agent class with 80+ constructor parameters.
Multi-crate Rust workspace; you embed it in whatever Rust binary you build. Core surface is focused (agent/executor/memory/tool/runtime); features gated via Cargo flags.
Thin (~5 kLOC) Python shim that subprocesses a bundled Claude Code Node/native binary which actually runs the agent loop. Closest to a wrapper around a vendor-managed CLI.
TypeScript shim (~2 MB JS) over a 200+ MB bundled Claude Code native binary. The loop, system prompt, tools and skills run inside the spawned subprocess; SDK is a control-protocol bridge.
Heavy Python framework bundling crew/flow runtime, memory (LanceDB), checkpointing, MCP, A2A, event bus, CLI, telemetry. Optional AMP SaaS adds hosted automations and triggers.
Go library (~12 kLOC compose+adk) with no HTTP server, UI or eval. Rich runtime primitives via eino-ext but you assemble the application. CloudWeGo-owned, ByteDance-internal use case driving roadmap.
Medium-heavy Go framework with registry, 18 first-party plugins, prompt loader, Reflection API server (dev-only) and stateless HTTP handler factory. JS dev-tools CLI is optional and dev-only.
OSS graph runtime (libs/langgraph) plus closed-source LangGraph Platform server (langgraph_api) for queue/auth/multitask/MCP routes. Pure-OSS is library; full product is hybrid OSS+SaaS.
Python library: agent/Workflow runtime in-process. No HTTP server, no scheduler, no UI. Production multi-agent serving punted to the separate llama_deploy project.
Heavy TypeScript framework. @mastra/core (200+ files, ~7k LOC for Agent) bundles agents, workflows, memory, storage, RAG, voice, MCP, deployers, scheduler, RBAC/FGA, scorers, playground.

Heavy SDK (~27 kLOC Python alone) for Python and .NET. Ships agents, workflows, sessions, compaction, MCP, middleware, observability, skills, security, evaluation, and 20+ provider connectors. Azure-tilted but core has no hard Azure dependency.
Medium-heavy Python library. Ships agents, 10 session backends, guardrails, MCP, sandbox runtime, tracing, realtime, REPL — but no dev UI, scheduler, deployer, or eval harness.
Lean TypeScript library: agents-core, agents-openai, agents-realtime, extensions. No bundled storage, eval, dev UI, or plugin system. The umbrella @openai/agents re-exports the parts.
Thin-to-medium Python library (~50 modules). Built atop pydantic_graph; ships Agent, hooks, toolsets and optional ASGI adapters. Durable execution via opt-in temporal/dbos/prefect/restate.
Medium-thick Rust library: Agent, AgentBuilder, Extractor, Pipeline, multi-turn/streaming loop, 26 provider integrations, 10+ vector stores, MCP client. No HTTP server or dev UI.
Medium-light Python library. ~30 sub-modules: agent, event_loop, hooks, multiagent (Graph/Swarm/A2A), sessions, MCP client, OTel telemetry, plugin system. AWS-leaning default but provider-agnostic.
Medium-heavy Node library (~2,100 LOC Agent class) with hooks, plugins, interventions, multiagent, sessions, telemetry. WASM build shared with strands-py via WIT contract.
Thin TypeScript SDK. generateText/streamText/toolLoop primitives plus 50+ provider adapters and UI stream protocol. No sessions, durable runtime, RAG, eval, skill loader or dev UI.

Loop is plain Go in your binary — internal/llminternal/base_flow.go drives Flow.Run, invoked by runner/runner.go. No subprocess, no sidecar. Only outbound HTTPS to the LLM provider. First-party REST/A2A servers run in the same process.
Agent.run dispatches to agno.agent._run inside your Python uvicorn worker. Memory/learning/cultural-knowledge run in background threads; no subprocess. AgentOS itself is the FastAPI app you serve.
Loop runs on the caller's tokio runtime (direct.rs and react.rs TurnEngine). LLM calls are plain async HTTP from the same process. Optional in-process ractor actor runtime; never a separate process.

Loop runs in a spawned Claude Code Node/native binary, not in your Python — Python is a JSON-over-stdio control-protocol shim. You cannot fork the loop without forking Claude Code; only hooks and canUseTool extend it. Acceptable for Claude-only tools, weak for benchmark's open multi-provider goal.

Same architecture as the Python SDK: agent loop, system prompt, tool dispatch, permissions, compaction, skill discovery and sub-agent fan-out all happen inside a spawned native binary. The TS package is a transport+RPC bridge. Hook callbacks and SDK MCP servers run in your Node heap.
Crew.kickoff → AgentExecutor (or legacy CrewAgentExecutor) runs in your Python process. LLM HTTP calls via LiteLLM or native SDKs go straight from the same process. No subprocess, no vendor binary.

ChatModelAgent.Run spawns a goroutine that runs a compose.Graph (Init→ChatModel→ToolNode) in your Go process. Workflow agents fan out goroutines coordinated by sync.WaitGroup. No subprocess at any layer.

ai.GenerateWithRequest at go/ai/generate.go is the single Go function that recurses model→tools→model in your binary. Reflection HTTP server on :3100 only starts when GENKIT_ENV=dev. Production binary is loop+registry+your HTTP server.

CompiledStateGraph.stream/invoke drives PregelLoop.tick directly in your Python process; tools and checkpointer I/O are in-process. The closed-source langgraph_api server wraps the same loop with queue/auth/multitask but does not subprocess it.

FunctionAgent.run resolves to Workflow.run which schedules @step methods on the asyncio event loop. No subprocess or vendor cloud round-trip. HTTP/distribution is BYO or via separate llama_deploy repo.

packages/core/src/loop/loop.ts builds a Mastra workflow stream that runs entirely in your TypeScript runtime (Node/Bun/CF Workers/Vercel Edge). No external scheduler; the agent loop is just a workflow on the in-process runtime.

Python agent.run uses BaseChatClient.get_response with FunctionInvokingChatClient tool loop; .NET uses Microsoft.Extensions.AI's FunctionInvokingChatClient via DelegatingAIAgent. Both run inside your host process — no subprocess, no bundled CLI.

Runner.run drives run_loop.run_single_turn / execute_tools_and_side_effects on the asyncio event loop you own. No bundled CLI, no Node sidecar, no sister-repo server. Shape comparable to Mastra or Vercel AI SDK.

Runner.run is a single while(true) loop in run.ts that calls prepareTurn → getResponseWithRetry → processModelResponseAsync → resolveTurnAfterModelResponse. No subprocess, no vendor binary; loop runs in Node/Deno/Bun.

Agent.run opens iter() which builds a pydantic_graph.GraphRun and walks UserPromptNode→ModelRequestNode→CallToolsNode→End. Every model call is host-process HTTPS; no subprocess. Durable variants (temporal/dbos) run the same graph under their workers.
Loop is plain Rust async — crates/rig-core/src/agent/prompt_request/mod.rs (non-streaming) and streaming.rs. Runs on your tokio runtime; WASM-compatible. No subprocess or IPC.

event_loop.event_loop_cycle is a pure-Python async generator called from Agent._execute_event_loop_cycle. No subprocess. A ConcurrencyException guards one stream_async per Agent instance, pushing one Agent per active session but many sessions per process.

Agent.stream is an async function* whose body loops until stopReason != toolUse, dispatching tools through the local ToolRegistry. Providers do outbound HTTP/SSE but orchestration is local. No subprocess.

generateText/streamText is a do/while loop in packages/ai/src/generate-text/generate-text.ts; ToolLoopAgent wraps it as a method-call entrypoint. No daemon, no subprocess — only HTTPS to provider APIs.
One Go binary; only Vertex AI/Gemini API (or BYO provider) mandatory. Postgres/SQLite/Spanner/GCS/Vertex Agent Engine all optional. No native libs, no JVM/Python/Node, no required subprocesses.

note: Python plus DB driver, MCP optional
details: Python 3.7+; agno[os] adds fastapi, uvicorn, sqlalchemy, PyJWT, opentelemetry-sdk, croniter, pytz. You pick a DB driver (Postgres/MySQL/SQLite/Redis/Mongo/DynamoDB/GCS) plus an LLM provider key. Heavier than thin SDKs but no daemons or native binaries.

Rust 1.75+, tokio mandatory; ractor for actor runtime. Optional Cargo features pull wasmtime, deno_ast/rquickjs, rmcp, qdrant-client, tch/burn/mistral-rs/llama-cpp. No mandatory DB or vendor; LLM providers gated behind features. Compile time is the real cost.

Python 3.10+ and a bundled Claude Code Node binary auto-discovered or system-installed. Anthropic API key mandatory. The CLI binary is large, and the loop only works with the CLI; you cannot replace it. Otherwise no Postgres/Redis/vector DB required.

Node 18+ (or Bun/Deno) plus a 207-233MB platform-specific Claude binary as optionalDependencies — practically mandatory; SDK throws on missing binary unless pathToClaudeCodeExecutable is set. Multi-arch Docker images ship 460+ MB of binaries. Anthropic API (or Bedrock/Vertex/Foundry) required.

Python ≥3.10 <3.14, pure Python — no bundled binaries, no Node, no vendor CLI. Default LanceDB writes to disk; checkpoints to JSON/SQLite. LLM provider HTTP endpoint required. Optional sandbox (E2B/Daytona) and MCP servers. AMP cloud is opt-in.
Go 1.25, no bundled binaries, no daemons. Postgres/Redis/vector stores only needed if you wire them via eino-ext. Lightest deployment story of any benchmarked stack alongside adk-go and rig.

Go ≥1.25, pure-Go modules. Optional Node.js + genkit CLI for dev UI/eval/init helpers only — not required at runtime. Optional GCP credentials, OTel exporter, Postgres/Firestore via plugins. ~30 MB binary, ~30 MB RSS idle.

Python ≥3.10. Storage (Postgres via psycopg, or SQLite) optional. LLM providers via langchain-* packages. For HTTP server you must add langgraph-cli[inmem] which pulls the closed-source langgraph-runtime-inmem/postgres; Platform deployments also need Redis for API/worker pub/sub.

Python 3.10+ with SQLAlchemy, httpx, pydantic, tiktoken, aiohttp, nltk, tenacity, banks, aiosqlite, llama-index-workflows. No bundled binaries. No mandatory infra; default Memory uses aiosqlite. Each provider/store integration adds its own SDK.

Node ≥18 (or Bun, Cloudflare Workers, Vercel Edge). 40+ AI SDK provider packages. Default in-memory store must be replaced for production (libsql/pg/redis/d1/dynamo/cloudflare/mssql). Optional vector store, Redis pubsub, Datadog/OTel.

Python ≥3.10 or .NET 8/9+. No external binaries the SDK subprocesses. Optional Redis/Cosmos DB/Azure AI Search/Foundry-hosted threads for persistence. One LLM provider required. No mandatory observability or eval vendor.

Python 3.10+, pure Python — no bundled binaries, no Node CLI. OpenAI API by default (or LiteLLM/any-llm for 100+ providers). All session backends (Sqlite/Postgres/Redis/Mongo/Dapr) optional; default in-memory. ~100-150 MB RAM baseline.

Node 22+, Deno or Bun. No bundled binaries, no subprocess. OpenAI API for default Model; AI-SDK extension brings Anthropic/Gemini/Bedrock. MCP server subprocesses opt-in. Cloudflare Workers experimental with nodejs_compat.

Python 3.10+, pydantic/pydantic-core/pydantic-graph/genai-prices/opentelemetry/anyio. No external binaries, no required infra. LLM provider key required. Durable execution via opt-in temporal/dbos/prefect/restate extras.

Rust edition 2024, tokio runtime, reqwest default HTTP client. WASM-compatible. No bundled subprocesses or CLIs, no required infra. Companion crates (rig-bedrock, rig-vertex, rig-memory, etc.) for opt-in extras.

Python ≥3.10 with boto3 in core (Bedrock default). Optional provider extras: anthropic/gemini/litellm/llamaapi/mistral/ollama/openai/writer/sagemaker. Optional S3 for sessions, OTLP collector for traces. No bundled CLI.

Node 20+, @aws-sdk/client-bedrock-runtime + small utilities. All other LLM providers and OTel/MCP/Express/S3 are optional peer-deps. No bundled CLI. FileStorage local dir or S3Storage; no mandatory Postgres/Redis.
Node v18/20/22 (v22 recommended). No native libs, no bundled binaries. Database BYO. Only an LLM provider account (or AI Gateway) needed. Cold start is essentially Node baseline.

README explicitly states "Easily containerize and deploy agents, with strong support for cloud-native environments like Google Cloud Run." cmd/launcher composes web UI + REST + A2A + agent-engine emulator. Multi-tenancy by (AppName,UserID,SessionID) composite key — one process many tenants is the natural shape.

Canonical pattern is agent_os.serve(app=..., reload=True) calling uvicorn.run. One process serves many concurrent sessions and agents; horizontal scaling by pointing multiple uvicorn workers at the same DB. Auth, RBAC, scheduling and tracing all in this single process.

Docs describe direct vs actor agents but do not prescribe container-per-tenant vs shared process. README's "horizontal scaling with multi-agent coordination" refers to the in-process actor runtime, not multi-process deployment. You embed it in whatever Rust binary you build.

Repo does not state a topology, but every query()/ClaudeSDKClient connection spawns a fresh CLI subprocess. Natural shape is container-per-tenant or many-CLI-subprocesses-per-Python-process with one CLI per active conversation. No production Dockerfile or hosted runtime shipped.

note: N workers per pod, alpha bridge
details: Vendor hosting doc recommends one CLI subprocess per session mediated by your HTTP server. attachBridgeSession/runAssistantWorker (alpha) document worker-per-session for claude.ai bridge. No first-party queue or scheduler; scheduling field polls a local file.

OSS docs assume one Python process per request running a Crew. AMP recommends GitHub-or-ZIP deploy to managed runtime (container per crew per automation). docs/en/concepts/production-architecture.mdx covers crew design, not horizontal scaling. No tenant primitive in OSS.

No vendor topology doc — it's a library. CloudWeGo docs implicitly assume one-process-many-tenants with horizontal Pod scaling and BYO ingress. Confirmed in production at Dailymotion: Eino embedded in single Go process per pod behind own router, shared DB state. Multi-tenancy guidance minimal.

Samples target Google Cloud Run as canonical hosting model — stateless container instances behind load balancer (samples/cloud_run_deploy.sh). One Go binary serving N HTTP routes via genkit.Handler. Sessions punted to your DB. Per-tenant identity flows in via headers→ContextProvider.

Platform docs recommend one-process-many-tenants: fleet of API pods sharing Postgres for state + Redis for pub/sub between API and worker pods. Self-host follows same pattern via langgraph up Docker compose or K8s Helm chart. Pure-OSS users BYO everything.

Official "deployment" tutorial literally says TODO. Recommended path for production multi-agent serving is the separate llama_deploy project, which is out of scope. No multi-tenant or scaling guidance shipped with the framework itself.

Documented one-process-many-tenants with stateless Hono server. Resumable streams remove session-affinity requirement. Deployers package for Vercel, Netlify, Cloudflare Workers, plus deployers/cloud for Mastra Cloud. Scheduler package for background work.

Multiple documented paths: Microsoft.Agents.AI.Hosting (AddAIAgent+AgentSessionStore+AIHostAgent) for ASP.NET, container-per-agent via FoundryHostedAgents, worker-pool/durable orchestration via DurableTask and Azure Functions, plus DevUI for local dev. Sample for each.

SDK has no vendor opinion. Examples assume one Python process per host hosting many sessions via asyncio. For horizontal scaling, run N stateless workers with a shared store (SQLAlchemy/Redis/Mongo). No first-party container-per-tenant recommendation.

Docs do not prescribe a topology. examples/nextjs/ shows one-process-many-requests in a Next.js Route Handler. No built-in worker pool, queue, or cluster mode. Cloudflare Workers documented as experimental.

Not opinionated; docs treat Agent like a FastAPI app. UI adapters assume one agent instance per ASGI app and one HTTP route per agent. Production durable patterns documented for Temporal/DBOS/Prefect under docs/durable_execution/. Default is one-process-many-tenants.

Rig is a library; docs offer no production deployment guidance. You ship a Rust binary (typically axum+tokio) and embed Rig. Container-per-tenant vs one-process-many-tenants is your call; state held in Arcs makes one-process-many-tenants the natural default.

Not prescribed by the SDK. Official guide is strandsagents.com docs on "operating agents in production". A ConcurrencyException raised on concurrent stream_async pushes one Agent instance per active session. Multiple sessions per process fine via distinct Agent instances.

Not prescribed in repo. README/examples treat the SDK as a normal Node library; no shipped "agent runtime daemon". Practical patterns one-process-many-agents (per-request instantiation) or container-per-tenant for strong isolation.

SDK doesn't ship hosting recipes. Vercel docs and examples/next-agent/ recommend mounting createAgentUIStreamResponse inside Next.js API route. One process per Node instance, many tenants per process; horizontal scaling via Next.js. All session state in your external DB.

Sub-second from main() to first r.Run; tens of MB RAM baseline. 20-40 MB compiled binary depending on whether Web UI is embedded. No JVM/Python/Node interpreter, no bundled vendor binary. Fastest cold start of any benchmarked stack.

Cold start dominated by Python interpreter + FastAPI app + AgentOS init (sync/async DB initialization, SQLAlchemy engine, optional table creation/migration). 100+ tool modules and 49 model adapters pulled in. Exact RAM/disk numbers BYO; pyproject suggests moderate footprint.

Release binary cold start ≈ process startup time (typically <100ms). Memory baseline small unless you enable llama.cpp/mistral-rs features. Compile time is the real cost — full cargo build with all features is heavy, but runtime is light.

Each connect() does version check + subprocess spawn + initialize handshake (60s timeout). CLI cold start dominated by Node startup; upstream issue #333 reports 20-30s cold start. 200-500 MB RAM per active session including model context. Session JSONL transcript on disk per session.

207-233 MB binary per platform in node_modules; multi-arch Docker images add up. Open issue #268 reports listSessions() spawn at 900 MB+; plan for ~1 GB resident per concurrent session. Cold start 5-20s warm-process resolve + initialize handshake; WarmQuery API exists to amortize.

Cold start ~0.5-1s dominated by openai+LiteLLM imports plus ~100ms LanceDB index init. RAM baseline ~150 MB Python interpreter + framework, growing with memory store. Disk ~50-100 MB wheels; LanceDB grows linearly with memory. No 20-30s penalty.

Negligible startup latency — Runner construction is just struct allocation. Eino runtime itself is ~12k LOC. Per-session memory dominated by runSession.Events accumulation during a run. Zero disk baseline (no on-disk cache, no JSONL). Massive cold-start advantage for serverless/horizontal scaling.

Init dominated by plugin Init() calls (googlegenai sync HTTP/credential check, typically <1s with cached ADC). Cloud Run instance cold-boot <<1s after image pull. ~30 MB RSS for minimal binary; growing with model SDKs (~50 MB once Vertex gRPC initialized).

Pure-OSS embedding: few hundred ms import, RAM baseline tens of MB beyond model client. Platform/self-host runs Starlette+Uvicorn worker pods; multi-tenant Postgres connection pool dominates RAM. Closed-source server hides exact numbers.

Pure-Python import overhead is non-trivial — SQLAlchemy, pydantic, tiktoken, nltk, banks, httpx, aiohttp all pulled in. No published baseline RAM. Cold start dominated by LLM SDK warm-up, not the framework. Reasonable but not measured.

note: tens of MB, slow on edge
details: @mastra/core is heavy (>200 source files). Realistic baseline for 5-agent app: tens of MB RAM, sub-second cold start on Node, ~1-2s on Cloudflare Workers due to bundle size. No public benchmark in-repo.

Thin .NET assembly / Python package; startup dominated by provider SDK init (AzureCliCredential, OpenAIClient) and context-provider loading. DevUI lists ports 8080/8090 but is dev-only. No documented multi-second cold-start surcharge.

import agents triggers openai SDK + pydantic imports; lazy SQLiteSession and extension backends amortize. ~100-150 MB RAM baseline. Tens of MB disk for the package. No 20-30s startup; sub-second cold start in practice.

No bundled binary. Pure JS/TS startup is typical Node baseline (~200-400 ms). Minimal RAM beyond Node baseline; MemorySession in-memory. Loop starts on run() invocation in milliseconds. No equivalent of Claude Agent SDK issue #333.

Pure-Python import; sub-second once Python interpreter is warm. RAM baseline tens of MB driven by pydantic + chosen provider SDK. No bundled binaries, no LLM subprocess. No documented multi-second startup overhead.

Rust binary startup typically <500 ms once compiled (no JIT, no Python interpreter). No vendor binary downloaded; no Node sidecar. Memory baseline small — Agent struct is a few Arcs plus a RwLock-wrapped ToolServerState.

Construction is light — ToolRegistry, HookRegistry, EventLoopMetrics, OTel tracer initialized in __init__. Cold start ~few hundred ms dominated by boto3/pydantic imports. No 20-30s subprocess warm-up. RAM baseline modest.

Not measured but expected light because no subprocess starts. Lazy-loaded peer-deps mean tree-shaken bundles stay small. CI includes browser bundle check, suggesting modest baseline footprint. No subprocess-spawn overhead.

Cold start of ai is just a JS import — typically tens of milliseconds. No bundled binaries or large native deps. Footprint essentially Node baseline. First LLM call dominated by provider API latency, not the SDK.

LLM: medium-high — model.LLM interface is open but request/response types embed *genai.Content directly, only first-party impls are gemini and apigee (Vertex proxy); BYO providers adapt to genai.Part. Hosting: low-medium — runs anywhere Go runs, README mentions Cloud Run. Eval: N/A in Go (Python-only). Observability: low — standard OTel.

note: 49 LLM providers, no hosting, no eval
details: LLM: minimal — 49 providers under agno/models/, abstract Model base. Hosting: none — just a Python process running uvicorn. Eval: none — BaseEval and Scorer classes in-repo, OTel tracing provider-neutral.

note: low LLM lock-in, OTel, no eval
details: LLM provider low — unified LLMProvider trait abstracts 10+ cloud + 3 local providers. Hosting none — runs anywhere Rust runs. Eval none — no eval framework. Observability OTel-standard via autoagents-telemetry with optional Langfuse provider, both swappable.

LLM: strongly Anthropic-locked — alternative providers route only via Anthropic gateway (Bedrock/Vertex), only Claude models first-class. CLI binary: strongly Claude-Code-locked — wire protocol closed-source, CLI-version-specific. Hosting low. Eval/observability OTel-only.

LLM provider high-to-medium — first-class Anthropic; Bedrock/Vertex/Foundry/anthropicAws/mantle/gateway enumerated. 3P providers (OpenAI/Gemini) require gateway adapters. Skill/sub-agent format CC-shaped — porting requires rewriting. Hosting low for self-host, high for claude.ai bridge. Eval/observability low.

OSS path open: 100+ providers via LiteLLM, none for hosting/eval/skills/memory/persistence. AMP path heavy lock-in: AMP-only deploys, automations, triggers, Studio, Traces dashboard, hallucination guardrail, PII redaction, RBAC, Agent Repositories. Stay OSS to keep portability.

LLM low — all providers behind model.BaseChatModel/ToolCallingChatModel interfaces, 11+ providers in eino-ext. Hosting none. Eval none — BYO. Tracing low — OTel via APMPlus, or first-party Langfuse/LangSmith/CozeLoop. Persistence none — CheckPointStore is two methods on []byte.

LLM multi-provider — googlegenai/vertexai/anthropic/compat_oai/ollama/modelgarden first-party; Fallback middleware for outages. Hosting slight GCP tilt — samples target Cloud Run, telemetry plugin is GCP-only, only Firestore session adapter ships. Nothing GCP-required: runs on any K8s/AWS/on-prem. Eval no lock-in. Tracing OTel-standard.

LLM low — any langchain-* chat model works via init_chat_model. Hosting/platform medium — HTTP server, auth, run queue, multitask coordination and /mcp routes ship only via closed-source LangGraph Platform; pure-OSS means BYO HTTP+queue+auth. Eval medium — cost USD requires paid LangSmith.

note: 104 LLMs, no hosting, no eval lock-in
details: LLM-provider: none — pluggable LLM abstraction with 104 implementations. Hosting: none for OSS framework (llama_deploy is OSS too; LlamaCloud is for parse/ingest, not serving). Eval-platform: none — BYO (LangSmith, Arize, Langfuse, Opik, Phoenix all have official integrations).

LLM low — uses Vercel AI SDK v5/v6 adapters (40+ providers). Hosting low — deployers for all major edge platforms, Hono runs anywhere. Storage low — 15+ adapters. Eval/observability medium — Mastra has own MastraScorer API and observability spans; OTel/Langfuse exporters exist but not default. Migrating to LangSmith would rewrite scorers.

LLM open — adapters for Azure OpenAI/Foundry/OpenAI/Anthropic/Bedrock/Gemini/Ollama/Claude/GitHub Copilot/Foundry-Local/Copilot Studio. Hosting: Azure stack clearly first-class (Foundry/Azure Functions/Cosmos/AI Search) but core packages have no hard dependency on Azure. ASP.NET Core hosting works against any LLM. Eval/observability OTel-native.

LLM: low — MultiProvider supports openai/litellm/any-llm prefixes (100+ providers). Hosting: none. Eval/observability: none — default OpenAI Traces exporter but 25+ partner exporters replace it. Session: none — 10 backends + Session Protocol. Only OpenAI-locked feature is server-managed conversation IDs (conversation_id/previous_response_id).

LLM medium — default OpenAI Responses API; pluggable via custom ModelProvider; Anthropic/Gemini/Bedrock/Vertex via @openai/agents-extensions/ai-sdk bridge. Hosted tools (webSearchTool, fileSearchTool, codeInterpreterTool, imageGenerationTool, toolSearchTool) OpenAI-only. Hosting low. Tracing defaults to OpenAI Traces dashboard but escapable.

LLM low — ~14 providers + FallbackModel chain + pydantic-ai-litellm direction; custom models via Model abstract base. Hosting none — library runs anywhere Python runs. Eval low — pydantic-evals is in-repo but optional, LangSmith/Braintrust work via OTel. Observability low — OTel-first, Logfire is one backend among many.

LLM low — 26 native providers (Anthropic, Azure, Cohere, DeepSeek, Gemini, Groq, HuggingFace, Mistral, Ollama, OpenAI, OpenRouter, Perplexity, xAI, Z.ai, etc.) plus Bedrock and VertexAI as companion crates. Hosting none. Eval none — in-tree evals.rs.

LLM low — 12+ providers (Bedrock, Anthropic, OpenAI, Gemini, LiteLLM, Llama, Llama.cpp, Mistral, Ollama, SageMaker, Writer, OpenAI Responses). Hosting low — pure Python, no managed runtime. Eval low — no built-in eval. Default-Bedrock posture biases AWS shops but nothing about SDK is AWS-only.

LLM low — Bedrock default but Model base class provider-agnostic; shipped adapters for Bedrock/Anthropic/OpenAI (Chat+Responses)/Google/VercelModel shim. Hosting none — pure library. Eval/observability OTel-native, so any OTLP backend (Datadog/Honeycomb/Tempo/Grafana/Phoenix) works.

LLM low — 50+ provider adapters, all behind LanguageModel interface; swap providers in one line. Hosting low — library only, runs anywhere Node runs; Vercel hosting and AI Gateway are conveniences not requirements. Eval N/A — SDK does not ship eval.

Bundles run loop, session stores (in-memory/GORM/Vertex), memory service, artifact store, REST API, A2A protocol, agent-engine emulator, embedded web UI, OTel, plugin system (11 hooks), skill loader, MCP client, configurable YAML loader, replay plugin, CLI. Comparable scope to Mastra; heavier than Vercel AI SDK; lighter than LangGraph.

Heavy. libs/agno/agno is ~50 subpackages: agent (10k+ LOC across 17 files), team, workflow, tools (130+), models (49), db (10), knowledge, memory, learning, eval, guardrails, hooks, skills, registry, scheduler, tracing, culture, compression, os FastAPI server (7k LOC). Agent constructor has 80+ parameters. Platform category, not thin SDK.

Heavy by total LOC (multi-crate workspace including speech, vector stores, derive macros, guardrails, WASM sandbox) but core surface (autoagents-core) is focused: agent/executor/memory/tool/context/hooks/runtime. You only pull what you use via Cargo features.

Thin Python SDK (~5 kLOC across src/claude_agent_sdk/): types.py (2,043 lines), _internal/query.py (899 lines), subprocess_cli.py (762 lines), client.py (627 lines), __init__.py (663 lines). Heavy lifting is in the bundled CLI binary, which is megabytes of Node bundle and not source-distributed.

TS shim ~862KB sdk.mjs, ~1.1 MB bridge.mjs, ~31 KB assistant.mjs total ≤ 2 MB pure JS. Bundled native CLI 207-233 MB per platform — heaviest of 11 stacks by bytes-on-disk. sdk.d.ts is 5722 lines (hook payloads, settings schema, control-protocol types). Neither a thin SDK nor a heavy framework conceptually.

Heavy. Bundles agent classes, executors (legacy + experimental plan-and-execute), memory, knowledge, RAG, MCP client, A2A client/server, event bus, hooks, telemetry, checkpoint engine, CLI, skill loader, tool catalog, training data, guardrails, planning, observation. 5 sub-packages, 151 event classes, ~70 kLOC core framework + 3 kLOC just for experimental executor.

12k+ LOC across compose/, adk/, schema/, callbacks/, components/. ADK alone is ~40 files plus 7 middlewares + 3 prebuilts. Zero platform code (no HTTP server, no UI, no eval, no marketplace). OSS runtime, no platform. Opposite philosophy from Mastra: rich runtime primitives, you assemble the application.

~317 Go files in go/. `Agent.cancel()` is in-process (sets a threading.Event checked at safe points). HTTP wiring is BYO.
`agent.cancel()` and `InvokeOptions.cancelSignal` are the in-process primitives; the recommended DELETE shape is described but not shipped.

Two BYO patterns: same-server uses `request.signal` → `streamText({ abortSignal })`; multi-server uses an example `DELETE /api/chat/:id/stream` route that writes `canceledAt` to a DB the running POST polls. Neither is a shipped framework endpoint.

`GET .../sessions/{session_id}` returns the full event list for replay. Resumption is implicit — call `/run_sse` again with the same `sessionId` and the runner picks up history. No dedicated `/resume` or `/replay` endpoint.

`POST /agents/{id}/runs/{rid}/resume` reconnects to an in-flight asyncio.Task and replays buffered SSE events then continues live. `GET /agents/{id}/runs/{rid}` returns persisted output; `GET .../sessions/{sid}/runs` lists session runs.
No HTTP API; no resume primitive even in-process.
`ClaudeAgentOptions.resume=<session_id>` is a parameter, not an endpoint. HTTP exposure is BYO.
`query({ options: { resume: sessionId } })` is the in-process logic, including `resumeSessionAt: messageUuid`. The endpoint is BYO.
OSS: `Crew.from_checkpoint` is in-process and you wire your own `/sessions/:id/resume`. AMP: re-deploy + re-kickoff via Studio UI.
`Runner.Resume(ctx, checkPointID)` exists in Go API; no HTTP wrapper ships.

Durable streaming via `StreamManager` and `X-Genkit-Stream-Id` header allows reconnecting clients to replay from a durable store. Experimental, requires a `StreamManager` impl (in-memory and Firestore samples ship). No general session-reopen endpoint.

`GET /threads/{tid}/runs/{rid}/stream?last_event_id=...` re-attaches to a stream from a given event id (requires `stream_resumable: true`). For HITL resume: `POST .../runs/stream` with `command: {resume: ...}`. Full state endpoints (`/state`, `/state/{checkpoint_id}`) round it out.
Pattern is to serialize `Context` keyed by `session_id` and pass it to `workflow.run`; no endpoint ships.

Three resume/replay routes: `GET /agents/:id/observe-stream` (attach as observer), `POST /agents/:id/resume-stream` (resume a suspended run), `GET /agents/:id/subscribe-thread` (SSE subscription to a thread's runs).
DevUI re-sends the same `conversation` ID and the server pulls thread history automatically. AG-UI propagates `availableInterrupts` and `resume` metadata. No dedicated resume endpoint.
`RunState.to_state().to_json()` / `RunState.from_json` are the primitives; you build the `/runs/{id}/resume` endpoint.
`RunState.toString()` / `RunState.fromString` exist; no endpoint shipped.

No dedicated resume endpoint — Vercel AI / AG-UI design sends the full `messages` history each request. Server-authoritative history requires you to persist by `conversation_id` and pass `message_history` to the adapter.
Resume via `ConversationMemory` is in-process only; no HTTP surface.
`FileSessionManager(session_id=...)` restores prior messages; `take_snapshot`/`load_snapshot` are building blocks. No endpoint ships.
`SessionManager.restoreSnapshot` and `agent.invoke([interruptResponseBlock])` are in-process; endpoint is BYO.
Example uses the external `resumable-stream` package + Redis with `createResumableStreamContext`. Not part of the `ai` package itself — recommended add-on only.

Approvals reuse `/run_sse` with a `functionResponse` payload named `adk_request_confirmation` carrying `{confirmed, payload}`. The runner matches the function response to the original call by ID and resumes. No separate `/approve` endpoint and no API-visible pause status — client infers pause from `LongRunningToolIDs`.

Tools decorated `requires_confirmation=True` cause `RunPausedEvent` with `status=paused`. `POST /agents/{id}/runs/{rid}/continue` (form field `tools=<json>`) resumes with verdicts. A separate admin `/approvals/...` namespace with persistent `agno_approvals` table also exists.
Only `HookOutcome::Abort` skips a tool call. No pause/wait-for-approval state, no persistence/resume primitive. HTTP surfacing is fully BYO.

`can_use_tool` callback is intra-process; cross-request HITL requires keeping `ClaudeSDKClient` alive across the user's round-trip. `PreToolUse` hook with `permissionDecision: defer` provides a weaker form. No HTTP endpoint ships.
`canUseTool` is the in-process primitive; your callback returns a Promise that you resolve when the operator's verdict arrives. No client-visible pause state and no shipped endpoint.

Flow-level `@human_feedback` with async `HumanFeedbackProvider` raising `HumanFeedbackPending` is the production pattern — auto-persists state and returns. Tool-level and task-level helpers are console-only (sync, not API-friendly). HTTP wiring is yours; AMP ships a Flow HITL UI.
`adk.Interrupt`/`adk.StatefulInterrupt` + `ResumeWithParams` are in-process. No HTTP route, no client-visible pause state beyond the serialized interrupt event.

Pause observable as `*ModelResponse` with `FinishReason=interrupted` and `metadata.interrupt`. Resume reuses the same flow endpoint with a request body carrying approval state, translated to `ai.WithToolResponses`/`ai.WithToolRestarts` in flow code. No dedicated approval endpoint.

`POST /threads/{tid}/runs/stream` with `command: {resume: "approved"}` (or per-interrupt map) resumes paused threads. State edits via `POST /threads/{tid}/state` first, then resume. Pause state observable via `StateSnapshot.interrupts`.
`Context.wait_for_event(HumanResponseEvent, ...)` + `InputRequiredEvent` is first-class in-process. Host routes the verdict to `handler.ctx.send_event(...)`; no endpoint ships.

Dedicated `POST /agents/:id/approve-tool-call` and `POST .../decline-tool-call` (streaming and non-streaming variants) plus `resume-stream` for generic suspend/resume. Each approval response returns a new SSE stream that continues execution.

Tools with `approval_mode=always_require` emit `function_approval_request` content; client builds `function_approval_response` and re-invokes via `agent.run`. DevUI exposes the request/response lifecycle as SSE events and conversation items. Tooling is first-class but resume is via the same endpoint, not a dedicated approval route.
`function_tool(needs_approval=True)` + `RunState.approve/reject` are in-process primitives. The wire format (POST endpoint, payload shape) is your responsibility.
`RunToolApprovalItem` returns from a run; `state.approve/reject` resumes. HTTP shape is whatever you design — the Next.js example uses a `decisions: { callId: 'approved' }` payload on the same POST.

Deferred Tools first-class in the SDK: `requires_approval=True` or `raise ApprovalRequired` triggers `DeferredToolRequests`. Resume passes `deferred_tool_results=DeferredToolResults(approvals={call_id: True})` on a follow-up run. UI adapters surface these in their dialects; exact field name varies by adapter.
No HITL primitive. `PauseControl` pauses stream polling but does not expose a tool-approval channel; closest pattern is `on_tool_call → Skip` to reject.

`InterruptException` raised from a hook is first-class in-process — agent stops with `stop_reason=interrupt` and persists pending state. Resume via `agent('...', InterruptResponseContent)`. HTTP endpoint shape is yours.

`context.interrupt` + `InterruptError` first-class in the SDK; resume by `agent.invoke([{type: 'interruptResponseContent', ...}])`. The `interventions` subsystem wraps this with structured `Confirm` actions. HTTP wiring is BYO.

Server emits `tool-approval-request` chunks; client calls `chat.addToolApprovalResponse({approved, reason})` which appends a `tool-approval-response` to messages. With `sendAutomaticallyWhen`, the chat re-POSTs to the same `/api/chat`, the agent loop sees the approval and resumes. No separate endpoint but pause state is observable client-side.

SSE frames are JSON `models.Event` objects covering text deltas (model partial events with `partial: true`), partial tool args (`FunctionCall.Args` forwarded from Gemini partial events), and lifecycle/activity frames (function call, function response). No explicit `start`/`end` SSE event types — stream starts on connect, ends on iterator return.

Rich SSE taxonomy with named events: `RunStarted`, `ToolCallStarted`, `ToolCallCompleted`, `RunCompleted` carrying metrics. Partial tool-arg streaming is provider-dependent; `ToolCallStartedEvent` carries the *complete* tool call at the moment it is parsed, not incremental JSON deltas.
No HTTP API. In-process `StreamChunk::ToolUseInputDelta`, text chunks, and lifecycle events do exist and would form a complete stream once you serialize them yourself.
No HTTP API. In-process all three dimensions are available (`include_partial_messages` for token deltas + `input_json_delta`, plus `Message` lifecycle frames).
No HTTP API. `includePartialMessages: true` exposes `SDKPartialAssistantMessage` with text + tool-arg `input_json_delta` + lifecycle in-process, but you serialize the wire format.

OSS ships no HTTP stream. AMP webhook events include `llm_stream_chunk` carrying partial tool-call arguments and full `BaseEvent` lifecycle, but webhook delivery isn't a live stream — order is not guaranteed without `realtime=true`.
No HTTP API. Tool-call deltas come through model chunks with `ToolCalls.Index` for merging — but no separate tool-arg-fragment event type and no wire framing ships.

SSE frames are `{message: ModelResponseChunk}` for chunks and `{result: ...}` for final. `ToolRequest.Partial` flag carries partial JSON for tool args (provider-dependent — Gemini supported). No dedicated tool-input start/delta/end sub-taxonomy.

SSE event taxonomy includes `messages/partial` carrying `AIMessageChunk.tool_call_chunks` (partial tool args), text-token deltas, plus `values`/`updates`/`checkpoints`/`tasks`/`metadata`/`end` lifecycle events. All three dimensions stream cleanly with explicit linkage by `tool_call_id`.
No HTTP API. In-process `AgentStream` carries text deltas and tool-call deltas; you serialize.

SSE forwards `fullStream` chunks: dedicated `tool-call-input-streaming-start`, `tool-call-delta` (carrying `argsTextDelta`), `tool-call-input-streaming-end`, plus text deltas and rich lifecycle events (`tool-call`, `tool-result`, `tool-output`, `tool-error`, `tool-call-approval`, etc.). All three dimensions stream with `toolCallId` linkage.

DevUI emits OpenAI-Responses-compatible SSE including `response.function_call_arguments.delta` for partial tool args, plus `response.output_item.added`, `response.created`, `response.completed` lifecycle. AG-UI typed events also cover the three dimensions.
No HTTP API. In-process the Responses API emits `response.function_call_arguments.delta` via `RawResponsesStreamEvent` plus `RunItemStreamEvent` lifecycle.
No HTTP API. `RunRawModelStreamEvent` exposes provider events but the SDK doesn't normalize into a typed tool-call-delta. Wire format is yours.

`ToolCallPartDelta.args_delta` carries incremental tool args, surfaced via `PartDeltaEvent`. UI adapter SSE frames cover text-delta, tool-call, tool-result, finish lifecycle (Vercel-AI / AG-UI dialects). Linkage by `toolCallId`.
No HTTP API. In-process `StreamedAssistantContent::ToolCallDelta` and `Delta(String)` content do support all three dimensions; serialization is yours.
No first-party chat HTTP. In-process `ToolUseStreamEvent` carries partial tool args and the stream yields message and lifecycle events; wire framing is yours.
No first-party chat HTTP. `ModelStreamUpdateEvent` carries `toolUseInputDelta` partial JSON in-process; you serialize.

UI Message Stream Protocol v2 ships explicit `tool-input-start`, `tool-input-delta` (`inputTextDelta`), `tool-input-available` plus `text-delta`, `start`/`start-step`/`finish-step`/`finish` lifecycle. `useChat` automatically transitions `ToolUIPart.state` from `input-streaming` to `input-available`. All three dimensions stream with explicit `toolCallId` linkage.

`server/adkrest/handler.go` registers no auth middleware. The example `examples/web/main.go` AuthInterceptor on the A2A path hardcodes the user. You wrap the REST router with your own JWT/tenant middleware.

JWT middleware (`os/middleware/jwt.py`) validates bearer tokens, fills `request.state.user_id`, `scopes`, `accessible_resource_ids`. Per-route `Depends(require_resource_access("agents", "run", "agent_id"))` enforces RBAC. Scope schema `agent-os:<os-id>:<resource-type>:<resource-id>:<scope>`. Fallback shared-secret mode also supported.
No HTTP API; auth is fully BYO.
SDK is unaware of HTTP; auth is your concern.
SDK does not validate JWTs, OAuth, or anything else. Auth termination is in your HTTP handler; tenant context is passed via `cwd`/`env`/closure-captured hooks.
OSS: BYO. AMP supports a bearer token per automation and webhook callbacks can carry their own auth. No tenant-aware RBAC at the HTTP boundary.
No HTTP API; auth is host responsibility.

SDK does not terminate JWT auth itself. `firebase.AuthContextProvider` ships for Firebase Auth; custom `ContextProvider` validates tokens and populates `ActionContext`. No first-class tenant/RBAC; stdlib middleware in front of the handler covers the rest.

`langgraph_api` calls `@auth.authenticate` on every request returning a `MinimalUserDict`; subsequent `@auth.on.*` handlers apply per-resource (thread/run/etc.) filters. Auth is fully terminated at the API boundary and identity reaches graph nodes via `runtime.context` / `ctx.user.identity`.
No HTTP API; auth is BYO.

`coreAuthMiddleware` terminates auth at `/api/*` with JWT/cookies/API keys and ships first-party integrations for Auth0/Clerk/WorkOS/Supabase/Firebase/Better-Auth/Okta/Studio. RBAC permissions auto-derived from path+method (`GET /agents/:id → agents:read`); FGA policies via `MastraFGAWorkos` enforce route-level checks.
DevUI ships bearer-token auth enabled by default (`DEVUI_AUTH_TOKEN`), `--no-auth` only for loopback. AG-UI/A2A/Foundry are BYO. No tenant scoping or per-resource RBAC at the HTTP boundary.
SDK consumes validated identity via `RunContextWrapper.context`; HTTP-layer JWT/Okta/API-key validation is yours.
Auth in your host middleware before calling `run()`.

Docs explicitly say "Treat the adapter endpoint as an internal backend service, running it inside your own authenticated route handler." Auth is the route's job — typical pattern is a FastAPI dependency validating JWT and building `TenantDeps` passed via `agent.run(..., deps=...)`.
No JWT validation, no tenant scoping at the network boundary.
The A2A server supports authentication via the upstream A2A SDK's user builder pattern but chat HTTP is BYO. Once authenticated, identity is pushed into `invocation_state`.
`A2AExpressServerConfig.userBuilder` integrates with `@a2a-js/sdk` for per-request user auth on the A2A path. Browser-chat auth is BYO middleware.
Helpers do not parse `Authorization` headers; auth and tenant scoping happen in your Next.js/Express/Hono middleware before invoking `createAgentUIStreamResponse`.

Runner is stateless per call; storage layer enforces isolation via GORM transactions plus stale-session optimistic concurrency (service.go:319-382). In-memory localSession uses sync.RWMutex. Strong single-writer-per-session guarantees but cannot fan out parallel turns on the same session. Live bidi sessions are pod-local and need sticky routing.

Each run()/arun() builds its own RunContext (_run.py:1323-1339) and reads/writes its AgentSession by session_id through BaseDb. Agent instance is shared and largely immutable post-construction so concurrent async invocations are safe. No automatic per-tenant isolation primitive but the per-call separation is solid.

Each BaseAgent owns its own Arc<Mutex<MemoryProvider>> (base.rs:63) so spawning one agent per session isolates naturally. There is no first-class Session concept — sharing one agent across sessions leaks memory because no per-call isolation exists. No tenant-scoped primitives.

Each ClaudeSDKClient/query() spawns its own claude CLI subprocess with its own cwd, env, JSONL transcript, and MCP connections. State cannot bleed across subprocesses except via shared filesystem or your shared SessionStore. Concurrent @tool handlers in the same Python process share closures/globals — engineer must avoid module-level mutable state.

Spawning one subprocess per (tenant, session) is the only safe model — sharing a subprocess across tenants bleeds cwd, MCP servers, settings, JSONL targets. The SDK does not enforce isolation; the host is responsible. Open issue #122 documents an in-process MCP host race when multiple query() calls share an SDK MCP server name — a real concurrency hazard with workaround (unique names).

Each Crew carries its own id, memory, and tools. However the event bus is a process-wide singleton and hooks register globally (hooks/llm_hooks.py:120), so a hook for tenant A fires for tenant B too. The contextvars runtime state is for state reconstruction, not tenant isolation. No (tenant, hook) scoping primitive.

ctxWithNewRunCtx (adk/runctx.go:387-401) seeds a fresh runContext per Runner.Run call and lives in context.Context. runSession mutexes guard internal maps; parallel sub-agents fork ctx via forkRunCtx and rejoin via joinRunCtxs. Risk remains for closures that capture singletons outside runSession.Values — framework does not enforce that.

Each request has its own context.Context; the *registry.Registry is shared but concurrency-safe for reads after Init. No shared mutable session state on the Genkit object — sessions live in your session.Store[S] implementation. Standard Go HTTP isolation.

OSS: each PregelLoop is a fresh Python instance per run; state is checkpointer-keyed on thread_id. BaseStore namespaces are tenant-scoped by convention but not enforced. Platform adds @auth.on.* filter chain enforcing resource scoping at the data layer, raising isolation to first-class for the hosted product.

Each workflow.run() creates a new Context (unless ctx=existing_ctx is passed to resume). Context.store is a per-context KV with no global sharing. Sessions are isolated by construction; no tenant primitives beyond that.

RequestContext and MessageList are per-call inside loop(); persistence is per-thread via SaveQueueManager keyed on threadId (save-queue/index.ts:6-49). Reserved request-context keys (MASTRA_RESOURCE_ID_KEY, MASTRA_THREAD_ID_KEY) are server-controlled so clients cannot spoof tenant identity at the HTTP layer — a first-class tenant-isolation primitive most peers lack.

Sessions hold mutable state (session_id, service_session_id, AgentSessionStateBag of concurrent-dictionary entries); agents are singletons by default in AddAIAgent. State bleed only happens if you store conversation state on the agent (anti-pattern) or share AgentSession across requests.

Session protocol binds one session_id per instance; SQLiteSession scopes every row by session_id. RunContextWrapper is a fresh dataclass per Runner.run; approvals are per-wrapper (run_context.py:60). Cross-session bleed is impossible inside the SDK unless engineer shares mutable TContext.

Each run() constructs a fresh RunState (run.ts:769-780). RunContext carries app context which is shared by reference — engineer controls what to put there. Approvals and usage are shared with forked nested contexts. No shared runtime means isolation is trivially correct if you don't share mutable objects.

Fresh RunContext per run() (deps, usage, metadata, conversation_id, run_id) plus a ContextVar _CURRENT_RUN_CONTEXT scoped via set_current_run_context (_run_context.py:122,138) so concurrent run() calls in the same process do not bleed. Toolset.for_run lets a toolset spawn a fresh instance per run for state isolation — first-class per-call isolation across the framework.

Agent state is largely immutable (model, preamble, static_context, hooks). PromptRequest clones agent data into local fields (prompt_request/mod.rs:101-123) so concurrent prompts do not see each other's new_messages. ToolServerHandle is an Arc<RwLock<>> shared across agent uses (read-lock for dispatch). Conversation memory isolation lives in the backend implementation.

Agent.stream_async holds a threading.Lock that raises ConcurrencyException if two invocations enter the same instance (agent/agent.py:823-828). Each Agent owns its own messages/state/registry/hooks/_invocation_lock/_interrupt_state/etc. ConcurrentInvocationMode.UNSAFE_REENTRANT is an opt-in foot-gun for advanced users.

acquireLock() throws ConcurrentInvocationError if invoke() is called while another invoke() is in flight (agent.ts:460). Each Agent instance owns its own messages, appState, modelState, registries, _interruptState. Multi-tenant fan-out should always be per-request new Agent() — sharing across tenants is unsafe by design.

Each request has its own JS scope, messages array, and runtimeContext. There is no shared mutable state in `ai` — provided you pass messages from external storage and runtimeContext from the request, isolation is guaranteed by the request handler boundary.

Session state is externalized to the database (session/database/) or Vertex Agent Engine (session/vertexai/) so N pods share the session pool. Stale-session optimistic concurrency (service.go:373-382) prevents lost updates between racing pods. No leader election; live bidi sessions are pod-local and need sticky routing.

Stateless workers can share a session pool via the same database (PostgresDb or AsyncPostgresDb), sessions keyed by session_id UUID. The scheduler uses DB-backed leader election via agno_schedules rows and SchedulePoller claiming locks (scheduler/poller.py) — a rare first-class coordination primitive.
Runtime is SingleThreadedRuntime (event-loop ownership; single_threaded.rs:35) — no leader election, distributed lock, shared store, or pod-pool pattern. Horizontal scaling is entirely BYO.

SessionStore adapter is the only shared-state primitive and it's append-only. Concurrent writes to the same session from two pods interleave unsafely — the SDK assumes one process owns one session at a time. SessionKey.project_key (types.py:1276-1295) is the documented sharding lever; no leader election, no coordinator.

SessionStore interface (sdk.d.ts:3738) plus a Postgres adapter (examples/session-stores/postgres/) lets any pod resume any session ID. forkSession is store-aware too. No leader election or shared coordinator; the local ~/.claude/projects JSONL is dual-written when sessionStore is set.

OSS has no shared-state, no leader election, no message-queue support. LanceDB/SQLite are local; CheckpointConfig only supports JSON-on-disk and SQLite. To scale you must externalize memory (Qdrant edge), build a worker pool yourself, and implement a custom BaseProvider for checkpoints. AMP hosts the runtime and manages concurrency for you.

Stateless Go binary; pods scale trivially. CheckPointStore is the cross-pod seam — point all pods at the same Postgres store and any pod can resume any session. Leader election, locking, and partition assignment are not provided — you layer optimistic concurrency or advisory locks on your store.

Standard Cloud Run/GKE replication. No leader election, lock, or coordination. FirestoreSessionStore (plugins/firebase/x/session_store.go) gives concurrency through Firestore; with a custom Postgres store you own the locking semantics.

OSS: shared PostgresSaver checkpointer with thread_id as partition key — any worker replays from any checkpoint. Platform: closed-source langgraph_api adds a Postgres-backed run queue serializing per-thread work via multitask strategy and re-attachable SSE streams. First-class horizontal scaling at both layers.

Serialize Context via ctx.to_dict(serializer=JsonSerializer()) and stash in Postgres/Redis/etc, then re-hydrate on the next request from any worker. No leader election or built-in coordination. llama_deploy (separate repo) provides a control-plane + queue if you need it.

Multiple Mastra processes behind a load balancer share the storage backend; no leader election. Resumable streams (/agents/:id/observe-stream) let any worker pick up an in-progress run because the workflow snapshot lives in storage. Suspended HITL state is durable via workflow snapshots — strong real-world horizontal story.

AgentSessionStore abstraction lets N pods share Cosmos or Redis; CosmosCheckpointStorage and CosmosChatHistoryProvider are designed for this. No leader election in the vanilla path, but DurableTask provides leader-elected, queue-backed orchestration as the explicit answer for stateful coordination.

Ships 10 session backends — SQLAlchemySession, RedisSession, MongoDBSession, DaprSession, OpenAIConversationsSession, etc. — all designed for stateless workers + shared store. Some retry logic exists for OpenAI-managed conversation locks (run.py:474-476). No leader election or centralized scheduler — application-level concurrency control is your responsibility.

As long as session state lives in an external store (custom Session backed by Postgres/Redis), any number of pods can serve the same session pool. RunState.toString()/fromString() lets you serialize a paused run to any KV store. No leader election, no shared in-process state.

Stateless: N workers serve the same logical Agent (designed for global reuse); message_history is user-owned storage re-passed per request. Durable execution via Temporal/DBOS/Prefect provides per-workflow horizontal recovery. No leader election or shared session pool in-tree.
Rig itself provides nothing for multi-pod scaling; the caller's deployment (axum + LB) plus a ConversationMemory backend you implement is the entire story.

Stateless workers rehydrate from a shared SessionRepository (session/session_repository.py:12). Ships FileSessionManager, S3SessionManager, and RepositorySessionManager. No leader election or cluster-aware coordination — the SDK is unopinionated.
N stateless Node processes behind a load balancer each load session state from S3Storage (or another SnapshotStorage) on-demand. No worker registration, heartbeat, or queue.

Spin up N Node processes (Next.js/Fargate/Cloud Run/Vercel Functions) each pulling session state from your shared store (Postgres/Redis/S3/Blob). The canonical durable-stream example uses the third-party resumable-stream package + Redis. No leader election or shared in-memory map.

First-party PubSub and Eventarc triggers in the REST server (server/adkrest/controllers/triggers/). PubSubController accepts Cloud Pub/Sub HTTP push messages with a concurrency semaphore (MaxConcurrentRuns); RetriableRunner wraps with exponential backoff. No in-box cron — you wire Cloud Scheduler → Pub/Sub → ADK trigger.

ScheduleManager + SchedulePoller + ScheduleExecutor are croniter-driven with DB-stored schedules (agno_schedules) and DB-backed leader election. agent.arun(..., background=True, stream=True) produces a resumable SSE stream surviving client disconnect with /resume reconnect (managers.py). FastAPI BackgroundTasks via @hook(run_in_background=True). Memory/learning futures spawn in threads/asyncio tasks. First-class on every axis.
No cron, no schedulers, no webhook receivers. Long-running background work via tokio::spawn + Topic<Task> is possible but there is no first-party primitive.
No cron, no webhook, no agent-as-background-worker primitive. The only first-party hook is AgentDefinition.background: bool (types.py:99) — a sub-agent hint for the CLI, not a host-level scheduler.

AgentDefinition.background and AgentInput.run_in_background give fire-and-forget sub-agents emitting task_notification when done. BashInput.run_in_background + TaskOutputInput polls completion. AssistantWorkerOptions.scheduling.dir polls .claude/scheduled_tasks.json every 10s and fires ~5s ahead — but local-only, tied to the worker's filesystem, not distributed cron. Webhook intake is BYO.

OSS: Crew.kickoff() is blocking; no scheduler module, no `crewai schedule` command. AMP ships Automations with triggers for Gmail/Calendar/Drive/Outlook/OneDrive/Teams/HubSpot/Salesforce/Slack/Zapier plus Webhook/API kickoff and cron — vendor-managed, no OSS equivalent.
No cron, no webhook trigger system, no scheduled-job framework. Use Go stdlib (time.AfterFunc, time.Ticker) or a job library (Asynq, Temporal, Cloud Tasks) in your host.

BackgroundModel abstraction (ai/background_model.go) and GenerateOperation for long-running model ops with CheckModelOperation polling — useful for video/Imagen jobs but not general scheduled tasks. core/x/streaming provides a StreamManager for resumable long agent runs but is marked experimental (servers.go:79). Cron/webhook triggers are BYO.

Pure OSS: not provided — BYO Celery/arq/Temporal/cron. Platform: first-party crons (crons.create/search/delete in langgraph_sdk/_async/cron.py) and webhooks (run create accepts webhook URL); Platform queue persists scheduled runs in Postgres. Strong story when the Platform is in scope; OSS-only is BYO.
No cron, scheduler, or webhook primitives in llama-index-core. BYO Celery, Temporal, RQ, asyncio. llama_deploy is a separate project.

Three first-party mechanisms: Schedulers (Mastra({ scheduler }) registers cron-like jobs under /api/scheduled-jobs), Background tasks with a dedicated chunk family and disableBackgroundTasks option (agent.types.ts:626), and Webhooks/channels packages (channels/slack, channels/discord) that wire agent runs into chat events.

Azure Functions hosting package (Microsoft.Agents.AI.Hosting.AzureFunctions) exposes Timer/HTTP/MCPTool triggers. DurableTask (DurableAIAgent, AgentEntity, EntityAgentWrapper) treats each run as a durable orchestration with replay-on-crash. Python wrapper exists in agent-framework-durabletask but is beta.

No scheduler, cron, webhook trigger, or background-agent runtime. The optional temporal extra (pyproject.toml:57) integrates Temporal workflows for durable orchestration but Temporal is a separate runtime you stand up. Called out as the single biggest architectural gap vs. Mastra/LangGraph.
No cron, webhook trigger primitives, or queues. Run a worker process (BullMQ, AWS SQS, etc.) and call run() from inside.

No first-party scheduler, cron, or webhook trigger. The agent runtime hooks into Temporal, Prefect, and DBOS for durable workflows (docs/durable_execution/) — these are external schedulers you stand up yourself, not first-party primitives.
No cron, webhook trigger, or background agent. Tokio runtime can spawn tasks but Rig offers no scheduling abstraction.

Invocation-driven library; nothing schedules cron or webhook triggers. strands-agents-tools ships a cron.py tool that the *agent* can use, but that is tool-side capability, not runtime-side scheduling.
No cron primitive, no webhook trigger surface. Use BullMQ/Cloudflare Queues/etc. and call agent.invoke() inside the worker handler.
No cron, scheduler, or webhook trigger primitive. Use your host (Vercel Cron, Cloud Scheduler, Trigger.dev) and invoke agent.generate() from there.

Triggers ship a semaphore-based concurrency limiter (pubsub.go:41: semaphore: make(chan struct{}, MaxConcurrentRuns)) — a thin worker pool. Beyond that, the runtime assumes short-lived HTTP request scope. For long-running work you either use IsLongRunning() HITL tools or fire-and-forget Pub/Sub triggers — no explicit queue or async dispatcher.

No first-party in-process queue (no Celery integration). The scheduler is DB-polling. For long-running runs you can use background=True for fire-and-forget with /resume, or schedules for cron-driven runs; richer queue models (Celery/RQ/Arq) are BYO.
Tasks are delivered to actors via actor_ref.cast(message) (in ractor). No durable queue, no retry semantics at the queue layer (LLM-level retries exist in optim::RetryLayer).
Runtime model is one CLI subprocess per active session, lifetime owned by the calling Python coroutine. For queue-shaped workloads layer your own (Celery, RQ, Temporal, AWS SQS workers).

Query.streamInput() and stopTask() (sdk.d.ts:2251,2256) give primitives for long-running streaming sessions but no shipped queue, no enqueue() API, no leasing semantics. Build with BullMQ/Cloud Tasks/etc.
OSS: none. AMP: implicit — each Automation is a separate managed deployment receiving trigger events. The OSS repository ships no queue primitive.
Framework assumes short-lived calls into Runner.Run from your HTTP handler. Typical pattern: enqueue, then have a worker pool call Runner.Run.

No built-in job queue. Expected model is HTTP request → run flow synchronously → respond. For async work, put requests on Cloud Pub/Sub/SQS yourself and have a separate worker call genkit.Generate on dequeue.

langgraph_api ships a Postgres-backed work queue with one logical lane per thread_id. Long-running runs (minutes/hours) are the default expectation; re-attaching clients pick up via GET /threads/{tid}/runs/{rid}/stream?last_event_id=... when stream_resumable: true. OSS-only mode has no queue — engineer wraps in their own.
Not provided in llama-index-core. llama_deploy is the separate vendor project providing control-plane + queue runtime around Workflows.

Not first-party for production queues — Mastra assumes you put it behind your normal Node/Edge HTTP infra. The pubsub/ directory contains a pub/sub abstraction used internally; for production queues you bring your own (BullMQ, SQS, etc.).

DurableTask is the explicit queue/orchestrator model with durable replay. Azure Functions triggers fan out work to a worker pool. Vanilla in-process agents do not expose a queue API, but the surrounding hosting ecosystem provides first-class options.

No internal task queue, no worker pool. For long-running agents expose a streaming endpoint over run_streamed() or persist RunState.to_json() and resume later from a worker pulling jobs off your own queue (Celery/RQ/SQS).
SDK assumes short-lived HTTP request scope by default. Long-running agents need a serialized RunState checkpoint pattern (HITL example at examples/agent-patterns/human-in-the-loop.ts:81-106).

No built-in queue. pydantic_ai.capabilities.ThreadExecutor lets you supply your own concurrent.futures.Executor for sync tool functions in long-running servers (docs/capabilities.md:83-95). Otherwise short-lived HTTP request scope is assumed.
Harness assumes short-lived agent.prompt() and await usage. No queue, no worker pool. Long-running runs can stream via agent.stream_prompt() to keep the client connected.
ConcurrentToolExecutor (tools/executors/concurrent.py:19) parallelizes tool calls within one cycle, but there is no inter-session queue. Session-level queueing is BYO.
SDK assumes you wrap agent.stream() in whatever request-scoped wrapper your host uses. The lone exception is the optional A2AExpressServer which assumes one-task-at-a-time per TaskStore.

No queue. The new @ai-sdk/workflow package (packages/workflow/src/) adds a WorkflowAgent abstraction with serializable step IO but is not a horizontal multi-tenant runtime. For long-running workloads you need an external queue (BullMQ, AWS SQS) and a worker calling agent.generate().

Strong typed session.Session interface plus storageSession/storageEvent GORM models with composite primary key (AppName, UserID, ID). Event-sourced model with separate scoped state tables (app/user/temp). No first-class tenant_id, but composite identity gives a natural multi-tenant key.

AgentSession dataclass with runs, session_data, metadata, agent_data, summary, created_at, updated_at, and sibling TeamSession/WorkflowSession types. Storage is per-run (not per-message). No first-class tenant_id but rich enough that you can scope sessions via session_id and user_id.

AutoAgents has no Session type. Closest equivalents are Task (input only), AgentState (in-memory for one Context run), and MemoryProvider (SlidingWindowMemory). No id, tenant_id, user_id, created_at, parent_session_id, metadata, usage, or model fields on any session-like type.

Sessions identified by session_id (UUID) plus project_key for tenant scoping in the SessionStore via SessionKey TypedDict. SDKSessionInfo carries summary, last_modified, custom_title, first_prompt, git_branch, cwd, tag, created_at. CLI writes opaque JSONL transcript entries; SDK treats entries as pass-through dicts.

SDKSessionInfo (sessionId, summary, customTitle, gitBranch, cwd, tag, createdAt) plus SessionKey (projectKey, sessionId, subpath). projectKey is explicitly documented as the multi-tenant scope. Per-message types carry session_id, uuid, parent_tool_use_id, subagent_type. Strong session model among the JS frameworks.

No session abstraction in the chat sense. Closest is a Crew/Flow/Agent kickoff identified by frozen UUID4 id. No tenant_id, no user_id, no parent_session_id field on Crew. Checkpoint serializes the entire runtime state (Crew/Agent/Task model + event DAG) but it is not a conversation session model.

No Session type per se. runSession is run-scoped (per Runner.Run call), with Values/Events/LaneEvents. The serialization checkpoint payload carries RunCtx + interrupt state. Traditional session fields (tenant_id, user_id, created_at, summary) are not in the framework.

Session[S any] is a typed user-defined state struct with id, state, store. No messages field, no built-in tenant_id, user_id, created_at, parent_session_id, or summary. You bring your own state shape and serialize via JSON; if you want conversation history persisted, you embed it yourself.

Thread is the session primitive with first-class Checkpoint TypedDict (v, id, ts, channel_values, channel_versions, versions_seen, updated_channels) and CheckpointMetadata (source, step, parents, writes). CheckpointTuple persists config/checkpoint/metadata/parent_config/pending_writes/pending_sends. Models full history (one per super-step), replayable.

No formal Session type. Memory class carries session_id, token_limit, memory_blocks, insert_method, sql_store. Workflow Context is a separately serializable state bag with KV store and queue position. Two-piece model (Memory + Context) covers conversation + run-state but lacks a unified Session entity.

Mastra calls the session a thread, paired with a resourceId (typically user/tenant id). MastraDBMessage has id, threadId, resourceId, role, content, createdAt, metadata, plus suspendedTools/pendingToolApprovals for HITL. resourceId gives natural per-tenant scoping at the model level.

AgentSession class (Python and .NET) with session_id, service_session_id (for provider-managed threads), state dict namespaced by ContextProvider.source_id. .NET uses AgentSessionStateBag (ConcurrentDictionary). No first-class tenant_id/user_id but state bag is extensible.

Session Protocol with session_id, optional SessionSettings, and items (TResponseInputItem). Concrete SQLiteSession adds created_at/updated_at columns. Minimal surface area on purpose; tenant scoping is BYO via session_id namespacing or TContext.

Session interface is just { sessionId, items: AgentInputItem[] } with 7 methods. No first-class tenant_id, user_id, cwd, model, metadata, usage, or summary fields. Reasoning-item IDs are persistable via opt-in. Slim by design.

No Session object. Closest equivalents are conversation_id (UUID7 per ModelRequest/Response), run_id, free-form metadata dict on RunContext, deps for typed dependencies, and caller-owned message_history. Persisting the session is entirely the caller's responsibility.

No Session type. ConversationMemory trait operates on (conversation_id, Vec<Message>). No tenant_id, user_id, cwd, parent_session_id, or metadata fields. Token usage, scratchpad files, attachments are not persisted by the memory contract.

Three dataclasses: Session (session_id, session_type, created_at, updated_at), SessionAgent (agent_id, state, conversation_manager_state, _internal_state), SessionMessage (message, message_id, redact_message, created_at, updated_at). Rich model but no tenant_id/user_id (BYO via agent.state).

Snapshot interface with scope (agent|multiAgent), schemaVersion, createdAt, framework data, and appData (caller-owned). SnapshotLocation tuple (sessionId, scope, scopeId). Snapshot is a JSON-serializable agent-state snapshot, not a wire chat session.

No SDK-provided Session or Thread type. Closest is the client-side Chat state machine. Per-call, you supply id, messages: UIMessage[], runtimeContext, toolsContext yourself. The SDK has zero opinion on what a session is.

Three first-party session.Service implementations: InMemoryService, GORM-backed database service (works with Postgres, SQLite, MySQL, Spanner dialectors), and Vertex AI Agent Engine. No first-party Redis, S3, or JSONL store, but GORM coverage makes any SQL backend viable.

Thirteen adapters ship under libs/agno/agno/db/: Postgres sync+async, MySQL, SQLite sync+async, Redis, Mongo, DynamoDB, Firestore, Singlestore, SurrealDB, GCS JSON, JSON file, in-memory. All inherit BaseDb/AsyncBaseDb with auto-provisioned tables. Best-in-class breadth.

No persistence stores ship. No JSONL, no SQLite, no Postgres, no Redis, no S3. Only the in-memory SlidingWindowMemory (VecDeque<ChatMessage>). MemoryProvider trait has clone_box/preload/export hooks for BYO storage.

Default is local-disk JSONL written by the CLI to ~/.claude/projects/. InMemorySessionStore reference. Postgres/Redis/S3 reference adapters live under examples/session_stores/ (added 0.1.64) but are not shipped in the wheel; you copy them in. Solid local story, but no first-class server-side adapters in the package.

Default JSONL on local disk plus InMemorySessionStore class. Postgres, Redis, S3 reference adapters under examples/session-stores/ with conformance tests. Marked @alpha. SQLite, MongoDB, DynamoDB, Cassandra, R2, Vercel Blob are BYO. Strong local default but production adapters are not first-party.

Two checkpoint providers ship: JsonProvider (one file per checkpoint) and SqliteProvider (WAL mode, one DB file). Flow persistence adds SQLiteFlowPersistence. No Postgres/Redis/S3/cloud-blob providers. Memory layer has LanceDB and Qdrant edge. Adequate for local dev, BYO for production.

None. CheckPointStore is interface-only and eino-ext ships no implementation (verified by grep). The bridgeStore is framework-internal in-memory only. Possibilities (Postgres/Redis/S3/SQLite/BoltDB) are all BYO.

Two stores: InMemoryStore[S] (experimental, process-local, not safe across replicas) and FirestoreSessionStore[S] (production-ready). No Postgres, SQLite, JSONL, Redis, S3, or GCS adapter. For a Postgres-backed multi-tenant agent you must implement session.Store[S] yourself.

Four production-grade checkpointers ship: InMemorySaver (dev), PostgresSaver + AsyncPostgresSaver, SqliteSaver + AsyncSqliteSaver. PostgresSaver also implements BaseStore for namespaced KV + vector search. No bundled Redis/S3/Mongo but the Postgres story is the gold standard.

Memory uses SQLAlchemyChatStore covering any SQLAlchemy-supported DB (SQLite default, Postgres, MySQL). Additional chat stores under storage/chat_store/ include Postgres, Redis, Azure, and others. Context serialization is BYO storage.

Fifteen-plus adapters under stores/: libsql (default), pg, mysql, mssql, dsql (Aurora DSQL), cloudflare, cloudflare-d1, dynamodb, mongodb, opensearch, couchbase, plus six vector stores (pinecone, qdrant, chroma, astra, lance, elasticsearch). Twenty storage domains under packages/core/src/storage/domains/. Breadth leader.

In-memory (both platforms), File (Python experimental), Redis (Python via agent-framework-redis), Cosmos NoSql (Python + .NET), Foundry Persistent Agents (server-side threads, both). Solid Azure-aligned coverage; uneven between Python and .NET for some adapters.

Ten first-party backends: SQLiteSession (default, WAL), OpenAIConversationsSession (hosted), OpenAIResponsesCompactionSession, AdvancedSQLiteSession, AsyncSQLiteSession, SQLAlchemySession (Postgres/MySQL via asyncpg), RedisSession, MongoDBSession, DaprSession, EncryptedSession (Fernet/HKDF wrapper). Largest set of any framework in the comparison.

Three session impls: MemorySession (in-process), OpenAIConversationsSession (OpenAI hosted), OpenAIResponsesCompactionSession (wraps another session for server-side compaction). No SQLite, Postgres, Redis, S3, or JSONL on disk built-in. Example adapters (file, Prisma) live under examples/.

None ship out-of-box. BYO Postgres/SQLite/Redis/S3 against result.all_messages_json(). The closest first-party option is the durable execution layer (Temporal/DBOS/Prefect/Restate), which provides its own state store under the agent loop.

Only InMemoryConversationMemory ships in-tree (Arc<Mutex<HashMap>>, single-process). The rig-memory companion crate ships policies (sliding window, token budget) that wrap an existing backend, not new backends. rig-postgres / rig-sqlite / rig-mongodb crates are vector stores, not session memory stores.

FileSessionManager (JSON files on local disk with session/agents/messages hierarchy), S3SessionManager (same hierarchy in S3), and RepositorySessionManager abstract base. Postgres/Redis are BYO via SessionRepository ABC. File + S3 covers a typical multi-tenant deployment.

Two SnapshotStorage implementations ship: FileStorage (local <baseDir>/<sessionId>/scopes/... tree with latest + immutable_history) and S3Storage (same layout, S3 keys). Postgres/Redis/DynamoDB are BYO via the interface.

None. No JSONL, SQLite, Postgres, Redis, or Blob adapter. The SDK has zero opinion on storage. You persist messages in your DB via onStepFinish/onFinish callbacks. The resumable-stream recipe uses Redis but it is example code, not a built-in store.

session.Service is a clean 5-method interface (Create, Get, List, Delete, AppendEvent) and the returned Session is itself an interface so you control the concrete struct. You can BYO Redis/S3/Cassandra/proprietary backends.

BaseDb / AsyncBaseDb is the plug point with ~50 abstract methods covering session, memory, eval, trace, knowledge, component, schedule, approval CRUD. Well-typed but heavy contract; implementing a new adapter requires more work than a 5-method interface.

MemoryProvider trait (remember/recall/clear/memory_type/size/clone_box/preload/export plus optional needs_summary/replace_with_summary/get_event_receiver/remember_with_role) is the BYO plug point. Async-friendly and ChatMessage is Serialize/Deserialize so wiring up a Postgres/Redis/S3 backing store is straightforward but every consumer needs to BYO.

SessionStore Protocol with two required methods (append, load) and four optional (list_sessions, list_session_summaries, delete, list_subkeys). Ships a 13-contract conformance test harness (claude_agent_sdk.testing.run_session_store_conformance). One of the strongest plug-store stories.

SessionStore interface mirrors Python — six methods (two required). Conformance suite in examples/session-stores/shared/conformance.ts (13 tests vendored across adapters). Marked @alpha. delete is no-op for WORM stores. Best plug-store ergonomics in the JS ecosystem.

Three separate interfaces: BaseProvider ABC for checkpoint state (discriminated union on CheckpointConfig.provider), StorageBackend Protocol for memory storage, and FlowPersistence ABC for Flow @persist decorator. Comprehensive but the surface area is wider than typical.

CheckPointStore interface is just Get/Set on []byte (gob-serialized). Minimal contract — you implement two methods. No schema, no migration helper, no versioning hook on the user side. Very BYO-friendly if you want full control.

Store[S any] is a 2-method interface (Get/Save on *Data[S]). Trivial to implement. The Firestore store is the canonical example. Tightly coupled to generic State S so reuse across state shapes requires generic specialization.

BaseCheckpointSaver abstract class with get_tuple/list/put/put_writes plus async siblings. Conformance harness lives in libs/checkpoint-conformance/. Postgres saver also implements BaseStore for cross-session KV. Gold-standard pluggability.

Two interfaces: BaseMemory (memory abstraction) and BaseChatStore (persistence interface for the message store). SQLAlchemyChatStore is the default reference, with community RedisChatStore, PostgresChatStore, AzureChatStore. Reasonable extension surface.

MastraStorage interface with sub-interfaces for each storage domain (memory, workflows, observability, scores, etc.). Custom adapter implements the domain interfaces and is passed via new Mastra({ storage: yourAdapter }). Powerful but more domain interfaces than typical.

Python HistoryProvider abstract base (get_messages/save_messages); .NET AgentSessionStore abstract class (SaveSessionAsync/GetSessionAsync) plus separate ChatHistoryProvider for message-history backends. Clean per-platform interfaces; small surface to implement.

Session Protocol (4 methods: get_items, add_items, pop_item, clear_session) or SessionABC. Minimal surface so a Datadog/BigQuery/Bun-backed custom store is short to write. Duck-typed structural typing means no inheritance needed.
