Session interface (getSessionId, getItems, addItems, popItem, clearSession, plus optional prepareHistoryItemForModelInput, preserveReasoningItemIdsForPersistence). examples/memory/sessions/file.ts is a 119-line reference. Extension interfaces add SessionHistoryRewriteAwareSession and OpenAIResponsesCompactionAwareSession.

No SessionStore / BaseCheckpointer interface to subclass. UI adapter docs show the recommended pattern (persist message_history keyed by thread id server-side and pass to next run) but there is no contract; you are entirely on your own to design the abstraction.

ConversationMemory trait (load/append/clear on async fn returning Vec<Message>) sits behind Arc<dyn ConversationMemory> on Agent::memory. Async-safe, WasmCompat bounds. Clean three-method contract for BYO Postgres/Redis/Mongo/S3 backends.

SessionRepository ABC (create/read/update on session, agent, message plus list_messages and optional multi-agent methods). RepositorySessionManager wires an arbitrary repository to the hook-based persistence flow. Reasonable surface for Postgres/Redis BYO.

SnapshotStorage interface with six methods (saveSnapshot, loadSnapshot, listSnapshotIds, deleteSession, loadManifest, saveManifest). FileStorage and S3Storage are reference implementations; tests show the BYO pattern for Postgres/Redis/DynamoDB.

No SessionStore or Checkpointer abstraction. Persistence is entirely your callback inside onStepFinish / onFinish. The SDK does not formalize how your DB exposes session reads/writes. Plug-store ergonomics are the weakest in the benchmark.

Every non-partial event is persisted synchronously inside a single GORM transaction (refetch, stale-check, state-delta routing, event row insert, session UpdateTime). A crash mid-tool-call loses that tool's progress but events before are durable. Per-event granularity, not per-task durability like LangGraph.

Limited. No per-tool-call checkpointing during a normal run. The only durable interrupt point is RunStatus.paused for HITL approvals via handle_agent_run_paused. A crash mid-tool-call on a non-paused run loses the run; only previously completed runs persist.
Not provided. Crash mid-tool-call loses all in-memory state. SlidingWindowMemory holds a bounded VecDeque<ChatMessage> only for the agent's lifetime.

Best-effort: CLI flushes JSONL per entry to local disk so a crash mid-tool-call leaves everything up to that point on disk; resume <id> re-loads it. No transactional commit-per-tool-write the way LangGraph's _runner.commit/put_writes does. SessionStore mirror is batched (~100ms) so external store may lag.

Subprocess writes each transcript entry to local JSONL line-by-line — that is the durability boundary. External SessionStore is post-local + batched + eventually consistent (100ms window). Per-task commit() like LangGraph does not exist. Recovery via importSessionToStore from the local file.

Strong: with on_events=[*] or tool_usage_started/finished, a checkpoint fires per tool call. Crew.from_checkpoint restores and _restore_runtime walks the event record to find tasks that started but did not complete, marks executor._resuming=True, and resumes on next kickoff(). Gold-standard mid-tool-call resumability.

Persistence fires on interrupt only, not on every message or tool result. Mid-tool-call resume requires you to explicitly call Interrupt/StatefulInterrupt inside the tool. A crash without a deliberate interrupt loses everything since the last interrupt. No equivalent of LangGraph's per-task put_writes.

Not provided. There is no checkpointer that snapshots mid-tool-call to resume after a crash. StreamManager persists output chunks for disconnected clients but a server crash mid-tool-call loses the in-flight state. BYO via WrapTool middleware that persists before each tool call.

Gold standard. _runner.commit() calls put_writes per task — so each parallel tool call's result is durable as it completes. _put_checkpoint runs once per super-step. Under durability=async (default) next super-step starts while previous persists. If 4 parallel tool calls run and the process crashes after 3 finish, on resume the 3 completed tool results are durable and not re-executed.

Not automatic. Workflow can be paused at ctx.wait_for_event for HITL and you ctx.to_dict to serialize, but a crash mid-tool-call loses the in-flight tool result. Weaker than LangGraph's per-task commit.

Mid-run durability is workflow-snapshot-based and fires only when a tool with requireApproval=true suspends. Resume via agent.approveToolCall replays from the suspended step. Survives process restarts if storage is durable but does not cover ordinary mid-tool-call crashes.

Three tiers: agent-level with PerServiceCallChatHistoryPersistingChatClient persists chat history between every LLM round-trip in the function-invocation loop (opt-in). Workflow-level CheckpointStorage between executor transitions (CosmosCheckpointStorage prod). .NET DurableAIAgent makes every agent step a durable orchestration step. Strong but per-tier opt-in.

RunState.to_json() is the durable checkpoint primitive (the 3,305-line run_state.py is the largest file in the SDK). Captures original input, current agent, current turn, generated items, session items, model responses, guardrail results, current step, tool-use tracker, approvals, sandbox resume state. Per-turn automatic via session_persistence; per-tool-call requires you to call result.to_state().to_json() yourself.

No automatic mid-tool-call durability. Closest is HITL state serialization: when a tool needs approval, state.toString() / RunState.fromString(agent, str) lets you serialize and re-run with run(agent, state). Not a substitute for per-tool checkpoints.

Agent itself has no checkpointer. Mid-run durability requires composing with Temporal, DBOS, Prefect, or Restate. Inside Temporal, the agent loop is a workflow and tool calls are activities — a crashed worker replays up to the last committed activity result.

Not provided. ConversationMemory.append fires only at end-of-turn after a successful response. If the loop errors mid-tool-call, append is not called (memory_unchanged_on_provider_error test verifies). Crash mid-tool-call loses the partial trajectory.

Experimental checkpoint at experimental/checkpoint/checkpoint.py with position ∈ {after_model, after_tools}. Stops with stop_reason=checkpoint, snapshot in AgentResult, resume via checkpointResume content block. Per-tool granularity within a cycle requires a custom ToolExecutor like TemporalToolExecutor.

Not durable mid-tool-call. Snapshot fires on lifecycle events (AfterInvocationEvent, MessageAddedEvent, AfterModelCallEvent) — no per-task commit inside executeTool. Interrupt subsystem stores pendingToolExecution on the agent which SessionManager persists at AfterInvocationEvent, so HITL pauses resume but crashes mid-tool-call do not.

Not provided. Crash mid-tool-call has no resume path. The resumable-stream recipe via Redis is resumable stream, not durable runtime — the tool call dies and the next request starts a new run with messages-so-far.

note: no fork, Branch is sub-agent path
details: No fork/branch model. The Branch field on Event is not a fork — it is a dotted-path label (agent_1.agent_2.agent_3) used by parallel sub-agents to scope which conversation history they see. Horizontal slice filter, not vertical fork.
No first-class branching/forking. Fork via manually reading a session, copying the runs you want, and writing under a new session_id. No helper or parent-child linkage.
No thread/branch model. To fork, clone_box the memory provider and start a fresh agent. No parent-child session relationship.

Forking supported: fork_session=True + resume=<id> creates a new session-id branching from a prior session. Top-level helper fork_session() in __init__.py does this from outside an active client. Not LangGraph-style multi-branch within one session, but a clean fork primitive.

forkSession(sessionId, { upToMessageId?, title?, sessionStore? }) branches at a specific message UUID with full UUID remapping and parentUuid chain preservation. Mints a fresh sessionId. No multi-branch graph per session but the UUID-aware fork is stronger than most.

Branching via checkpoint fork: Crew.fork(config, branch=experiment-1) restores from a checkpoint then forks the underlying RuntimeState to a new branch label. Same for Flow.fork and Agent.fork. Conceptually similar to LangGraph's checkpoint forks.
No fork/branch model — you cannot session.fork() LangGraph-style. Thread of execution is linear; only parallel sub-agents inside one run get lanes. A new checkPointID equals a new session.
No native fork/branch model. No parent-child session relationship. If you need branching, you encode it in your state struct.

First-class: graph.get_state_history(config) returns every step; graph.update_state(config_at_step_N, values) creates a new branch from step N. Multiple branches per thread are first-class via Pregel checkpointer. The reference design for this row.
No fork/branch primitive in the OSS framework. Workflow Context resume after pause is the closest mechanic. To branch, you copy the session in your DB and feed messages to a new run.
Fork/branch is not first-class. cloneThread (see packages/memory/src/clone-thread-om.test.ts) exists as a helper — you copy a thread to a new id. No multi-branch per thread.

No fork/branch model on AgentSession. Branching exists at the workflow layer via CheckpointStorage — you can resume a workflow from any checkpoint, but that is checkpoint-replay rather than a parent-child session tree.
No native fork() semantics. For parallel branches (A/B testing) you create separate session_ids and copy the prefix items yourself. RunState.to_json is interruption resume, not session forking.
Single linear conversation per session. No fork / branch model and no parent_session_id. To branch you would implement a graph layer on top.
Branching = pass conversation_id='new' to fork while keeping prior message_history. Basic; no LangGraph-style first-class fork/checkpoint tree.
Linear conversation per conversation_id. No fork/branch model.
Single linear conversation per (session_id, agent_id) pair. No branching/forking primitive. Multi-agent sessions are supported but each agent under a session has its own message log.
Forking is take a snapshot, hand it to another Agent instance, load it — the Snapshot is a JSON blob you copy. Not a first-class branch model.
Single linear conversation per id. No branch/fork model. No checkpoint graph. If you want branching, you implement it as N sessions in your DB.

Event-sourced model means you can List/Get sessions and walk events, but no first-party replay engine. To replay you would re-feed events to a new runner with mocked LLM responses. Tracing exports OTel.
Export via AgentSession.to_dict() + db.get_session(session_id) returns a fully-serializable dict. No replay_session helper — you read the runs list and walk it manually.
Partial: MemoryProvider.export() returns Vec<ChatMessage> and preload() re-hydrates one. Replay (deterministic re-execution of past events) is not provided — events are emitted but not stored.

Top-level list_sessions/get_session_messages/list_subagents helpers plus _from_store siblings. On-disk JSONL is transparent append-only and can be replayed by passing resume=<id> to a new query. import_session_to_store migrates local to remote. Strong export/replay among the field.

getSessionMessages and listSessions for read; deterministic replay via query({ options: { resume, sessionStore } }). resumeSessionAt: messageUuid replays up to a specific point. listSubagents lists subagent transcripts. foldSessionSummary helper for summary sidecars.

crewai replay -t <task_id> CLI lets you re-run from a saved task output. RuntimeState.event_record is fully serializable JSON, captures emission sequence, restored on from_checkpoint. crewai_event_bus._replaying contextvar signals listeners to suppress side effects. Replay is deterministic enough to reconstruct UI state but not to remake real HTTP calls.

Export via r.store.Get(ctx, checkPointID) returns the gob blob. Replay via Runner.Resume re-enters from the saved point. No deterministic replay-from-start framework (frozen RNG, recorded LLM responses) — BYO with a mock model.

No first-party export/replay tooling for sessions. Tracing emits OTel spans. To replay you reconstruct messages from your DB and pass them to Generate via ai.WithMessages. Dev UI replays individual actions, not full sessions.

Strongest replay story. graph.get_state(config) returns current StateSnapshot; graph.get_state_history(config) returns every step. Both serialize via langgraph-checkpoint's codec. Replay: pass config['configurable']['checkpoint_id'] to graph.stream(None, config). is_replaying observable on the loop.

Context.to_dict(serializer=JsonSerializer()) / Context.from_dict is the canonical export/import pattern. For deterministic replay you re-feed chat_history to a new run with mocked LLM responses. No built-in record/replay harness.

Export via storage.getMessages({ threadId }) plus resumable-stream / observe-stream endpoints. _llm-recorder package (packages/_llm-recorder) is used for test fixture replay. Solid export, replay is more test-fixture-oriented than user-facing.

AgentSession.to_dict() returns a typed JSON envelope. Workflow checkpoint export via CheckpointStorage. .NET DurableTask provides replay-from-checkpoint (Microsoft.Agents.AI.DurableTask). Strong on .NET side, lighter on Python side.

RunResult.to_input_list(mode=preserve_all|normalized) exports the run as TResponseInputItems. RunState.to_json/from_json enables full state replay across processes. CURRENT_SCHEMA_VERSION + SCHEMA_VERSION_SUMMARIES is OpenAI's explicit compatibility contract. No first-party replay viewer (tracing dashboard or external exporter).

RunResult.history and RunResult.state are serializable via JSON (state.toJSON across runState.ts). RunState.fromString(agent, json) rebuilds state for replay. Traces dashboard at platform.openai.com/traces is a hosted replay viewer. Solid baseline.

AgentRunResult.all_messages_json() exports the full conversation as JSON bytes. Replay = construct a new Agent.run(..., message_history=...). Pydantic ModelMessagesTypeAdapter round-trips messages. No deterministic record/replay engine.

Not first-class. PromptResponse.messages gives the new messages added during the turn. Replay = construct a PromptRequest::with_history(...). Tests use MockCompletionModel but there is no record/replay against real providers.

Agent.take_snapshot(preset=session, include=..., exclude=..., app_data=...) returns a Snapshot dataclass capturing messages, state, conversation_manager_state, interrupt_state, system_prompt. Agent.load_snapshot restores. Experimental checkpoint wraps this for durable pause/resume.

agent.takeSnapshot({ preset: 'session' }) returns a Snapshot you JSON.stringify for export. agent.loadSnapshot restores. Replay-from-event-stream is not first-class; you can re-issue agent.invoke against a restored snapshot but there is no deterministic event-by-event replay engine.
Export is JSON.stringify(messages) — you already have the messages. Replay = pass the same messages and pin model + seed. Determinism is not a first-party feature.

llmagent.New wires llminternal.Flow, the canonical ReAct loop (call -> tool -> repeat) at base_flow.go:101-127; harness owns continuation via IsFinalResponse() and supports agent transfer and HITL pauses out of the box.

Each Model adapter ships the LLM-tool-LLM cycle internally; `agent.run()` drives it with tool_call_limit, HITL pause/resume, and optional reasoning=True ReAct steps (libs/agno/agno/agent/_run.py:382-712). User only configures tools and hooks.

Prebuilt ReActAgent uses the shared TurnEngine.run_turn (turn_engine.rs:148) bounded by max_turns; also ships BasicAgent and CodeActAgent variants and lets users implement custom AgentExecutor. Loop fully owned by framework.

The ReAct loop runs inside the Claude Code CLI; Python harness only ingests the JSONL frames. It is the canonical Anthropic agent loop with tool-use, hooks, permission gating, sub-agents and resume — but you cannot intercept call->tool->call at the Python layer.

Same CLI-hosted ReAct loop as the Python SDK, with hook fan-out (PreToolUse, PostToolUse, PostToolBatch), maxTurns, maxBudgetUsd, and SDK MCP round-trips back to the host (sdk.d.ts:2281). Fully framework-owned.

Both legacy CrewAgentExecutor and the new Flow-based AgentExecutor implement the LLM-tool-LLM cycle (crew_agent_executor.py:306-325; experimental/agent_executor.py:157); ReAct text path also shipped for non-tool-calling LLMs. Caveat: executes only the first tool_call per turn (crew_agent_executor.py:649), so multi-tool-per-turn parallelism is lost.

adk.NewChatModelAgent compiles a fixed Init -> ChatModel -> ToolNode -> ChatModel ReAct graph (adk/react.go:302-437) with MaxIterations cap, returnDirectly support and full middleware chain. ReAct is the default loop with no graph-building required.

note: automatic tool loop, no explicit ReAct prompt
details: ai.GenerateWithRequest runs an automatic call->tool->call loop bounded by MaxTurns (default 5, generate.go:374-492) with parallel tool dispatch via goroutines; relies on native function-calling, no Reason/Act/Observe scaffolding.

create_react_agent ships a ReAct loop but is @deprecated in favor of langchain.agents.create_agent (chat_agent_executor.py:274-277). Pregel super-step engine is the real primitive; you typically assemble the agent/tools nodes yourself for production.

ReActAgent (react_agent.py:38) parses Thought/Action/Observation for non-tool-calling models; FunctionAgent uses native function-calling. Both drive the same workflow event graph (init_run -> setup_agent -> run_agent_step -> parse_agent_output -> call_tool* -> aggregate_tool_results) bounded by max_iterations (default 20).

loop() compiles an executionWorkflow chain (llmExecutionStep -> tool calls -> llmMappingStep -> backgroundTaskCheckStep -> isTaskCompleteStep) supporting HITL, completion scorers and background tasks (agentic-execution/index.ts:73-100). Fully framework-owned with strong ReAct semantics.

Python _try_execute_function_calls + .NET FunctionInvokingChatClient drive the call->tool->call loop until finish_reason != 'tool_calls' (_tools.py:1632; _types.py:1651) with inline approval gating and middleware. ReAct is automatic but most of the loop lives in Microsoft.Extensions.AI, not in MAF itself.

Runner.run / run_streamed implement the documented ReAct cycle (run.py:215-222) with handoffs, tool_use_behavior modes (run_llm_again / stop_on_first_tool / StopAtTools / ToolsToFinalOutputFunction), max_turns and resumable RunState. Framework owns every step.

run() implements the same canonical loop as the Python SDK (run.ts:476-495): final_output -> stop, handoff -> swap agent, else dispatch tools and re-run. Bounded by DEFAULT_MAX_TURNS=10 (null disables since 0.10.0); fully framework-owned.

Agent graph nodes UserPromptNode -> ModelRequestNode -> CallToolsNode form the ReAct cycle (_agent_graph.py), terminated by configurable end_strategy (early/graceful/exhaustive) and UsageLimits. First-class ReAct without user wiring.

PromptRequest.send (agent/prompt_request/mod.rs:351-718) drives a multi-turn LLM-tool loop bounded by max_turns, with parallel tool dispatch via futures::stream::iter().buffer_unordered and a ThinkTool primitive for visible reasoning. Effectively ReAct without explicit thought channel.

event_loop_cycle (event_loop/event_loop.py:120-282) plus recurse_event_loop drive the call -> tool -> call cycle with rich hook fan-out (BeforeModelCall, BeforeToolCall, After*) and tool-as-async-generator yields. Multi-agent and conversation manager all plug into the same loop.

Agent._stream() (strands-ts/src/agent/agent.ts:816) is the while(true) ReAct loop with deferred append for crash-safety, BeforeInvocation/BeforeModelCall/BeforeTool* hooks, concurrent or sequential tool dispatch and StopReason-driven termination.

generateText/streamText contain a do { } while(...) ReAct loop (generate-text.ts:653) with parallel tool execution. ToolLoopAgent defaults stopWhen to isStepCount(20); raw generateText defaults to one-shot unless stopWhen is set, so callers must configure the loop primitive explicitly.

handleFunctionCalls (base_flow.go:878-980) spawns a goroutine per FunctionCall, calls BeforeToolCallback / tool.Run / AfterToolCallback, then merges all FunctionResponse parts into one session.Event. Results matched by FunctionCall.ID; LongRunningToolIDs surface HITL pauses cleanly.

Each Model adapter (e.g. agno.models.anthropic.claude) drives FunctionCall.execute() with pre/post tool hooks and writes ToolExecution back into messages (libs/agno/agno/tools/function.py:1019-1080). Approval gating built-in via pause/requires_confirmation. Concurrency depends on each provider adapter.

ToolProcessor.process_single_tool_call_with_hooks dispatches via tool.execute(parsed_args), fires on_tool_call/on_tool_start/on_tool_result/on_tool_error hooks and emits ToolCallRequested/Completed/Failed events (tool_processor.rs:50-108). Linear name lookup, results stored as ChatMessage Tool entries.

Three dispatch paths inside CLI: built-in tools, MCP processes, and SDK MCP tools that round-trip back via control_request: mcp_message to run @tool-decorated handlers in-process. Results returned as ToolResultBlock matched by tool_use_id (query.py:548-721). Caller cannot intercept dispatch beyond MCP/hook surface.

Same three dispatch paths as Python SDK; SDK MCP tools defined via createSdkMcpServer + tool() run inside the Node host (sdk.d.ts:5592). PreToolUse/PostToolUse/PostToolBatch hooks gate every call. ToolResult blocks matched by tool_use_id.

note: first tool call only per turn
details: execute_tool_and_check_finality wraps before_tool_call -> tool.run -> after_tool_call; result_as_answer ends loop immediately. Hard limitation: executes only tool_calls[0] per turn even when the LLM emits multiple parallel calls (crew_agent_executor.py:649; experimental/agent_executor.py:1480), reducing throughput. Parallelism only across plan todos.

compose.ToolsNode (tool_node.go:63-72) dispatches each ToolCall to the matching tool by name (default ExecuteSequentially=false -> goroutine per call) and emits one schema.Message per call, matched back via ToolMessage.ToolCallID == ToolCall.ID. UnknownToolsHandler covers hallucinations; rich middleware chain available.

handleToolRequests (go/ai/generate.go:942-1046) spawns one goroutine per Part.ToolRequest, runs WrapTool middleware, folds responses into a single tool-role message with ref-matched ToolResponse parts. Interrupts are first-class and surface FinishReason=interrupted.

ToolNode.invoke (tool_node.py:743) splits tool_calls into parallel executions via Send in v2 ReAct, appends one ToolMessage(tool_call_id=...) per tool to the messages channel. Linkage always explicit; you can also build custom dispatch nodes in any StateGraph.

parse_agent_output emits one ToolCall event per call; the workflow runtime fans them out to parallel @step call_tool invocations (base_agent.py:610-619) and aggregate_tool_results fans them in via ctx.collect_events. Context-aware FunctionTool wiring injects the workflow Context where requested.

toolCallStep validates tool name, runs tool.execute with full ToolExecutionContext, supports requireApproval/needsApprovalFn (emits tool-call-approval chunk and suspends), and llmMappingStep folds results back into the next prompt. Approval suspension is durable via workflow snapshots.

Python _execute_function_calls (_tools.py:1781) invokes FunctionTool with FunctionInvocationContext; .NET delegates to Microsoft.Extensions.AI's FunctionInvokingChatClient routing AIFunction instances. Inline approval gating produces function_approval_request and surfaces user_input_requests. Most loop logic lives outside MAF.

Dedicated dispatch modules: execute_function_tool_calls, execute_computer_actions, execute_shell_calls, execute_apply_patch_calls, execute_mcp_approval_requests. Each call gets a ToolContext (tool_name, tool_call_id, arguments, RunContextWrapper); FunctionToolResult threaded back via run_items_to_input_items.

runner/toolExecution.ts runs concurrent function tool calls up to toolExecution.maxFunctionToolConcurrency (run.ts:180-202) with input/output guardrails around tool.invoke (tool.ts:1876-1933). Results become RunToolCallOutputItem fed back next turn.

CallToolsNode -> ToolManager.handle_call validates JSON args via SchemaValidator and fires before_tool_validate -> wrap_tool_validate -> before_tool_execute -> wrap_tool_execute -> after_tool_execute hooks; ToolReturnPart or RetryPromptPart (on ModelRetry) is appended to the next ModelRequest.

Tool calls dispatched via futures::stream::iter().buffer_unordered(self.concurrency) (mod.rs:567-699) with on_tool_call (Skip/Terminate) and on_tool_result hooks, results wrapped in UserContent::tool_result_with_call_id. Solid concurrency but no first-class approval/HITL primitive.

ToolExecutor._stream (tools/executors/_executor.py:93-289) dispatches via selected_tool.stream(tool_use, invocation_state) — tools are AsyncGenerators yielding intermediate ToolStreamEvents ending with ToolResultEvent. Hook fan-out lets BeforeToolCall swap tools, mutate input, cancel, or retry.

executeTool (agent.ts:1807) builds ToolContext, runs tool.stream(toolContext), wraps each yield in ToolStreamUpdateEvent. BeforeToolCallEvent hooks can mutate input or swap the tool; AfterToolCallEvent can retry. toolExecutor: 'concurrent' | 'sequential' selects parallelism.

executeTools (generate-text.ts:1284) runs approved client tool calls in parallel via Promise.all; resolveToolApproval gates each call (approved/denied/user-approval). tool.toModelOutput lets you reshape raw output, and ToolUIPart state machine tracks each tool call from input-streaming through output-available.

Streaming is first-class via the same iter.Seq2[*session.Event, error] iterator; partial assistant deltas have Partial=true on LLMResponse, are not persisted, and live alongside tool/state events. RunLive adds bidi audio/video streaming via channels wrapped back into the iterator.

_run_stream is a generator yielding RunOutputEvent instances including RunContent for text deltas, ReasoningContentDelta for reasoning, and ModelRequestStarted/Completed for usage. Stream is plain Python yield with 39 distinct event types in RunEvent (run/agent.py:143-194).

TurnEngine.stream_with_tools accumulates LLM StreamChunks (Text, ReasoningContent, ToolUseStart/Delta/Complete, Done, Usage) and emits Event::StreamChunk per chunk plus Event::StreamToolCall. Delivered via tokio mpsc::Sender stored on Context.tx.

Token streaming is opt-in via include_partial_messages=True; SDK then yields SDKPartialAssistantMessage / StreamEvent carrying raw Anthropic SSE events. Default iterator only sees assembled assistant messages, so consumers must opt in to get token-level deltas.

Same as Python — includePartialMessages: true makes the Query iterator yield SDKPartialAssistantMessage (type: 'stream_event') carrying raw BetaRawMessageStreamEvent. Off by default; consumers re-stream over their own SSE/WS.

Crew(stream=True) wires the singleton CrewAIEventsBus into a queue and yields StreamChunk(content, chunk_type=text|tool_call, ...) via CrewStreamingOutput. LLMStreamChunkEvent and LLMThinkingChunkEvent flow on the bus for richer observability.

Streaming is the default representation: ChatModel.Stream returns *schema.StreamReader[*schema.Message], MessageVariant.IsStreaming surfaces it in the AgentEvent, and the graph reducer concatenates chunks. Tool calls also stream via streamToolCallMiddlewares.

ai.WithStreaming(cb) lets the model invoke ModelResponseCallback per chunk; GenerateStream returns iter.Seq2[*ai.ModelStreamValue, error] for range-over-func consumption. Chunks carry Role and accumulated Index; tool results also flow as chunks (generate.go:1031-1040).

stream_mode='messages' yields (AIMessageChunk, metadata) tuples per token via StreamMessagesHandler.on_llm_new_token (pregel/_messages.py:150-163); multiple modes can be combined ('values', 'updates', 'tokens', 'custom', etc.). Per-call SyncQueue/asyncio.Queue is the in-process delivery.

_get_llm_response writes AgentStream events as tokens arrive (base_agent.py:329-339); handler.stream_events() yields them. AgentStreamStructuredOutput streams structured output progressively. Per-token delta surfaced on event.delta.

agent.stream returns MastraModelOutput exposing fullStream (ReadableStream<ChunkType>) with text-start/text-delta/text-end, reasoning-*, tool-call-delta, etc. ~40 chunk types in the ChunkType union (stream/types.ts:931). Plus per-property promises for text/usage/toolCalls.

stream=True returns ResponseStream[AgentResponseUpdate, AgentResponse]; .NET RunStreamingAsync returns IAsyncEnumerable<AgentResponseUpdate>. Each update is a partial Message; DevUI mapper splits these into OpenAI Responses-shaped frames (response.output_text.delta etc.).

run_streamed returns RunResultStreaming whose stream_events() yields StreamEvent = RawResponsesStreamEvent | RunItemStreamEvent | AgentUpdatedStreamEvent. Raw text deltas, function-call-arg deltas and reasoning deltas all surfaced via the underlying OpenAI Responses API events.

StreamedRunResult yields async iterable of RunStreamEvent including RunRawModelStreamEvent (e.g. output_text_delta) and RunItemStreamEvent for assembled items. Sub-agent stream events can be forwarded via Agent.asTool({ onStream }).

Each graph node implements async def stream(ctx) yielding PartStartEvent/PartDeltaEvent/PartEndEvent (messages.py:2697-2784); Agent.run_stream_events() yields AgentStreamEvent + AgentRunResultEvent. The event capability hook lets you intercept the stream.

StreamingPromptRequest returns Pin<Box<dyn Stream<Item = MultiTurnStreamItem<R>>>> with StreamedAssistantContent variants (Text delta, ToolCall, ToolCallDelta, Reasoning, ReasoningDelta, Final) plus StreamedUserContent::ToolResult. Non-streaming path has no event stream at all.

Agent.stream_async yields AsyncIterator with TextStreamEvent for token deltas, ToolUseStreamEvent for streaming tool-arg JSON, ReasoningTextStreamEvent for thinking, and ModelStreamChunkEvent for raw Bedrock chunks. Pure async generator under the hood.

Agent.stream() is a native AsyncGenerator yielding AgentStreamEvent class instances; ModelStreamUpdateEvent carries token deltas (textDelta, reasoningDelta, toolInputDelta) and ContentBlockEvent yields assembled blocks. Hooks invoked synchronously before each yield.

streamText(...).fullStream yields TextStreamPart (~24 variants including text-start/-delta/-end, reasoning-*, tool-input-*); toUIMessageStream emits wire-format UIMessageChunk (~28 variants) on SSE. Both push (callbacks) and pull (iterator) surfaces (notify.ts).

A turn ends when event.IsFinalResponse() returns true (session/session.go:124-130). Every event carries InvocationID and Branch, so 'invocation' is the modeled outer cycle; there is no dedicated Turn type but boundaries are explicit and observable via the event stream.

Agno explicitly calls a turn a 'run': one run() call = one turn = one LLM cycle. RunOutput.run_id is the turn-level identifier (UUID) and AgentSession.runs is a list of RunOutputs (libs/agno/agno/session/agent.py:37). RunStarted/RunCompleted events demarcate boundaries.

TurnEngine.run_turn is one explicit turn; Event::TurnStarted{turn_number, max_turns} and Event::TurnCompleted{final_turn} bracket each iteration (autoagents-protocol/src/protocol.rs:128). max_turns cap is first-class. Among the clearest turn taxonomies in the benchmark.

ResultMessage marks the end of a turn and carries num_turns (count of internal LLM<->tool exchanges), stop_reason, total_cost_usd, model_usage and permission_denials. max_turns caps the internal loop. No explicit start-of-turn event, but boundaries are reliable.

SDKResultMessage (discriminated by subtype: success / error_max_turns / error_max_budget_usd / ...) ends each request loop with num_turns, total_cost_usd, usage, modelUsage, permission_denials, terminal_reason. Same observable boundary as Python SDK.

self.iterations increments per LLM call inside the executor; new AgentExecutor caps via _get_max_step_iterations per-todo. max_iter (default 25) is the budget. No first-class Turn object exposed, but LLMCallStarted/Completed and TaskStarted/Completed events on the bus provide implicit boundaries.

ChatModel -> ToolNode -> ChatModel iteration count is governed by MaxIterations (default 20) but there is no Turn type and no TurnStarted/TurnCompleted event. AgentEvent is the smallest emitted unit; the loop branch is the only boundary signal.

A turn is one trip through runGenerate; MaxTurns counts these (generate.go:473) but is just an int carried through recursion. No Turn type and no lifecycle event marking start/end of a turn — boundaries are observable only via tracing spans.

No 'Turn' object; the closest first-class boundary is the Pregel super-step. A ReAct turn is roughly: agent node (one LLM call) -> tools node (one or more ToolMessages). stream_mode='tasks' or 'updates' surfaces super-step starts/ends but you must reconstruct a 'turn' yourself.

A turn is one LLM call -> N parallel tool calls -> fan-in. max_iterations (default 20) caps the count, early_stopping_method = 'force' | 'generate' tunes overflow behavior (base_agent.py:519-541). AgentInput/AgentSetup/AgentOutput events bracket each turn on the stream.

A turn (called a 'step' in Mastra) is one full pass through the 6-step workflow chain. The fullStream emits start-step / step-finish / finish chunks demarcating turn boundaries; isStepCount-style stop conditions and isTaskCompleteStep scorers control termination.

Implicit: a turn ends when the LLM returns a non-tool-call response (finish_reason in {stop, length, content_filter}) or when MiddlewareTermination is raised. No explicit Turn type; the run accumulates updates until terminal.

Documented: 'A turn is defined as one AI invocation (including any tool calls that might occur)' (run.py:237). max_turns (default 10, configurable, None unlimited) is first-class; resumed runs do not increment the counter. Boundaries are explicit and serializable via RunState.

A turn is bounded by prepareTurn -> model call -> resolveTurnAfterModelResponse -> applyTurnResult; state._currentTurn (runState.ts) increments at the start of each turn. maxTurns defaults to 10 (null disables since 0.10.0). Loop terminates only on next_step_final_output or next_step_interruption.

A turn is one trip around the graph until another ModelRequestNode is queued or End fires. RunContext.run_step (_run_context.py:74) increments per iteration; UsageLimits bounds total turns; end_strategy controls termination but there is no Turn lifecycle event type.

A turn is one LLM call plus its tool dispatches; current_max_turns counter (mod.rs:410) bounds the loop. No Turn type or event; only the streaming FinalResponse marks end-of-loop. Hooks fire at known points but turn boundaries themselves are not first-class events.

One event_loop_cycle ~ one model call + zero-or-many tool calls; EventLoopStopEvent yielded when stop_reason in {end_turn, max_tokens, cancelled, interrupt, stop_sequence} and no further tool use (event_loop.py:267). Each tool batch recurses into a fresh cycle, so cycle boundaries are observable.

A cycle is one model call plus any tools it triggered; Meter.startCycle / endCycle demarcate boundaries (agent.ts:890, 1023). StopReason union (endTurn / toolUse / maxTokens / interrupt / cancelled / ...) tells you why the cycle ended.

A 'step' is one LLM call + parallel tool executions; stopWhen (isStepCount, hasToolCall, custom) defines termination. start-step / finish-step stream parts bracket each step and step-event hooks fire onStepStart/onStepFinish. Step boundaries are first-class.

Idiomatic Go 1.23 iter.Seq2[*session.Event, error] returned by Runner, Agent and Flow at every layer (runner/runner.go:131-268). Composable via for-range, no EventEmitter or callback hell. RunLive layer below uses channels wrapped back into iter.Seq2.

_run_stream is a Python generator yielding RunOutputEvent; _arun_stream is an AsyncIterator. Events produced by helpers in agno.utils.events and passed through handle_event respecting agent.events_to_skip and agent.store_events. 39 distinct event types in RunEvent enum.

Events emitted via mpsc::Sender<Event> on Context.tx, wrapped by EventHelper. Two consumption modes: DirectAgent fans out via EventFanout (BoxEventStream), ActorAgent uses runtime Environment.take_event_receiver or subscribe_events. DEFAULT_CHANNEL_BUFFER bound.

Single anyio memory-object stream with max_buffer_size=100 (query.py:121-123). Transport read loop pushes typed dataclasses; receive_messages pops. Backpressure via the bounded buffer means a slow consumer blocks the read loop after 100 buffered messages — one taxonomy on one iterator, deliberately simple.

Query extends AsyncGenerator<SDKMessage, void>; consumer iterates with for-await-of and dispatches on msg.type. Single discriminated union (~30 SDKMessage variants) covers stream events, turn results, tool/sub-agent/hook/notification lifecycle. Same simple design as Python SDK.

CrewAIEventsBus is a process-wide singleton with sync handlers dispatched to a ThreadPoolExecutor and async handlers on a daemon asyncio thread (events/event_bus.py:83). 151 event classes across 19 files cover crew/agent/task/LLM/tool/memory/MCP/checkpoint/HITL/skill/reasoning/guardrail/OS-signal categories. Singleton design limits horizontal isolation.

*AsyncIterator[*AgentEvent] backed by an unbounded internal channel (adk/utils.go:31-56) returned by Runner. Consumer loops with iter.Next(). One event per assistant/tool message; sub-agent events multiplex via RunPath. Callback hook events are a separate subsystem and not mixed in.

Streaming uses a ModelStreamCallback (one function, generate.go:72) or GenerateStream's iter.Seq2 wrapper. No async EventEmitter or topic bus; lifecycle events (start, step-start, finish) are observable only via tracing spans, not the stream itself.

Per-run SyncQueue / asyncio.Queue (pregel/main.py:2719) plus a parallel LangChain callback handler chain for token streaming (pregel/_messages.py:150-163). stream() yields between super-step ticks; seven explicit StreamPart TypedDicts (values, updates, messages, custom, checkpoints, tasks, debug).

Two complementary mechanisms inside the workflow runtime: (1) @step routing via return / ctx.send_event with ctx.collect_events fan-in, (2) ctx.write_event_to_stream pushes onto handler.stream_events() consumer iterator. Rich event taxonomy with HITL InputRequiredEvent/HumanResponseEvent first-class.

loop() returns a web-standard ReadableStream<ChunkType>; MastraModelOutput exposes fullStream plus per-property promises (text, usage, toolCalls, finishReason, messageList). Processors push custom data-* chunks via ProcessorStreamWriter; transient chunks streamed but not persisted.

Python returns AsyncIterable<AgentResponseUpdate>; .NET returns IAsyncEnumerable<AgentResponseUpdate>. Middleware composes via with_transform_hook / with_result_hook; ContextProvider lifecycle hooks fill the gap. No in-process event bus or observer pattern — the only fan-out is middleware.

Internal asyncio.Queue[StreamEvent | QueueCompleteSentinel] (result.py:483) plus separate _input_guardrail_queue. Three event flavors (RawResponsesStreamEvent / RunItemStreamEvent / AgentUpdatedStreamEvent) cover token deltas, run-item generation, and agent handoffs. RunHooks fire synchronously inside the loop.

Dual surface: AgentHooks/RunHooks EventEmitter for lifecycle (agent_start/end/handoff/tool_start/end, lifecycle.ts:101-181) and StreamedRunResult async iterable of RunStreamEvent (events.ts:1-83). Asymmetric but flexible.

Agent.run_stream_events() returns an AgentEventStream async context manager yielding AgentStreamEvent + AgentRunResultEvent. Each graph node implements async def stream(ctx) yielding events. The 'event' capability hook and wrap_run_event_stream let you intercept the stream end-to-end.

note: Stream for streaming, no events otherwise
details: Streaming path returns a futures::Stream<MultiTurnStreamItem<R>>; non-streaming path returns only PromptResponse after the loop finishes — no event stream at all. Hooks (7 PromptHook callbacks) and tracing spans are the only observability when not streaming.

Agent._run_loop is a Python async generator yielding TypedEvent instances; stream_async routes each through event.prepare and callback_handler (agent/agent.py:857-868). Rich hook event bus (BeforeInvocation/BeforeModelCall/BeforeToolCall/MessageAdded/etc.) layered alongside the stream.

Native AsyncGenerator<AgentStreamEvent, AgentResult, undefined> from Agent.stream(). Every yielded value is a discriminated AgentStreamEvent class; hooks invoked synchronously via _invokeCallbacks before each yield, so hooks can mutate events before they leave the generator.

Two parallel mechanisms via notify(): push (experimental_onStart/StepStart/LanguageModelCallStart/End, onToolExecutionStart/End, onStepFinish, onFinish) and pull (streamText().fullStream: AsyncIterableStream<TextStreamPart>). 24-variant TextStreamPart in-process plus 28-variant UIMessageChunk on wire.

Only native adapters are Gemini (`model/gemini/gemini.go`) and an Apigee Vertex proxy. No first-party OpenAI, Anthropic, Bedrock, Azure OpenAI, or LiteLLM adapters; BYO by implementing the `model.LLM` interface, which still forces marshalling through Gemini's `genai.Content` shape.

`libs/agno/agno/models/` ships ~49 native providers including Anthropic, OpenAI (Chat + Responses), Gemini, Bedrock, Vertex, Azure, Cohere, Mistral, Ollama, Groq, Fireworks, DeepSeek, LiteLLM, vLLM, OpenRouter, xAI, and many more. Among the broadest native catalogues in the benchmark.

Native backends in `crates/autoagents-llm/src/backends/` cover OpenAI, Anthropic, Azure OpenAI, OpenRouter, DeepSeek, xAI, Phind, Groq, Google, MiniMax, Ollama, plus local-model crates (llama.cpp, mistral-rs, Burn/Onnx). Misses Bedrock/Vertex first-party and has no LiteLLM aggregator.

SDK is Anthropic-only (Sonnet/Opus/Haiku). Bedrock and Vertex routing exist at the underlying CLI layer but the SDK is opaque to them; no OpenAI/Gemini/etc. path. Multi-provider is effectively out of scope.

`AccountInfo.apiProvider` covers `firstParty | bedrock | vertex | foundry | anthropicAws | mantle | gateway` — all Anthropic-API surfaces selected via env vars, not config. No native OpenAI or Gemini; reaching them needs a LiteLLM-style gateway you run yourself.

Native providers under `lib/crewai/src/crewai/llms/providers/` cover OpenAI, Anthropic, Azure, Bedrock, Gemini, plus an `openai_compatible` adapter (DeepSeek, OpenRouter, Ollama, vLLM, Cerebras, Dashscope). Anything else routes through LiteLLM (`LLM.__new__` in `llm.py:350-443`) for 100+ models.

`eino-ext/components/model/` ships adapters for OpenAI (and Azure via OpenAI-compatible), Anthropic, Gemini (Vertex + AI Studio), Ollama, DeepSeek, Qwen, Qianfan, Ark, Arkbot, OpenRouter. No bundled LiteLLM gateway; missing Bedrock first-party.

Plugins in `plugins/`: `googlegenai` (Gemini + Vertex), `anthropic`, `compat_oai` (OpenAI / Azure OpenAI / vLLM / Anyscale), `ollama`. No first-party Bedrock plugin, no LiteLLM/AnyLLM aggregator, and each new provider is ~500 LOC of plugin code.

`init_chat_model("anthropic:...")` / `openai:` / `google:` / `bedrock:` / Azure / Vertex / LiteLLM-as-OpenAI-proxy — native via the langchain ecosystem, not a third-party shim. Effectively unlimited provider breadth.

`llama-index-integrations/llms/` houses ~104 LLM packages: Anthropic, OpenAI, Azure OpenAI, Bedrock (and Bedrock Converse), Vertex, Google GenAI, Cohere, Mistral, Groq, Together, Fireworks, DeepSeek, Cerebras, Databricks, Cloudflare AI Gateway, HuggingFace, IBM, Ollama, vLLM, and many more. Broadest native coverage in the benchmark.

Inherits the Vercel AI SDK's 40+ provider adapters — Anthropic, OpenAI, Gemini, Bedrock, Vertex, Azure, Cerebras, Groq, Cohere, Mistral, etc. — through one `LanguageModelV2` interface. README explicitly markets "40+ providers through one standard interface".

Provider modules across Python/.NET: OpenAI, Azure Foundry, Foundry Local, Anthropic, Bedrock (Python), Gemini (alpha), Ollama, Claude (Code-style), GitHub Copilot SDK, Copilot Studio, Hyperlight. Solid breadth but Gemini is alpha and some providers are Python-only.

Custom prefix→provider maps are supported via `MultiProviderMap`.

All other providers — Anthropic, Gemini, Bedrock, Vertex, Mistral, LiteLLM-compatible — flow through the `@openai/agents-extensions/ai-sdk` adapter wrapping a Vercel AI SDK `LanguageModelV2`. Wide coverage but heavily mediated.

`crates/rig-core/src/providers/` lists 26 native providers: Anthropic, Azure, ChatGPT, Cohere, Copilot, DeepSeek, Galadriel, Gemini, Groq, HuggingFace, Hyperbolic, Llamafile, MiniMax, Mira, Mistral, Moonshot, Ollama, OpenAI, OpenRouter, Perplexity, Together, VoyageAI, xAI, Xiaomimimo, Zai. Bedrock/Vertex live in companion crates (`rig-bedrock`, `rig-vertexai`, `rig-gemini-grpc`).

`strands-ts/src/models/` has `BedrockModel`, `AnthropicModel`, `OpenAIModel` (Chat + Responses), `GoogleModel`, and `VercelModel` (which wraps any `@ai-sdk/provider`). Smaller native surface than the Python sibling but the Vercel adapter unlocks the full Vercel ecosystem.

Ships 50+ first-party provider packages: OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Azure OpenAI, Bedrock, Vertex, Mistral, Cohere, DeepInfra, DeepSeek, Fireworks, Groq, Together, Replicate, xAI, Perplexity, Alibaba, ByteDance, Moonshot, Cerebras, Baseten, HuggingFace, OpenAI-compatible, AI Gateway, and image/audio/speech/embed sister providers. No model-fallback primitive. The `retryandreflect` plugin retries on tool errors only, not on model errors. To fall back on outage you write an `OnModelErrorCallback` that re-issues the request against another model — entirely host-built.

`FallbackConfig` (`libs/agno/agno/models/fallback.py:20-40`) classifies failures into `on_error`, `on_rate_limit`, and `on_context_overflow` with separate fallback model lists per class plus a callback for instrumentation. Wire via `Agent(fallback_config=...)` or the `fallback_models=[...]` shortcut. Best-in-class for this row.

`FallbackLayer` (`crates/autoagents-llm/src/optim/fallback.rs:64`) composes with `RetryLayer` in a `PipelineBuilder`: `PipelineBuilder::new(openai).add_layer(RetryLayer).add_layer(FallbackLayer::new(vec![anthropic, ollama]))`. `default_is_fallbackable` triggers on HttpError, ProviderError, Generic, ResponseFormatError, NoToolSupport while auth/invalid-request errors propagate. Streaming only falls back on the initial call.

`ClaudeAgentOptions.fallback_model` (`types.py:1679-1680`) provides one-shot fallback on overage/outage; `ResultMessage.model_usage` shows the split. Not a multi-rung chain — and only useful within the Anthropic ecosystem since multi-provider is out of scope.

`Options.fallbackModel` (sdk.d.ts:1301) triggers on API errors and rate-limit responses; `modelUsage` reflects which model served the turn. Single-step only — no chain — and issue #313 is open for richer retry policy. Restricted to Anthropic-family models.

No built-in "if provider A fails, retry on provider B" config. `Agent.max_retry_limit=2` retries the task on the same model. Workarounds are LiteLLM (intra-provider retries) or AMP connection management — both host-built.

`ModelRetryConfig` (`adk/chatmodel.go:307`) retries on the same model with backoff. To fall back to a different model on outage you write a `WrapModel` middleware that catches `next.Generate` errors — fully BYO.

`middleware.Fallback{Models: []ai.ModelRef{...}}` (`plugins/middleware/fallback.go:59-70`) accepts an ordered list of `ModelRef`s and triggers on UNAVAILABLE, DEADLINE_EXCEEDED, RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED, ABORTED, INTERNAL, NOT_FOUND, UNIMPLEMENTED — overridable via `Statuses`. Composes with `middleware.Retry` (`retry.go:71-87`) for exponential backoff + jitter via outer-to-inner `Retry{Fallback{model}}`.

`langchain-core`'s `Runnable.with_fallbacks([...])` wraps the model passed to `create_react_agent` and fires on `Exception`. Generic — no built-in rate-limit-aware or error-class policy; you encode classification yourself.

No first-class fallback primitive in core. The `llama-index-llms-cloudflare-ai-gateway` integration delegates to Cloudflare's AI Gateway; otherwise you wrap an `LLM` with retry/fallback logic yourself.

`loop()` accepts a `models` array (`packages/core/src/loop/loop.ts:13`) and retries on the next entry when the first model fails; `MODEL_GENERATION` OTel spans are re-stamped to reflect the fallback (`llm-execution-step.ts:650-660`). First-class ordered chain with observability.

MAF ships no fallback chain. `Microsoft.Extensions.AI` has `DistributedCachingChatClient` and `LoggingChatClient` decorators and community fallback decorators exist, but nothing first-party. BYO via a custom `IChatClient` decorator.

`RetryPolicy` (`src/agents/retry.py`) with `ModelRetryAdvice` / `ModelRetryBackoffSettings` handles intra-provider retries (see `examples/basic/retry.py`, `retry_litellm.py`). Cross-provider fallback (OpenAI down → Anthropic) is not provided — wrap `Runner.run` in try/except and re-issue with a different `RunConfig.model`.

`getResponseWithRetry` / `getStreamedResponseWithRetry` (`packages/agents-core/src/runner/modelRetry.ts`) retry inside one provider. No automatic provider-fallback chain — you'd implement it inside a custom `ModelProvider` that orchestrates multiple `Model` instances.

`FallbackModel` (`models/fallback.py:69`) wraps an ordered list of `Model` instances and falls through on `ResponseRejected` or configurable exception types, e.g. `FallbackModel(OpenAIModel('gpt-5.2'), AnthropicModel('claude-sonnet-4-6'))`. Pydantic AI Gateway adds load-balanced routing groups on top.
No retry-on-fallback-model mechanism shipped. You write your own wrapper around the provider clients to swap on error.

`ModelRetryStrategy` (`event_loop/_retry.py`) is the default hook with `max_attempts=6, initial_delay=4s, max_delay=240s` — retries on the same model. Cross-provider fallback requires a custom `Model` wrapper or a hook that mutates `agent.model` on `AfterModelCallEvent.exception`.

`DefaultModelRetryStrategy` (`strands-ts/src/retry/default-model-retry-strategy.ts`) retries the same model on throttling/transient errors with exponential backoff. To swap providers on failure you write a custom `ModelRetryStrategy` or react to `AfterModelCallEvent.error` by setting `event.agent.model = backupModel; event.retry = true`.

`customProvider({ fallbackProvider })` (`packages/ai/src/registry/custom-provider.ts`) only falls back when a model id is missing — not when a call errors. For true error fallback you write a `LanguageModelMiddleware.wrapGenerate/wrapStream`. AI Gateway (hosted) has policy fallback internally but it's not configurable from the SDK.

ADK-Go ships no auto-summarization or rolling-window compaction. The `llmagent.Config.IncludeContents` knob is only `default` (full history) or `none` (current turn). Engineers must wire a `BeforeModelCallback` to summarize when `len(req.Contents)` exceeds a threshold.

`CompressionManager` compresses tool results when `compress_tool_results=True`, but there is no automatic message-history compaction when context fills up. Hard caps (`num_history_messages`, `num_history_runs`) and optional session summaries are the only history controls; you compose them yourself.

`SlidingWindowMemory` with `TrimStrategy::Summarize` only flips a `needs_summary` flag on overflow; it does not actually summarize. You must call `MemoryProvider::replace_with_summary(...)` yourself after generating the summary externally — no built-in summarizer agent ships.

Auto-compaction is built into the Claude Code CLI subprocess and runs when context nears the model window. The Python SDK exposes `PreCompact` hook (with manual/auto trigger discrimination and custom instructions), `autoCompactThreshold`, and `get_context_usage()` for live inspection. The algorithm itself is opaque but the integration is first-class.

Same CLI-driven auto-compaction as the Python sibling, plus `PreCompact` and `PostCompact` hooks. `SDKCompactBoundaryMessage` (`type: 'system', subtype: 'compact_boundary'`) cleanly marks where compaction happened and lists `preserved_segment`/`preserved_messages` for resume. First-class but trigger is implicit (no SDK threshold option).

`Agent.respect_context_window=True` calls `handle_context_length()` to summarize/truncate when the LLM raises a context-length-exceeded error. It is reactive only — no compaction before the limit is reached and no `PreCompact` hook. Adequate but not proactive.

Ships `adk/middlewares/summarization/` with a configurable token-threshold trigger (default 190k), pluggable `TokenCounter`, customizable summary prompt, and optional transcript-file pointer so the model can re-read full history. Fires inside `BeforeModelRewriteState` and replaces the message list. Best-in-class for a Go framework.
No built-in summarization or truncation. BYO by writing a `WrapGenerate` middleware that watches `len(messages)` or token count and rewrites earlier messages into a summary.

`pre_model_hook` is the documented place to wire trimming/summarization, but the OSS runtime ships no first-party summarizer — engineers compose `trim_messages` (LangChain-core) or `langgraph-deepagents`'s third-party `compress` tool. Primitive is excellent; built-ins are missing.

`Memory` has a token-budget-driven FIFO flush — when chat history exceeds `chat_history_token_ratio * token_limit`, oldest messages are flushed into memory blocks. `ChatSummaryMemoryBuffer` (deprecated) does explicit summarization and `FactExtractionMemoryBlock` can summarize ejected messages. Usable but rougher than first-class strategies.

Built-in `TokenLimiterProcessor` and `BatchPartsProcessor` trigger when token budget is exceeded, with a drop-oldest user/assistant pair strategy. LLM-summarized compaction has to be composed yourself. Solid but lighter than CLI/strategy approaches.

First-class `CompactionProvider` with `ContextWindowCompactionStrategy`, `SummarizationCompactionStrategy`, `ToolResultCompactionStrategy`, `ChatReducerCompactionStrategy`, and `PipelineCompactionStrategy`. `HarnessAgent` (.NET) wires this by default and triggers on context-window pressure before each chat call. ADR-documented architecture.

`OpenAIResponsesCompactionSession` (~521 LOC) runs server-side compaction on the OpenAI Responses API with `auto`/`previous_response_id`/`input` modes. Restricted to OpenAI; for LiteLLM/Any-LLM you BYO via `session_input_callback` or `call_model_input_filter`.

Same OpenAI-only pattern as Python: `OpenAIResponsesCompactionSession` wraps `responses.compact` with `force`, `compactionMode`, `responseId` knobs. Not built into the generic `MemorySession`; other providers require BYO.

Provider-native compaction via `OpenAICompaction` and `AnthropicCompaction` capabilities. No provider-agnostic compaction in core; `ProcessHistory` lets you plug a custom summarizer. Reasonable but tied to provider features.

Core ships nothing; `rig-memory` (separate crate) provides sliding-window and token-budget policies that filter history during memory `load`. No summarizer agent or auto-compaction strategy. BYO summarization.

`SlidingWindowConversationManager` (default window 40, optional `should_truncate_results`, optional `per_turn`) and `SummarizingConversationManager` (configurable summarization prompt) are first-class. Triggers proactively at end of cycle and reactively on `ContextWindowOverflowException`. `NullConversationManager` available for stateful models.

Mirrors Python: `SlidingWindowConversationManager` (default `windowSize: 40`), `SummarizingConversationManager` (calls configured `Model` to summarize), and `NullConversationManager`. Proactive trigger when `projectedInputTokens / contextWindowLimit > compressionThreshold` (default 0.7). Reactive on overflow. Pluggable abstract base.

No built-in summarize-and-truncate. Engineers truncate `messages` in `prepareStep`, compact at provider level via `LanguageModelMiddleware.transformParams`, or compose with `@ai-sdk/langchain`. Full BYO.

Twelve callbacks across plugins and llmagent: `OnUserMessageCallback`, `BeforeRunCallback`, `AfterRunCallback`, `OnEventCallback`, `BeforeAgentCallback`, `AfterAgentCallback`, `BeforeModelCallback`, `AfterModelCallback`, `OnModelErrorCallback`, `BeforeToolCallback`, `AfterToolCallback`, `OnToolErrorCallback`. Plugins fire across all agents; per-agent variants exist too.

`pre_hooks`, `post_hooks`, `tool_hooks` (middleware chain), per-tool `pre_hook`/`post_hook`/`tool_hooks`, `BaseGuardrail` subclasses, and `@hook(run_in_background=True)`. Covers run, tools, and per-tool slots; no per-LLM-call slot or `SessionStart`.

`AgentHooks` trait with 10 methods (`on_agent_create`, `on_run_start/complete`, `on_turn_start/complete`, `on_tool_call`, `on_tool_start`, `on_tool_result`, `on_tool_error`, `on_agent_shutdown`). Covers the lifecycle adequately but most slots are read-only.

11 first-class hook events (`PreToolUse`, `PostToolUse`, `PostToolUseFailure`, `UserPromptSubmit`, `SessionStart`, `Stop`, `SubagentStop`, `SubagentStart`, `PreCompact`, `Notification`, `PermissionRequest`). Hook matchers can target tool names; outputs schema is rich.

29 hook events from `HOOK_EVENTS`, including the Python set plus `PostToolBatch`, `UserPromptExpansion`, `SessionEnd`, `StopFailure`, `PostCompact`, `PermissionDenied`, `Setup`, `TeammateIdle`, `TaskCreated/Completed`, `Elicitation`/`ElicitationResult`, `ConfigChange`, `WorktreeCreate/Remove`, `InstructionsLoaded`, `CwdChanged`, `FileChanged`. Strictly the broadest surface in the comparison.

Four typed hook types (`before_llm_call`, `after_llm_call`, `before_tool_call`, `after_tool_call`) plus `before/after_kickoff_callbacks`, `step_callback`, `task_callback`, decorator-style `@before_kickoff`/`@after_kickoff`, agent-scoped wrappers, listeners on the 151-event bus, and `BaseInterceptor` at the httpx transport layer. No `SessionStart`, no `PreCompact`.

Three layers: graph-level `callbacks.Handler` (5 timings), deprecated `AgentMiddleware` struct, and new `ChatModelAgentMiddleware` interface with 8 methods (`BeforeAgent`, `BeforeModelRewriteState`, `AfterModelRewriteState`, 4 `Wrap*ToolCall` variants, `WrapModel`). Embed `BaseChatModelAgentMiddleware` for no-op defaults.

Three composable middleware points: `WrapGenerate` (per tool-loop iteration), `WrapModel` (per model API call), `WrapTool` (per tool exec). No traditional `SessionStart`/`BeforeMessage`/`AfterMessage`/`OnTurnComplete` lifecycle hooks; intentionally hook-light.

`pre_model_hook` and `post_model_hook` on the prebuilt `create_react_agent` (read+mutate+block+branch), `wrap_tool_call`/`awrap_tool_call` around every tool dispatch (override request, return synthetic ToolMessage, re-execute), `GraphCallbackHandler` for interrupt/resume, plus full LangChain `BaseCallbackHandler` observe-only set.

No Claude-style hook system. You subclass `BaseWorkflowAgent`'s `@step` methods (`init_run`, `setup_agent`, `run_agent_step`, `parse_agent_output`, `call_tool`, `aggregate_tool_results`) and use `FunctionTool(callback=...)`. Dispatcher tracing is read-only.

`Processor` interface with 8 method slots (`processInput`, `processInputStep`, `processLLMRequest`, `processLLMResponse`, `processOutputStream`, `processOutputStep`, `processOutputResult`, `processAPIError`) plus loop-level `onChunk`, `onStepFinish`, `onFinish`, `onError`, `onAbort`, `onIterationComplete`, delegation callbacks. Covers every stage of the loop.

`AgentMiddleware`, `ChatMiddleware`, `FunctionMiddleware` around run/chat/tool plus `ContextProvider` lifecycle (`before_run`, `after_run`, `before_chat_call`, `after_chat_call`). `HistoryProvider` for persistence. Decorator sugar and .NET pipeline builder hooks complete the surface.

Global `RunHooks` and per-agent `AgentHooks` with `on_llm_start/end`, `on_agent_start/end`, `on_handoff`, `on_tool_start/end`. Plus `call_model_input_filter`, `session_input_callback`, `tool_error_formatter`, and four guardrail decorators (`input`, `output`, `tool_input`, `tool_output`).

`RunHooks`/`AgentHooks` with `agent_start/end/handoff/tool_start/tool_end`, `InputGuardrail`/`OutputGuardrail`/`ToolInputGuardrail`/`ToolOutputGuardrail`, plus `callModelInputFilter`, `sessionInputCallback`, `toolErrorFormatter`, `errorHandlers`, `HandoffInputFilter`. No `SessionStart` or PreCompact.

`Hooks` capability gives decorator sugar over 20+ slots: `before_run`/`after_run`/`run`(wrap)/`run_error`, per-node variants, `before_model_request`/`after_model_request`/`model_request`(wrap), `prepare_tools`/`prepare_output_tools`, `before/after_tool_validate`(+wrap), `before/after_tool_execute`(+wrap), `before/after_output_validate/process`(+wrap), `deferred_tool_calls`, `run_event_stream`, `event`. Tool hooks support filtering and timeouts.

`PromptHook` trait with 7 methods: `on_completion_call`, `on_completion_response`, `on_tool_call`, `on_tool_result`, `on_text_delta`, `on_tool_call_delta`, `on_stream_completion_response_finish`. All read-only; only `HookAction::Terminate` and `ToolCallHookAction::Skip` are available control verbs.

Lifecycle events (`AgentInitializedEvent`, `BeforeInvocationEvent`, `AfterInvocationEvent`, `MessageAddedEvent`, `BeforeModelCallEvent`, `AfterModelCallEvent`, `BeforeToolCallEvent`, `AfterToolCallEvent`) plus multi-agent (`MultiAgentInitializedEvent`, `BeforeMultiAgentInvocationEvent`, `BeforeNodeCallEvent`, `AfterNodeCallEvent`, `AfterMultiAgentInvocationEvent`) and experimental Bidi events. Sync/async supported.

Hookable events for invocation, model, tools (`Before*`/`After*` for invocation, model, tools-batch, individual tool call), plus content/model/tool stream updates, message events, result events, interrupt events, and 9 multi-agent events. `HookOrder` enum (`SDK_FIRST`, `INTERVENTION_OUTPUT`, `DEFAULT`, `INTERVENTION_INPUT`, `SDK_LAST`).

`prepareCall`/`prepareStep` (mutate model/tools/instructions/messages), `experimental_onStart`/`onStepStart`/`onLanguageModelCallStart`/`onLanguageModelCallEnd`, `experimental_repairToolCall`, `experimental_refineToolInput`, per-tool `onInputStart/Delta/Available`, `resolveToolApproval`, `onToolExecutionStart/End`, `onStepFinish`, `onFinish`, `LanguageModelMiddleware.transformParams/wrapGenerate/wrapStream`. Broad and granular.

Callbacks can mutate `*model.LLMRequest`, tool `args map[string]any` in place, and `result map[string]any`. Returning a non-nil value short-circuits the underlying call (e.g. LLM cache or tool fast-path). `OnModelErrorCallback` and `OnToolErrorCallback` can convert errors to responses/results.

`pre_hooks` mutate `run_input` and raise `InputCheckError` to block; `post_hooks` mutate `run_output` and raise `OutputCheckError`. `tool_hooks` form a `functools.reduce`-built nested middleware chain that mutates args and results and can swap implementations. Guardrails enforce blocks.

Hooks are observe-and-abort. `on_run_start` and `on_tool_call` can return `HookOutcome::Abort` but receive immutable `&Task`/`&ToolCall`. None of the mutate scenarios (force tool args, summarize tool result, rewrite messages) are supported as first-party; you must wrap the executor or hide context inside tool struct fields.

Hooks can return `updatedInput`, `updatedToolOutput`, `additionalContext`, and `decision: 'block'` / `permissionDecision: allow|deny|ask|defer`. `continue_: False` halts. The in-flight messages array is not directly mutable from Python — the CLI owns it — so message-array surgery is restricted to `additionalContext`.

Same `updatedInput`/`updatedToolOutput`/`additionalContext`/`decision: 'block'`/`permissionDecision` surface, plus `AsyncHookJSONOutput` to defer with `asyncTimeout`. Matchers fire per tool name; last-wins merge on `updatedInput`. Messages list still owned by the CLI.

`before_llm_call` and `before_tool_call` mutate `ctx.messages`/`ctx.tool_input` in place (warned against replacing the list) and return `False` to block. `after_llm_call`/`after_tool_call` return a `str` to replace the response/result. Event listeners cannot block.

`BeforeModelRewriteState` mutates the message list before each model call; `WrapModel` can replace the model entirely (routing, retry, mid-stream tool filtering); `WrapInvokableToolCall` wraps tool endpoints to mutate args and results; `BeforeAgent` mutates Instruction/Tools/ReturnDirectly. Real-world `summarization` middleware proves the mutation depth.

`WrapGenerate` mutates `params.Request.Messages` (Skills uses this for `injectSkillsPrompt`); `WrapTool` mutates `params.Request.Input` and rewrites `resp.Output`/`resp.Content`; `WrapModel` short-circuits with cached responses. Hooks can interrupt and emit extra stream chunks via `params.Callback`.

`pre_model_hook` emits `messages` or `llm_input_messages` (one-shot) updates; `post_model_hook` can append `AIMessage` with new `tool_calls`, route, block, or short-circuit. `wrap_tool_call` can return synthetic `ToolMessage` without executing, call `execute()` zero/one/many times, return `Command(goto=Send(...))` to fan out. `ToolRuntime`/`InjectedState` strip+inject trusted args.

note: subclass to mutate, callback to rewrite
details: Subclassing `@step` methods (`init_run`, `setup_agent`, `run_agent_step`, `call_tool`, `aggregate_tool_results`) gives full read/mutate/block/branch. `FunctionTool(callback=...)` can return a new `ToolOutput` or string to override. `partial_params` only fills defaults — LLM values still win. Verbose vs. dedicated hooks.

note: tripwire abort, replace LLM with cached, retry with feedback
details: `processInputStep` replaces `model`/`tools`/`toolChoice`/`activeTools`/`messages`/`systemMessages`/`messageList`/`providerOptions`/`modelSettings`/`structuredOutput`/`messageId`. `processLLMRequest` returns `{ response }` to skip the LLM (response caching). `processOutputStream` drops or rewrites chunks. `ctx.abort({ retry: true })` self-corrects with feedback. `processAPIError` can request controlled retry.

`AgentMiddleware`/`ChatMiddleware` mutate `AgentContext.messages` and can raise `MiddlewareTermination`; `FunctionMiddleware` mutates `arguments` and `result` around tool calls; `ContextProvider.before_run` injects instructions/context messages/tools/middleware. Sequential chain via `await call_next()`.

note: filter mutates input, output guardrail replaces
details: `call_model_input_filter` is the only first-class mutate-before-LLM hook (replaces `input`/`instructions`). `RunHooks`/`AgentHooks` are read-only (raise to abort). `@tool_output_guardrail` + `reject_content(message=...)` replaces tool results. No mutate-args hook for tool input; rely on `ctx.context` reads inside the function.

`callModelInputFilter` mutates `{ input, instructions }`. `RunHooks`/`AgentHooks` are read-only. `ToolInputGuardrail` can block but mutating LLM-emitted JSON args via a hook is not directly supported. `ToolOutputGuardrail` can replace results. Adequate but narrower than Mastra/CASDK.

Every stage exposes `before_*`/`after_*`/`wrap_*` variants. `SkipModelRequest(response)`, `SkipToolValidation(args)`, `SkipToolExecution(result)` short-circuit cleanly. `before_model_request` mutates the request; `before_tool_validate`/`before_tool_execute` mutate args; `after_tool_execute` returns replacement results. Fold semantics across hooks and recovery via `on_*_error`.

All seven `PromptHook` methods receive immutable refs (`&Message`, `&CompletionResponse`, `&str` args, `&str` result). The only control verbs are `HookAction::Terminate { reason }` and `ToolCallHookAction::Skip { reason }`. None of the three benchmark patterns (force args, rewrite results, message surgery) work — all require baking logic into the tool body or wrapping the agent.

note: writable events incl. tool_use/result, retry, resume
details: `BeforeInvocationEvent.messages`, `BeforeToolCallEvent.{cancel_tool, selected_tool, tool_use}`, `AfterToolCallEvent.{result, retry}`, `AfterModelCallEvent.retry`, `AfterInvocationEvent.resume` are all writable. Interrupts via `InterruptException`. Hooks can mutate `agent.messages` directly. Strong mutate+block surface.

`BeforeToolCallEvent` mutates `toolUse.{name,input,toolUseId}`, sets `selectedTool` to swap tool, `cancel`, or `interrupt(...)` for HITL; `AfterToolCallEvent.result` writable plus `retry`. `BeforeInvocationEvent`/`AfterInvocationEvent` can cancel or `resume`. `BeforeModelCallEvent` mutates `event.agent.messages`.

note: prepareStep mutates almost everything; tool result via toModelOutput
details: `prepareStep` returns overrides for `model`, `toolChoice`, `activeTools`, `instructions`, `messages`, `toolsContext`, `runtimeContext`, `providerOptions`, `sandbox`. `experimental_refineToolInput[name]` mutates tool args (Q6.4). Tool result mutation is per-tool only via `toModelOutput`; no harness-level post-tool mutate hook. `LanguageModelMiddleware.wrapGenerate` can block/retry/cache.

No automatic breakpoint placement. `model.LLMRequest.Config` (`*genai.GenerateContentConfig`) can include `CachedContent` (a Gemini feature) but you configure it by hand; no stable-prefix preservation policy ships.

Reports `cache_read_tokens`/`cache_write_tokens` in `Metrics` and surfaces them in `ModelRequestCompletedEvent`, but does not place Anthropic/OpenAI cache breakpoints. Stable-prefix arrangement (via `instructions` and `add_history_to_context`) is BYO.

`CacheLayer` in `crates/autoagents-llm/src/optim/cache.rs` is a response-level cache for identical message+tool+schema inputs, not a stable-prefix breakpoint mechanism. No `cache_control` markers; you would manage in your provider wrapper.

CLI handles Anthropic prompt-caching automatically; cache tokens surfaced on `AssistantMessage.usage`. `SystemPromptPreset.exclude_dynamic_sections` strips per-user dynamic sections out of the system prompt and re-injects them into the first user message — explicit support for cross-user multi-tenant cache amortization.

Three first-class mechanisms: (1) `Options.systemPrompt: string[]` with `SYSTEM_PROMPT_DYNAMIC_BOUNDARY` splits static cacheable prefix from dynamic suffix; (2) `excludeDynamicSections: true` strips per-user content for cross-user cache hits — the killer multi-tenant feature; (3) CLI auto-places breakpoints on stable-prefix content. Cache stats on `SDKResultMessage.usage`.

`mark_cache_breakpoint(message)` helper is auto-applied in `_setup_messages` to tag the system prompt and per-task user prompt as stable prefixes. Provider adapter translates to Anthropic `cache_control: {type: 'ephemeral'}`; OpenAI/Gemini cache implicitly. Solid but you cannot add your own breakpoints from a `before_llm_call` hook without re-applying the marker.

Provider-cache-aware indirectly: framework preserves message-list stability so Anthropic/OpenAI caching lands naturally on repeated prefixes. No first-class `cache_control` placement helper — engineers write it themselves via `schema.Message.Extra`. `TokenUsage.PromptTokenDetails.CachedTokens` lets you observe hit rate.
Plugin-specific not generic: `googlegenai/cache.go` lets you attach `cachedContents`. No generic `cache_control` mechanism across providers — each plugin handles its own cache features.

Engineers wire Anthropic `cache_control` flags into specific `SystemMessage`/`HumanMessage` content blocks; `pre_model_hook` is where you ensure the stable-prefix invariant. No automatic breakpoint placement.
`ChatMessage` supports a `CachePoint` content block which Anthropic/OpenAI providers honor — but the framework does not auto-place breakpoints; the developer inserts them. Not first-class.

Processor pipeline supports caching via `processLLMRequest` returning `{ response: <cached chunks> }` (skip LLM entirely). Built-in `ResponseCacheProcessor` ships. Anthropic-style cache breakpoints are not auto-managed — you place them in the system prompt yourself or via a processor.
No first-party prompt-cache breakpoint controller. Providers (Anthropic ChatClient in `agent-framework-anthropic`) set breakpoints internally; MAF exposes no generic stable-prefix knob.

`PromptCacheKeyResolver` generates a per-run cache key threaded through model settings to opt into OpenAI's prompt-caching pricing tier. Visible on `RunResult._generated_prompt_cache_key`. Anthropic `cache_control` not natively wired; via LiteLLM you pass provider-specific extras.

Passes `previousResponseId` to OpenAI's Responses API for server-side caching benefit but does not manage Anthropic-style `cache_control` breakpoints. `ai-sdk` extension inherits whatever the Vercel AI SDK provider supports.

Cache breakpoints first-class: `CachePoint` message part, `cache_write_tokens`/`cache_read_tokens` on `RequestUsage`, provider-specific model-settings flags (e.g. `bedrock_supports_prompt_caching`). `InstructionPart` is split into static vs dynamic so the stable prefix is cache-friendly by default. Placement still manual.

`Usage` exposes `cached_input_tokens` and `cache_creation_input_tokens` for observation but there is no automatic cache-breakpoint placement. You configure provider-side caching (e.g. Anthropic `cache_control`) via the provider's `additional_params`.

`system_prompt` accepts `list[SystemContentBlock]` including `cachePoint` blocks; `Message` content blocks also accept `cachePoint`. `BedrockModel`/`AnthropicModel` wire these through. Placement is manual but the AgentSkills plugin demonstrates a real strategy for preserving cache points while injecting skills XML.

Per-provider `Model.CacheConfig` with `strategy: 'auto' | 'anthropic'` — `auto` injects cache points after tools and the last user message. `CachePointBlock` content blocks carry markers; Bedrock and Anthropic wire it in; OpenAI doesn't need markers. More automated than Python sibling.

`LanguageModelUsage.inputTokenDetails` exposes `noCacheTokens`/`cacheReadTokens`/`cacheWriteTokens` — better visibility than most stacks. But the SDK does not place Anthropic-style cache breakpoints; you set them via `providerOptions` (e.g. `{ anthropic: { cacheControl: { type: 'ephemeral' } } }`) on a system message or via `LanguageModelMiddleware.transformParams`.
No first-party clearing primitive. `AfterToolCallback` can mutate the result `map[string]any` in place (e.g. replace with a pointer string), giving a manual path to clearing. BYO.

`compress_tool_results: bool` + `CompressionManager` compress tool outputs in place. `store_tool_messages: bool` drops tool messages from `RunOutput` entirely. Both are first-party knobs aimed exactly at this benchmark.
Tool results go directly into `MemoryAdapter::store_tool_interaction`; the only knob is the sliding-window size which evicts old messages but does not target tool results specifically.

`PostToolUse.updatedToolOutput` lets you replace a large tool output with a summary/stub before the model sees it (works for any tool since 0.1.74). Ergonomic and first-class; no separate filesystem-stash helper but the primitive itself is clean.

`PostToolUse.updatedToolOutput` (any tool) and `updatedMCPToolOutput` (MCP, deprecated) replace the tool result in-place before it reaches the model — the canonical use is truncating/summarizing/redacting. `getContextUsage()` and per-category breakdown help decide when to clear.
`after_tool_call` returns a `str` to replace the result — e.g. `return ctx.tool_result[:5000] + '... [truncated]'` for any oversized output. Manual but ergonomic; the docs show the exact pattern.
`adk/middlewares/reduction/` ships a built-in middleware that truncates oversized tool outputs in the message list and leaves a summary. First-party, zero-code, configurable. Best Go example.
Filesystem middleware has a `fileUnchangedStub` to short-circuit re-reads of unchanged files. No generic clearing/summarization primitive for tool results — BYO.

`wrap_tool_call` can rewrite the `ToolMessage` to a summary plus a pointer string; `BaseStore` is a natural stash. No first-party 'tool result clearing' primitive but the wrapper hook is general enough that the pattern lands in a few lines.
`FunctionTool(callback=...)` or `async_callback=...` can return a summary string and stash the full payload elsewhere. Manual; no first-party clearing primitive.

Tools declare `toModelOutput(output)` to return a truncated/summarized version to the LLM while persisting the full result in storage — sub-agent wrapper uses this exactly. `processOutputStream` can drop or rewrite `tool-result` chunks at the processor layer.

`ToolResultCompactionStrategy` explicitly clears or summarizes tool results once they exceed a threshold — a first-party compaction strategy dedicated to this benchmark row. Wired into `CompactionProvider` so it runs automatically.

`@tool_output_guardrail` with `reject_content(message=summary)` replaces a tool result with a synthetic message — usable for clearing/summary. Codex/Shell tools have `tool_output_trimmer` extension that truncates output before it goes back to the model. Solid but not branded as such.
`ToolOutputGuardrail` can replace the result via its `execute` return. No first-party tool-result-clearing primitive outside of Sandbox Agents (which have workspace files for large outputs).
`after_tool_execute` hook returns a replacement value (typically a summary instead of raw result). Hook-driven, clean to compose with the `tools=` filter. Ergonomic for any specific tool.
`on_tool_result` is read-only (`&str`, `&str`); you cannot rewrite the result. The only workaround is doing summarization inside the tool's own `call` body — i.e. not a framework feature.

`SlidingWindowConversationManager(should_truncate_results=True)` truncates large tool results to first+last 200 chars and swaps images for placeholders. Plus the vended `context_offloader` plugin. Two complementary first-party paths.

`ContextOffloaderPlugin` registers an `AfterToolCallEvent` hook that stores large payloads in configurable `Storage` keyed by `mem_<id>` and replaces in-context content with a preview + reference. Plus sliding/summarizing managers as a secondary path.
`tool.toModelOutput` lets you summarize at tool-author time but there's no harness-level 'after step N, drop the tool result from history' hook. `onToolExecutionEnd` is read-only. Per-tool only.

No artifact-handle pattern ships. Engineers can write to an artifact store inside `AfterToolCallback` and return a pointer string, but there is no first-party stash + summary + on-demand re-read primitive.

Skills are a textbook progressive-disclosure pattern: only skill metadata is in the system prompt; full body is fetched on demand via `get_skill_instructions`/`get_skill_reference`/`get_skill_script` tools. First-party and well-integrated.
No progressive-disclosure primitive — no skills, no filesystem stash, no lazy fetch. Tool outputs go straight into memory.

Skills register only metadata in the system prompt; full body is fetched on demand. Built-in `Read`/`Write`/`Edit` filesystem tools naturally encode the progressive-disclosure pattern (large outputs land on disk, model receives a path and can `Read` slices). No dedicated 'stash large tool result and return summary handle' primitive in the SDK itself — the pattern is straightforward to layer but not branded.
