Skills + file scratchpad pattern with built-in `Write`/`Edit`/`Read` (large outputs go to disk, model receives a path and `Read`s on demand). `getContextUsage()` per-category breakdown (system/tools/messages/MCP/memory/agents/skills/commands) supports decisions. MCP tool definitions deferred by default (`alwaysLoad: false`) so descriptions are not in the prompt until tool-search runs. Multiple complementary mechanisms.

Skills with `RESOURCES` disclosure level catalog file lists in the prompt — but the agent has to fetch contents via a separate tool you provide. No filesystem-stash/on-demand-re-read pattern shipped (no equivalent to Claude Code's `Read` with line numbers).

note: filesystem middleware for large tool results
details: `adk/middlewares/filesystem/large_tool_result.go` automatically stashes oversized tool results into the configured `filesystem.Backend` and replaces the tool message with a short reference plus a first-10-lines preview, then suggests the LLM use `read_file` with offset/limit for more. Closest match in any Go framework to Claude Code's progressive disclosure.
Filesystem middleware has a `fileUnchangedStub` to avoid re-reading unchanged files — narrow re-read elision, not a general stash+handle pattern. No skills handle catalogue or lazy fetch.

`wrap_tool_call` can rewrite the `ToolMessage` to a summary plus a 'full result available via <resource_id>' pointer using `BaseStore` as a natural stash. The mechanism exists but there is no first-party progressive-disclosure primitive — engineers compose it by hand.

note: stash via callback, no built-in pattern
details: BYO — `FunctionTool` `async_callback` can return a summary string while stashing the full payload elsewhere. No shipped stash+handle+re-read pattern; no skills metadata catalog.

Workspace + Skills system explicitly encourages the filesystem-stash pattern: a tool writes its full output to a workspace file and returns a short summary plus path; the LLM calls `skill_read` later to fetch slices. `toModelOutput` separates persisted full result from model-visible summary. First-class staged-handle architecture.

Skills follow the progressive-disclosure pattern: metadata-only in the prompt with the body loaded on demand via `load_skill`. First-party and integrates with `CompactionProvider`. Not as wide as Mastra/Eino's filesystem stash for tool results but the Skills pattern is core.

`defer_loading: bool` on `FunctionTool` hides the tool definition from the Responses API until `ToolSearchTool` loads it. Coupled with `ToolSearchCallItem`/`ToolSearchOutputItem` items — the LLM searches a catalogue and explicitly loads what it wants; the rest never enter the prompt. First-class progressive disclosure for tool catalogues.

Outside Sandbox Agents (which have a filesystem workspace for large tool outputs referenced by path), there is no progressive-disclosure primitive. Non-sandbox tools return their result string directly to the LLM.

Tool Search capability defers tool *loading* — tools marked `defer_loading=True` are included only after the agent calls `search_tools` (a meta-tool). Available native (Anthropic, OpenAI Responses) or local; `defer_loading()` on any toolset. Targeted at tool catalogue rather than tool result bodies, but first-class.
No filesystem-stash strategy, no auto-summarization of large tool outputs, no skills handle pattern. Use a `rig-memory` policy or implement on-the-fly truncation inside the tool body.

Vended `context_offloader` plugin is the explicit progressive-disclosure path: stashes large content out-of-context with a fetch-on-demand pattern. Plus `SlidingWindowConversationManager(should_truncate_results=True)` for in-place truncation. The offloader is the matching primitive.

`ContextOffloaderPlugin` stores full content in configurable `Storage` keyed by `mem_<id>`, swaps inline with preview + reference, and exposes a sibling `retrieve_offloaded_content` tool with grep / line-range access. Textbook lazy-fetch staged handle, first-party, plug-in shape.

`tool.toModelOutput` lets the tool author return a summary while keeping the full result in storage they manage — but there is no harness-level stash + handle + re-read primitive. No skills catalogue or deferred tool loading.

`memory.Service` interface with two implementations: in-memory keyword search and Vertex AI RAG. Namespaced per AppName+UserID. Population requires explicit `AddSessionToMemory` call (not automatic). The `loadmemorytool` is the agent-facing entry point. Usable but limited backends and manual lifecycle.

First-class `MemoryManager` with `enable_agentic_memory` (tool-call write/recall) and `update_memory_on_run` (auto-extract user facts). `UserMemory` rows keyed by user_id with topics, feedback, timestamps. Recall via `add_memories_to_context`. Production-ready out of the box.

No first-party long-term memory abstraction with persistence. `VectorStore` trait with in-memory and Qdrant backends plus embedding abstraction lets you build it. You write a `MemoryProvider` calling into the vector store yourself; no pre-built memory subsystem.

Memory limited to `CLAUDE.md` files loaded by the CLI when `setting_sources` includes `project`. `AgentDefinition.memory: 'user' | 'project' | 'local'` scopes which CLAUDE.md a sub-agent sees. No vector store, no embeddings, no semantic recall.

CLI surfaces memory files from `~/.claude/agent-memory/<agentType>/`, `.claude/agent-memory/`, and `.claude/agent-memory-local/`. `SDKMemoryRecallMessage` supports `mode: 'select' | 'synthesize'` — selector returns full file bodies, synthesizer returns a Sonnet-authored paragraph distilled from many tiny memories. No own vector index; for true vector-search RAG bring an MCP tool.

Sophisticated `crewai.memory.unified_memory.Memory` with LLM-driven `remember` (extract atomic facts, infer scope/categories/importance, consolidate above similarity threshold) and adaptive `recall` (deeper exploration when confidence low). Tunable recency/semantic/importance weights, hierarchical `root_scope`, LanceDB or Qdrant backends. First-class subsystem.

No `Memory` type, no `MemoryStore`, no auto-recall. You build cross-session memory by combining `components/retriever` (vector search) with a custom system-message-injection middleware. Primitives exist but assembly is host-built.

Genkit does not ship a memory abstraction (no semantic, episodic, or working memory). The closest pieces are `x/session` for state (not vector recall) and retrievers for query-time semantic search — but you must encode the memory yourself as documents.

`BaseStore` provides namespaced KV with optional vector search. Tools access via `runtime.store.put` / `runtime.store.search`. Vector search backed by Postgres pgvector (in `langgraph-checkpoint-postgres`) or in-memory. Memory shape and lifecycle policies are host-built but the primitive is first-class.

First-class `Memory.memory_blocks` accepts `BaseMemoryBlock` subclasses: `StaticMemoryBlock` (fixed system content), `VectorMemoryBlock` (vector search over past messages), `FactExtractionMemoryBlock` (LLM-extracted facts). Blocks processed in priority order; ejected short-term messages pushed into blocks. Comprehensive memory primitive.

`@mastra/memory` ships four memory modes: conversation history (per-thread log), working memory (LLM-summarized rolling notes per resource), semantic recall (vector-store-backed retrieval of relevant prior messages), and observational memory (patterns across many threads). Vector adapters for Pinecone, Qdrant, Chroma, Astra, Lance, Elasticsearch. Direct fit for the benchmark.

note: Mem0, Azure AI Search, harness store
details: Multiple first-party adapters: `agent-framework-mem0`/`Mem0Provider.cs` (beta), `agent-framework-azure-ai-search` as context provider, harness `MemoryFileStore`/`MemoryStore` (experimental, added 1.3.0), and .NET `TextSearchProvider` for generic text-search. Pluggable provider model. Some pieces still experimental/beta.

The 10 Session backends store conversation history at the turn level only. No vector-search-backed long-term memory primitive. For semantic recall you wire your own `@function_tool` over your vector store.

No built-in cross-session semantic memory. The only memory surface beyond `Session` (in-conversation history) is the Sandbox Agents `memory()` capability — a filesystem-backed scratchpad inside the workspace useful for cross-turn notes inside one sandbox run, not semantic recall across sessions.

Built-in `MemoryTool` is Anthropic-native with no in-tree local fallback — only works through providers that support the native tool. For provider-agnostic memory you fall back to third-party `pydantic-ai-memory` / `pydantic-ai-backend` capability packages, which are out-of-tree.

`ConversationMemory` is in-conversation only (linear history under a single id). For cross-conversation recall you combine `ConversationMemory` with `dynamic_context(sample, vector_store_index)` — the vector store is your semantic-memory substrate. No memory subsystem; you rebuild it via the RAG path.

Not in the SDK core but `strands-agents-tools` ships `mem0_memory`, `agent_core_memory`, `elasticsearch_memory`, `mongodb_memory`, and `memory` as explicit tools the LLM calls. Multiple production-grade backends available, but lifecycle/recall is LLM-driven via tool calls rather than automatic.
No vector store integration, no embeddings primitive, no memories/facts object. Cross-session continuity = re-hydrate from a `SessionManager` snapshot. Pure BYO.
No `Memory` class, no semantic-recall primitive. The SDK has no concept of cross-session memory. Reports contrast this with Mastra and LangGraph, which ship dedicated abstractions.

Vertex AI RAG via `memory/vertexai/` is the only first-party RAG adapter. No first-party Pinecone/Weaviate/Qdrant/pgvector integration — write your own `memory.Service` impl. `loadmemorytool` is the agent-facing RAG entry point. No built-in chunkers or rerankers.

note: Knowledge with many stores, embedders, readers
details: First-class `Knowledge` class with vector DB integrations (Chroma, Qdrant, Pinecone, Weaviate, Milvus, MongoDB Atlas, Lance, PgVector, Singlestore, Cassandra, ClickHouse). Embedders for OpenAI, Gemini, Cohere, Ollama, HuggingFace, Bedrock, Voyage, Mistral, JinaAI, AWS Titan. Readers for text, markdown, pdf, docx, csv, json, sitemap, website, S3, GCS. Filters let the agent choose at runtime; `search_knowledge=True` adds an automatic tool.

`autoagents-core` ships `VectorStore` trait (in-memory and Qdrant), embedding abstraction, document type, and PDF readers. Examples cover Qdrant and in-memory RAG agents. You assemble retrieval yourself but the building blocks are present.
No first-party RAG. Layer it as an MCP server or SDK tool. No vector store, chunker, retriever, or citation primitive.
Not first-party. No built-in vector store, chunker, retriever, or citation primitive. The supported pattern is defining an `mcp__myrag__search` tool that hits Qdrant/Pinecone/etc.

Separate `crewai.knowledge.Knowledge` subsystem. Source types: String, TextFile, CSV, JSON, PDF, Excel, Docx, CrewDoclingSource for general doc parsing, plus `BaseKnowledgeSource` for custom. Each source is chunked + embedded + stored. ChromaDB default with Qdrant supported. `EmbedderConfig` supports OpenAI, Azure, Cohere, HuggingFace, Bedrock. Set at Agent or Crew level.

First-class primitives: `components.retriever.Retriever`, `components.indexer.Indexer`, `components.embedding.Embedder`, plus `components.document.{Loader,Parser,Transformer}` for ingestion. Eino-ext adapters: Qdrant, Milvus v1/v2, Redis, OpenSearch v2/v3, Elasticsearch v7/v8/v9, Volc VikingDB, Dify, Volc Knowledge. Wired via graph nodes or wrapped as a tool. No first-party citation primitive.

Retrievers are an action type. Built-in plugins: `localvec` (in-process), `pinecone`, `weaviate`, `postgresql` (pgvector), `alloydb`, `firebase` Firestore. Plus chunkers, embedders (per model provider), and a `Reranker` abstraction (`RerankerRequest`/`RerankerResponse`). `ai.WithDocs` inlines retrieved docs as grounding/context blocks. Strong end-to-end primitives.

LangGraph does not ship its own retriever but the broader langchain ecosystem (Chroma, Pinecone, Weaviate, Postgres+pgvector) is separately packaged. `BaseStore.search()` covers basic semantic recall in-tree. No first-party chunking or citation primitive in the LangGraph package itself.

Historical core competency. 60+ vector store integrations under `llama-index-integrations/vector_stores/`. Index types include VectorStoreIndex, SummaryIndex, TreeIndex, KeywordTableIndex, KnowledgeGraphIndex, PropertyGraphIndex, ComposableIndex. Retrieval primitives `BaseRetriever`, `RouterRetriever`, `FusionRetriever`. Citations built in via `CitableBlock`/`CitationBlock`. Expose retrieval as `QueryEngineTool`.

`@mastra/rag` ships retrievers, chunkers (`recursiveChunker`, etc.), and citation support. Integrates with vector store adapters (Pinecone, Qdrant, Chroma, Astra, Lance, Elasticsearch). Full end-to-end RAG out of the box.

`TextSearchProvider` (.NET) is the generic primitive with `TextSearchProviderOptions`. For semantic search, plug it into Azure AI Search or any IR backend via `IVectorStore` (Microsoft.Extensions.AI.Vector). Strong Azure path but lighter coverage for non-Azure backends in-tree.

`FileSearchTool` integrates with OpenAI's hosted Vector Stores (re-exported from the OpenAI SDK). For non-OpenAI RAG you write a `@function_tool` that queries your own vector store. No chunker, embedder, or citation primitive in-tree.
`fileSearchTool` (OpenAI hosted file search over vector stores) is the closest built-in. Otherwise BYO retriever as a function tool. No first-party chunker/embedder/citation primitive.

Embeddings package with providers OpenAI, Cohere, Google, Bedrock, sentence-transformers, voyageai. RAG examples in docs. Vector stores are BYO (Chroma, pgvector, Pinecone). Framework focuses on the embeddings interface, not full retrieval/citations.

First-class `crates/rig-core/src/vector_store/`: `VectorStoreIndex` and `VectorStoreIndexDyn` traits, `InMemoryVectorStore`, and `EmbeddingsBuilder`. Companion crates: rig-mongodb, rig-lancedb, rig-qdrant, rig-sqlite, rig-surrealdb, rig-milvus, rig-scylladb, rig-postgres, rig-s3vectors, rig-helixdb, rig-vectorize, rig-neo4j. `agent.dynamic_context(num_samples, vector_store_index)` is the documented RAG path with automatic search + inline. No explicit citation primitive.
Via `strands-agents-tools/retrieve.py` (Bedrock Knowledge Base) and the memory tools. No first-party chunker or embedder primitives in the SDK. Bedrock-centric.

Not provided as a first-class subsystem. Build a retrieval tool: `tool({ name: 'retrieve', callback: async ({ query }) => doVectorSearch(query) })`. The `ContextOffloaderPlugin` is the closest built-in retrieval pattern (offloads tool results to disk/blob, exposes `retrieve_offloaded_content` for grep/page).

SDK ships `embed`/`embedMany` and `rerank` plus `cosineSimilarity` — but no vector store, no chunker, no retriever, no citation rendering. Use `@ai-sdk/langchain` or `@ai-sdk/llamaindex` for higher-level RAG primitives, or roll your own with a vector DB.

`SearchRequest.AppName` + `SearchRequest.UserID` give per-user scoping naturally. For tenant scoping, use `AppName` as the tenant key (paying the cost of fully-isolated memory across apps). Natural shape but not a dedicated tenant axis.

`UserMemory.user_id` is the scoping key. Per-tenant scoping means setting `user_id` to a tenant-prefixed value (`user_id='acme:alice'`) or filtering at query time using `metadata`. No dedicated tenant axis.
Not provided — BYO. You'd namespace your vector-store collections per tenant. No framework primitive.
Filesystem-shaped: per-tenant CLAUDE.md lives under `tenants/<tid>/CLAUDE.md` and the SDK loads it via `cwd`. Works but only as deep as the filesystem-only memory layer.

Memory dirs are global-per-machine (`~/.claude/agent-memory/`) or project-scoped (under `cwd`). To scope per-tenant: use a per-tenant `cwd: /tenants/${tenantId}` so memory lives under `.claude/agent-memory/`. For vector-DB cross-tenant memory, BYO an MCP tool.

Hierarchical `root_scope` is the natural fit: `Memory(root_scope='/tenant/acme')` scopes all `remember`/`recall` to that prefix. Different tenants need different `Memory` instances with different `root_scope` values. BYO wiring — no `Memory.with_tenant(id)` runtime filter.

Not automatic. `Retrieve(ctx, query, opts...)` receives ctx so you pass tenant scope through and the retriever adapter's `Options.SubIndexes` or query filter respects it. Framework does not enforce — the adapter does.

Not provided automatically. Retrievers accept a free-form `RetrieverRequest.Options` field you'd use to encode tenant filters (e.g. `Pinecone.namespace`, `Postgres WHERE tenant_id = $1`). Each plugin's `Retrieve` implements its own filter pass-through. No Mastra-style automatic namespacing.

Convention via `BaseStore` namespace tuples (`runtime.store.search((runtime.context.tenant_id, 'memories'), query=...)`). Critically, at the HTTP layer `@auth.on.store` injects the tenant prefix server-side so external API callers cannot escape it. First-class enforcement when running under the LangGraph server.

`Memory.session_id` is the only first-class scoping key. For per-tenant separation you encode `tenant:user:session` in `session_id` or use a per-tenant `SQLAlchemyChatStore` instance (different DB, table, or schema via `db_schema=`). No dedicated tenant axis.

Memory is naturally scoped per `resourceId` (in the `memory: { thread, resource }` tuple). The reserved `MASTRA_RESOURCE_ID_KEY` makes it server-controlled so a client cannot read another tenant's memory. For cross-tenant separation at the vector level, prefix index names with tenant id.
Memory adapters expose `scope` options (e.g., `Mem0ProviderScope` with values `User`, `Session`, `Global`). Tenancy = scope-by-user with your tenant ID encoded into the user. No deeper tenant axis.
BYO — namespace your vector indexes by `tenant_id`. No framework primitive for tenant scoping.
Not provided. You namespace yourself by setting per-tenant vector store IDs in `fileSearchTool(vectorStoreIds)`, or by partitioning your custom `Session` impl.
Per-tenant scoping is your responsibility — namespace by `tenant_id` in your vector index. No framework primitive.
Not first-class. You scope vector-store collections per tenant yourself (e.g. namespace by `tenant_id` in your Postgres/Qdrant schema).
BYO. The memory tools accept user/agent IDs but tenancy must be encoded in those IDs. No tenant axis.
BYO. Namespace your vector store / DB / S3 prefix by `tenantId` from `invocationState`.
BYO — namespace yourself in your vector DB (prefix keys with `tenantId:`, or use a separate index per tenant).

First-class SKILL.md loader (tool/skilltoolset/) following the agentskills.io v1.2 spec. YAML frontmatter (name, description, license, compatibility, metadata, allowed-tools) with strict validators and a standard skill-name/SKILL.md plus references/, assets/, scripts/ layout enforced at load time.

Top-level Agent.skills parameter backed by libs/agno/agno/skills/. SKILL.md uses YAML frontmatter (name, description, license, metadata, compatibility, allowed-tools) and validate_skill_directory enforces required fields plus optional scripts/ and references/ subfolders.

AutoAgents has no SKILL.md analogue, no Skill trait, no skills directory convention. The framework's only abstractions are Rust agent structs and tools; a markdown workflow skill would have to be hand-rolled outside the framework.

Skills are a native concept in the underlying Claude Code CLI; the Python SDK exposes only the skills option to filter them (types.py:1812-1830). The SDK itself does not define or validate the SKILL.md schema, but markdown skills with YAML frontmatter (name, description, tools) are the canonical Claude Code format.

Same as the Python SDK — SKILL.md with YAML frontmatter is the canonical Claude Code format, but it is CLI-validated, not SDK-validated. The TS SDK only surfaces an Options.skills filter and an SDKSystemMessage.skills field.

lib/crewai/src/crewai/skills/ is a full subsystem (parser, loader, validator, models). SkillFrontmatter is a frozen Pydantic model enforcing name regex, length limits, directory-name match, plus optional allowed-tools, metadata, license, compatibility. Standard scripts/, references/, assets/ layout.

First-class via adk/middlewares/skill/. SKILL.md uses YAML frontmatter typed as FrontMatter struct (name, description, context mode, optional agent/model). Markdown body is the skill instructions or sub-agent prompt; closest match in any Go framework to Claude Code's SKILL.md model.

Skills middleware (plugins/middleware/skills.go) reads SKILL.md with YAML frontmatter, but the schema is minimal: only name and description are typed (skillFrontmatter struct, skills.go:78-82). No license, compatibility, allowed-tools fields; body has no validated schema.

Grep for SKILL.md, loadSkills, class Skill across libs/ returns zero matches. Skills (a la Claude Code's SKILL.md) are not a first-class concept; engineers BYO via BaseStore + pre_model_hook or by routing through the separate langgraph-deepagents template repo.
LlamaIndex has no SKILL.md analogue. The closest community offering is LlamaPacks, but those are pip-installable codebases, not lightweight markdown workflow skills.

Mastra implements the Anthropic Agent Skills spec end-to-end (cited at workspace/skills/types.ts:7). SkillMetadata is fully typed (name, description, license, compatibility, user-invocable, metadata), validateSkillMetadata enforces the schema, and skills support local, external, and managed content sources.

First-class _skills module (Python 3269 LOC, .NET 10 files) aligned with the agentskills.io spec (ADR 0021). SkillFrontmatter validates name, description, license, compatibility, allowed_tools, metadata. Standard SKILL.md plus references/, assets/, scripts/ layout. Marked experimental at the package level.

Skill BaseModel (sandbox/capabilities/skills.py:401) implements the canonical SKILL.md frontmatter, but skills are scoped to sandbox / shell execution rather than as general workflow templates. Standard scripts/, references/, assets/ fields supported.

Skills are a SandboxAgent capability only (sandbox/capabilities/skills.ts). SKILL.md with YAML frontmatter is parsed via parseSkillFrontmatter; SkillDescriptor types name, description, content, scripts, references, assets, compatibility, deferred. Outside SandboxAgent the concept does not exist.

No in-tree SKILL.md loader. The in-tree analog is AgentSpec YAML (agent.yaml) loaded via Agent.from_file. The third-party pydantic-ai-skills package implements the agentskills.io standard but ships outside the core framework.

Rig has no SKILL.md primitive, filesystem scanner, or WorkspaceSkills equivalent. The word skill does not appear in the documented API; the closest analogs are ToolDefinition.description and Agent.preamble, both hand-rolled.

AgentSkills vended plugin (vended_plugins/skills/) implements the agentskills.io spec. SKILL.md with YAML frontmatter (name, description, allowed-tools, metadata, license, compatibility) is validated by _validate_skill_name and directory-name match (lenient or strict mode).

AgentSkills vended plugin (@strands-agents/sdk/vended-plugins/skills) compatible with Claude Code's SKILL.md. YAML frontmatter validated by Skill.fromContent: name regex, length limits, allowed-tools, license, compatibility, metadata. Directory-name match enforced.

The packages/ai/src/upload-skill package is only a thin relay to Anthropic's /v1/skills HTTP endpoint. The SDK never reads SKILL.md from a local filesystem, has no frontmatter schema, no SDK-side skill loader, and no skill concept beyond passing an opaque providerOptions.anthropic.skills array.

Toolset exposes three first-class tools (list_skills, load_skill, load_skill_resource) plus a system-prompt XML listing of skill name+description appended on every request (toolset.go:107-117). Agent discovers via the injected list and invokes via load_skill.

Hybrid invocation: metadata (name, description, scripts list, references list) injected as <skills_system> XML in the system prompt; bodies fetched via auto-generated get_skill_instructions, get_skill_reference, get_skill_script tools. The Anthropic Agent Skills pattern, fully realized.

CLI exposes a built-in Skill tool to the model; calling Skill(name=X) loads the SKILL.md body into the conversation. Observable from Python as ToolUseBlock(name=Skill). Discovery is CLI-driven and gated by options.skills filter; SDK does not expose programmatic registration.

Same Claude Code mechanism as the Python SDK: skill list (name+description) injected in the system prompt; LLM invokes by emitting tool_use with name Skill. Filtered by Options.skills; SDKSystemMessage.skills surfaces the filtered set.

Loaded skills are rendered directly into the agent's system prompt via format_skill_context wrapped in <skill name=...> tags. No first-class read_skill or load_skill tool — once activated, the full instructions live in the prompt and resources are only listed (not auto-fetched).

Pluggable Backend interface exposes a single skill tool (renameable) to the LLM. Three invocation modes via frontmatter context field: inline (returns markdown body), fork (spawns sub-agent with skill as system message), fork_with_context (sub-agent inherits parent history).

Middleware injects a <skills> system prompt block listing names+descriptions and exposes a use_skill(skillName) tool. Calling it reads the SKILL.md from disk and returns the body as the tool result. Filesystem rescanned on each Generate call.

No skill discovery or invocation primitive in the framework. BYO via BaseStore + pre_model_hook to inject skill bodies as SystemMessage, or a custom skill_read tool — every piece must be built by the host.
No skill invocation mechanism in the framework. The closest first-party mechanism is tool_retriever on a FunctionAgent for dynamic tool retrieval, but those are tools, not skills.

Three first-class tools (skill, skill_search, skill_read) plus a SkillsProcessor that injects <available_skills> XML metadata into the system prompt with an explicit instruction. Adds BM25/vector/hybrid search across skill content — beyond the basic load mechanism shipped by other stacks.

Three tools surfaced to the LLM per ADR 0021: load_skill (fetch body), read_skill_resource (fetch supplementary file), run_skill_script (execute a script, only registered when any skill has scripts). Skill names+descriptions also injected into the system prompt.

Skill metadata injected as a ### Skills section in the system prompt; for lazy mode a synthetic load_skill tool is added. Invocation is system-prompt instructions plus shell/file-read access in the sandbox — not a dedicated skill tool per Mastra's model.

Capability.instructions injects an available-skills section into agent instructions; when lazy, a load_skill tool materializes a skill on demand into .agents/<skill>/. Eager mode materializes everything up front.

No in-tree skill invocation. AgentSpec capabilities load eagerly at construction. Third-party pydantic-ai-skills SkillsCapability reportedly uses progressive disclosure via a skill_read tool, but the framework itself does not ship a skill invocation primitive.
No skill invocation primitive in Rig. The LLM only sees what is in the preamble or dynamic_context; there is no skill-as-tool or skill-as-hook mechanism.

Hybrid: <available_skills> XML block injected into the system prompt with name+description+location, plus a skills(skill_name) activation tool that returns full instructions and a listing of bundled resource files. Activated skills are tracked in agent.state and persist across turns.

Same pattern as the Python plugin: BeforeInvocationEvent hook injects <available_skills> XML into the system prompt; a registered skills tool accepts skill_name and returns the full body. Activation tracked in agent.appState across turns.

Invocation is provider-side (Anthropic). The LLM internally decides when to consult the skill body; the SDK only passes an opaque providerOptions.anthropic.skills array. Neither tool call nor SDK-side system-prompt injection from the user perspective.

Only frontmatters (name+description) are appended to the system prompt; bodies are fetched only when the agent calls load_skill, and resources only via load_skill_resource. Matches Claude Code's lazy loading model.

Body never enters the system prompt — only metadata does. agent_skills.py:117-125 explicitly documents the Browse / Load / Reference / Scripts progressive workflow. Bodies and references are fetched only on tool invocation, including a get_skill_script tool with optional subprocess execution.

Frontmatter (name+description) goes in the system prompt; full body loads on Skill(name=X) invocation. Confirmed by ContextUsageResponse.skills exposing the frontmatter breakdown. Driven entirely by the underlying CLI.
Same as Python SDK: metadata in system prompt, body fetched on Skill tool use. Options.skills filters which skills appear in the prompt. Driven by the underlying Claude Code CLI.

Three disclosure levels (METADATA, INSTRUCTIONS, RESOURCES) in skills/models.py:24, but once a skill is activated the full instructions are written into the system prompt. Resources are only listed in the prompt, not auto-fetched, so it is half-progressive: prompt-eager for activated skills, lazy for resource files.

Tool description sent to the LLM enumerates available skills (name + 1-line description) via renderToolDescription; the full markdown body is only loaded when the LLM invokes the skill tool. Keeps initial context small with hundreds of skills.
System prompt lists available skill names+descriptions only; body fetched only when LLM calls use_skill(skillName). Files are read on every invocation (no in-memory cache between Generate calls).
No skill primitive, hence no progressive disclosure. BYO patterns (vector search + pre_model_hook, or a skill_read tool) can implement it but the framework provides nothing.
No skill loading mode. tool_retriever provides progressive disclosure for tools, but not for markdown skill workflows.

Only <available_skills> metadata is injected via SkillsProcessor; bodies are fetched via the skill tool, resources via skill_read with optional line ranges, and skill_search with BM25/vector/hybrid is offered. Stateless: if context is compacted, the model calls again.

Skill names+descriptions go into the system prompt (~100 tokens per skill per ADR 0021); bodies fetched on demand via load_skill, resources via read_skill_resource, scripts via run_skill_script. Standard Anthropic progressive-disclosure model.

Both eager (Skill(...) inlined, scripts/references/assets materialized into sandbox) and lazy (LazySkillSource exposes index up front, body fetched via load_skill tool) supported. Progressive-disclosure prompt explicitly tells the LLM to open scripts/ instead of retyping code.

Two modes: eager (materialize everything into .agents/<skill>/ and show full metadata) and lazy (lazyFrom: localDirLazySkillSource shows only the index; LLM calls load_skill to materialize). Skills can also be marked deferred.

AgentSpec loads everything eagerly at construction (config, not a runtime catalog). The third-party pydantic-ai-skills plugin reportedly does lazy loading via a skill_read tool, but that is not in-tree.
No progressive disclosure for skills. Closest BYO would be dynamic_context with a vector store of skill embeddings to RAG-select snippets at prompt time.

Only descriptions and names appear in the system prompt up-front; bodies loaded on demand via the skills tool. Activated skills tracked in agent.state['agent_skills']['activated_skills'] and survive across turns in a session.
Only metadata (name+description+location) goes into the system prompt; body fetched on-demand via the skills tool. Activation tracked in agent.appState[stateKey].activatedSkills.
Progressive disclosure happens entirely server-side at Anthropic; the SDK only stores an opaque skillId. No way to inspect or steer disclosure from the SDK.

Standard skill-name/SKILL.md plus references/, assets/, scripts/ layout is first-class. Composition via MergedSource lets you stitch sources together (errors on duplicates), and a skill body can reference its own bundled files. No first-class skill-includes-skill mechanism — bodies must call each other through tool descriptions.

Skills bundle scripts/ and references/ as first-class (validated via validate_skill_directory). get_skill_script can read or execute (subprocess) bundled scripts with path-traversal protections. No imports: [other-skill] in frontmatter; cross-skill composition is text-driven only.

Cross-skill references are implicit via skill bodies that mention each other, plus plugins (SdkPluginConfig) which bundle multiple skills, plus AgentDefinition.skills which scopes which skills a sub-agent sees. No SDK-side composition primitive — bundling lives at the CLI/plugin layer.

Can reference other skills via plugin-qualified names (<plugin>:skill-name per sdk.d.ts:1708). Can call sub-agents (skill body decides). Bundled assets accessed via Read/Bash on relative paths inside the skill directory. CLI-layer composition; SDK does not add primitives.

scripts/, references/, assets/ directories are first-class with RESOURCES disclosure level cataloging them in the prompt. But they are not auto-fetched: the LLM needs a Read tool to access them. No skill-imports-skill mechanism.

Strongest composition story: fork mode lets a skill spawn a sub-agent that itself has tools, sub-agents, and skills (full recursion). Skill body can reference files in its BaseDirectory passed via the sub-agent's instruction template. Skills can call other skills if the sub-agent has the skill middleware installed.

use_skill reads the SKILL.md body and returns it as the tool result; no first-class scripts/, references/, or assets/ subfolders in the loader. Composition is purely text-driven via skill bodies that mention other skills.
No skill composition primitive.
No skill composition primitive.

Skills bundle references/, scripts/, and assets/ as first-class; skill_read accesses any path with optional line ranges and binary detection. skill_search across content (BM25/vector/hybrid) lets skills find each other indirectly. No skill-imports-skill directive.

Skills ship references/ and assets/ alongside SKILL.md plus scripts/*.py executed via a pluggable SkillScriptRunner, with optional require_script_approval HITL gating. AggregatingSkillsSource / FilteringSkillsSource / DeduplicatingSkillsSource enable source-level composition. No extends: mechanism between skills.

Skill model has typed scripts, references, assets dicts. Progressive-disclosure prompt explicitly instructs the LLM to open scripts/ and reuse assets/. Skills do not cross-reference each other directly, but a body can mention other skill names for the LLM to load.

SkillDescriptor carries scripts, references, assets entries. Sources include inline, filesystem dir, and gitRepo. Injected instructions explicitly steer the LLM to load only specific reference files and reuse scripts/assets. Lazy loader can request loading another skill at runtime.

CombinedCapability allows ordering and overlap of capabilities — a capability can ship its own toolset, hooks, instructions, native tools, model settings. But skill-to-skill includes and bundled-asset directories are not first-class; an AgentSpec file can reference filesystem paths without an enforced layout.
No skill composition primitive.

Skills bundle scripts/, references/, assets/ which are listed in the activation response (capped at maxResourceFiles, default 20). Skills cannot directly call other skills, but the activated instructions can instruct the LLM to invoke other skills via the skills tool (text-driven chaining).

Skills bundle scripts/, references/, assets/ subdirectories; activation response includes a listing capped at maxResourceFiles (default 20). LLM reads them via separate file-reading tools. Skills cannot directly reference other skills or call sub-agents.
Anthropic's skill bundle may include scripts and references, but the SDK has no knowledge of them and no composition rules. From the SDK's view, the entire skill is an opaque providerReference.
Three first-class mechanisms: agents-as-tools (agenttool.New), workflow agents (parallel/sequential/loop), and LLM-driven transfer_to_agent handoff. Sub-agents are an integrated part of the runner.

First-class Team primitive auto-injects delegation tools (delegate_task_to_member, forward_task_to_member, broadcast). Four orchestration modes (coordinate/route/broadcast/tasks) cover most fan-out patterns out of the box.

No SubAgent/handoff/delegate primitive. Multi-agent is expressed via actors subscribing to a shared runtime Topic; parent publishes a Task and matches TaskComplete events by sub_id/actor_name. Agent-as-tool wrapper is BYO.

Sub-agents are first-class via the CLI's built-in Task tool plus AgentDefinition (description, prompt, tools, model, skills). Parent LLM emits a tool_use that the CLI dispatches; sub-agent runs its own loop with isolated context.

First-class via CLI's built-in Agent tool (renamed from Task in 0.3.142) + AgentDefinition. Configurable from inline Options.agents map or markdown files under .claude/agents/. Can't disable the special semantics.

Two awkward paths: Crew with hierarchical process + DelegateWorkTool (LLM picks coworker), or Flow @start/@listen with explicit Python orchestration. No first-class agent-as-tool primitive for in-process fan-out. A2A protocol adds heavyweight cross-org option.
Three first-class mechanisms: SetSubAgents handoff, NewAgentTool wrapper, and workflow agents (Sequential/Parallel/Loop). Prebuilt patterns supervisor/deep/planexecute layered on top.
No SubAgent/handoff/delegate primitive. Idiomatic pattern is to write a tool whose execute body internally calls genkit.Generate with a different prompt+tools. No agent registry or markdown manifest.

No first-class SubAgent/handoff primitive. Subgraphs are added as nodes or wrapped as tools (langgraph-supervisor third-party). Static compile-time registration; flexible but require state-schema design.

First-class AgentWorkflow + can_handoff_to declarative handoff graph (auto-injected handoff tool), plus agents-as-tools by wrapping .run() in a FunctionTool. Configuration is Python-only (no markdown manifest).

First-class agents field on Agent (statically, dynamically per request, or via SubAgent interface). Runtime synthesizes agent-<name> tools via listAgentTools(). Network mode wraps supervisor pattern explicitly.

Agent.as_tool() in Python wraps any agent as a FunctionTool. .NET adds SubAgentsProvider exposing six tools (StartTask, WaitForFirstCompletion, GetTaskResults, etc.). Workflows also offer declarative orchestration via WorkflowBuilder.
Two first-class mechanisms: Agent.as_tool() and typed Handoff with HandoffInputFilter. Both fully integrated into the runner; no special-tool hack.

Both handoff (synthesized transfer_to_<agent> tool) and Agent.asTool() are first-class. asTool exposes structured parameters and customOutputExtractor; handoffs switch state._currentAgent in the loop.
Agent delegation pattern: parent has a @tool whose body calls await child_agent.run(...). No first-class Task/Swarm primitive in core; agents can be loaded from spec files (Agent.from_file).

Agent<M> implements the Tool trait directly (agent/tool.rs:16-50), so parent_agent.tool(child_agent) registers the child as a normal tool. Single mechanism (agents-as-tools); no handoff, workflow, or transfer primitive.
Multiple first-class mechanisms: agent.as_tool() for LLM-driven fan-out, Graph for deterministic DAGs, Swarm for collaborative handoff, plus A2AServer for cross-process orchestration.
Three first-class patterns: agent.asTool() (auto-applied when an Agent is passed in tools[]), Graph DAG with parallel scheduling, and Swarm with structured HandoffResult. Comprehensive coverage.

No subAgent/handoff/delegate primitive in the SDK. The endorsed pattern is BYO: wrap a child ToolLoopAgent.generate() inside a tool({ execute }). No registry, no markdown manifest, no runtime integration.
ParallelAgent uses errgroup goroutines (parallelagent/agent.go:82-99); agents-as-tools dispatched in parallel by Flow.handleFunctionCalls. Two complementary parallelism paths covered.
Sync delegate_task_to_members iterates members sequentially. Async adelegate_task_to_members uses asyncio.gather for fan-out, so you must use team.arun and an async model to get concurrency.

Each actor receives published messages in its own tokio task; subscribers process concurrently after the publish loop returns. Parallel is the natural mode; no dedicated parallel-agent primitive but pub/sub gives it for free.

Parallel sub-agent fan-out is first-class in the CLI; the SDK ships _SubagentContextMixin for hook attribution when multiple sub-agents interleave on the control channel. background flag and stop_task add explicit control.

Parent LLM can emit multiple Agent tool_use blocks in one turn; CLI dispatches them concurrently and fires PostToolBatch once with the full batch. background:true and TaskOutput polling add explicit control over async sub-agents.

Sequential by default. Crew hierarchical picks one delegate at a time. Native executor explicitly runs only the first tool per turn (crew_agent_executor.py:649). Parallel persona fan-out requires hand-rolled Flow + asyncio.gather.
ParallelAgent runs sub-agents via sync.WaitGroup + goroutines (workflow.go:471-516). Agents-as-tools also parallel by default through ToolsNode. Strong coverage with explicit framework-level fan-out.

Within a single Generate call, tool dispatch fans out via goroutines (go/ai/generate.go:957-999). If the parent LLM emits 3 sub-agent tool calls, they run concurrently. No parent-level rate limit and no dedicated parallel primitive.

Send API dispatches each item to its own task (PregelRunner.tick). create_react_agent v2's tools node uses this to run multiple tool calls in parallel. Strong primitive but you assemble the graph yourself.

AgentWorkflow itself is serial (single active agent). Parallel fan-out happens through agents-as-tools: the parent LLM emits parallel tool calls and the workflow runtime executes them concurrently via @step + ctx.collect_events.

Sub-agent invocations are tool calls dispatched via foreach(toolCallStep, { concurrency: 10 }). Concurrency drops to 1 only when approval/suspend is in play. Parallel by default, opt-out via requireApproval.

SubAgentsProvider (.NET) is concurrent — StartTask is non-blocking, WaitForFirstCompletion blocks on any. Python _execute_function_calls iterates sequentially; provider-driven parallel tool calls only help when the model emits them.

When the LLM emits multiple as_tool calls in one turn, execute_function_tool_calls dispatches them concurrently bounded by max_function_tool_concurrency. Programmatic fan-out is BYO via asyncio.gather; no swarm()/fan_out() helper.
Multiple asTool invocations in one turn dispatch in parallel via Promise.all up to toolExecution.maxFunctionToolConcurrency. Strong default behaviour.
Parallelism is whatever you write — asyncio.gather(child_a.run(...), child_b.run(...)) inside the parent tool. No built-in Promise.all wrapper or WaitGroup-style primitive.

Parent loop uses buffer_unordered(self.concurrency) (agent/prompt_request/mod.rs:695), so multi-tool turns run in parallel up to the configured concurrency. Default concurrency=1 (sequential); requires opt-in via with_tool_concurrency.
ConcurrentToolExecutor creates asyncio.Task per tool call by default. Graph layers run concurrently via asyncio.gather. Comprehensive parallel coverage; Swarm is sequential by design.
Parent uses toolExecutor:'concurrent' by default with Promise.race scheduler. Graph schedules ready nodes up to maxConcurrency:Infinity with AND-edge semantics. Strong default fan-out.
No SDK-level fan-out primitive. Parallel sub-agent execution is hand-rolled inside the parent tool body via Promise.all. Multiple tool calls within a single step are parallel at the parent level.
Sub-agent configs (system prompt, tools, model) cannot be generated by the LLM on the fly. SubAgents []Agent is set at agent.New time and immutable thereafter.

Members must be pre-registered. members can be a Callable[..., List] factory for per-request resolution under host control, but the parent LLM cannot author a new sub-agent with a custom system prompt.
Each agent is a Rust type with #[agent(...)] macro. No markdown configs, no inline per-call configs, no runtime synthesis.

AgentDefinition is a dataclass the Python harness can build per-request per-tenant (no requirement that the dict be static at boot). The parent LLM itself cannot generate a new AgentDefinition mid-run, but host-side dynamic registration is supported.

Options.agents must be set at session start (or via on-disk markdown). The parent LLM can only choose subagent_type from registered agents — it cannot generate a fresh config with a custom system prompt. Deliberate Claude Code design.
Sub-agents must be statically registered (in code, YAML, or fetched from AMP repository at boot). DelegateWorkTool only lets the LLM pick among pre-registered coworkers.
Sub-agents must be constructed as Go structs before Runner.Run; no per-call inline. taskTool lets the LLM pick subagent_type from a fixed registry but cannot synthesize the agent itself.

Sub-agent configurations are inlined per call (Go code calling Generate with a persona's prompt). No agent registry or markdown format. Host can vary per request but the LLM cannot author a new sub-agent.
parent.add_node(name, agent) is build-time. No inline-per-call config. Closest is dynamic-model selection inside an existing sub-agent (chat_agent_executor.py:325-356).
Not first-class. You can build a FunctionAgent dynamically inside a tool, but there's no markdown-loader analogue to Claude's Task tool.

agents can be a DynamicArgument returning the map per request, enabling per-tenant persona fan-out. The LLM picks an existing agent-<name> tool; it can pass additional instructions/maxSteps/threadId/resourceId merged onto the sub-agent's defaults.
Parent LLM cannot create a new sub-agent with a custom system prompt at runtime. Sub-agents must be registered ahead of time. Workaround: BYO custom tool constructing Agent from a dict.
Sub-agent configs are static Python Agent objects. The parent LLM cannot synthesize a system_prompt for a fresh sub-agent at runtime. Would require BYO meta-tool.
Sub-agents are statically declared TypeScript at module load time. Closest is parameterizing via asTool({ parameters, inputBuilder }), but the sub-agent code itself is fixed.

Not directly. A capability factory can synthesize an Agent at runtime from ctx, but no built-in primitive lets the parent LLM author a sub-agent spec. Parent tool can call Agent.from_spec(dict) if you wire it.
Sub-agents are statically registered Rust structs built via AgentBuilder. The parent LLM cannot dynamically generate a sub-agent's preamble or toolset.
Not natively. strands-agents-tools provides use_agent.py letting a parent LLM call a tool that constructs a new Agent, but there's no in-loop primitive to synthesize a sub-agent description.
AgentConfig is fully programmatic — no markdown sub-agent file format. Swarm routes are dynamic (LLM picks agentId), but the set of agents is fixed at swarm construction.
No native support. A meta-tool can instantiate a ToolLoopAgent from LLM-provided arguments, but the SDK has no opinion or telemetry/streaming integration for it.

Each sub-agent gets a new InvocationContext with its own Branch field; events share storage but ContentsRequestProcessor filters by branch. agent-tool gets stronger isolation via a brand-new InMemoryService session (agenttool.go:168-198).

Each member call passes a copy of run_context.session_state (team/_default_tools.py:831) so mutations don't bleed back. All members share session_id; knowledge filters fall back to leader's if member has none.

Each agent owns its own BaseAgent with its own memory/tools/context. Parent's memory is not shared; isolation enforced by Arc<Mutex<Box<dyn MemoryProvider>>> ownership and no shared mutable state at the framework level.

Each sub-agent has its own transcript JSONL under subagents/agent-<id>.jsonl. Parent sees only final summary; sub-agent's system prompt is its own (AgentDefinition.prompt) and parent's context is not inherited.

Sub-agent starts fresh: only its own system prompt, optional initialPrompt, and its own tool catalog. Parent only gets the final result (or with forwardSubagentText:true, the intermediate text). Separate session subpath on disk.

Each Agent has its own executor.messages list — Crew agents do not share message history unless explicitly wired via context in Task.execute_sync. Delegated coworker receives only the task+context strings.

Parallel branches fork runContext (shared Values, isolated LaneEvents). agent-tool shares parent session values by default; transfer agents inherit the same context. ClearRunCtx is available for explicit isolation.

Sub-agent's Generate has its own Messages (whatever the parent's tool passes in); parent message history is not automatically inherited. Only context.Context flows through (so ActionContext propagates).

Not enforced — depends on how you design state_schema. Same schema means subgraph sees parent's full messages; own schema isolates except for explicit channel mapping. Command(graph=Command.PARENT) lets subgraph write to parent state.
Each sub-agent invocation via .run() gets its own Context by default — fresh memory, fresh state. Can opt-in to ctx=parent_ctx for sharing.

Sub-agent gets a sanitized copy of parent message history via stripParentToolParts (removes parent's tool-call/tool messages). MASTRA_THREAD_ID/RESOURCE_ID keys cleared so sub-agent writes to its own thread. Default-on isolation with reasonable inheritance.
as_tool(propagate_session=False) default gives fresh session; propagate_session=True forwards parent state. SubAgentsProvider runs each sub-task in its own session by default. Configurable isolation.

as_tool gets a fresh ToolContext derived from parent RunContextWrapper; sub-agent sees only the input string (or structured parameters). Handoffs are the opposite (full history, optional HandoffInputFilter).

Nested asTool runs share parent's RunContext.context, approvals, and usage by default (runContext.ts:140-152 _cloneSharedState). Useful if children should write back to a shared todo list, dangerous if you want strict separation.
By default each agent.run() gets a fresh RunContext and empty message_history — full isolation. To share, you explicitly pass message_history=ctx.messages or shared deps/usage.
Sub-agent starts with its own Vec<Message> (just args.prompt) — parent's history is not passed through. Enforced at agent/tool.rs:43-45 where self.prompt builds a fresh PromptRequest.

as_tool(preserve_context=False) (default) snapshots initial messages/state and resets before every invocation. Graph/Swarm nodes follow same pattern. Sub-agent doesn't see parent's agent.messages either way; only the input string crosses.

AgentAsTool.preserveContext defaults to false (sub-agent reloads initial snapshot before each call). Sub-agent does not see parent's agent.messages either way; only the input string crosses the boundary.
Each child ToolLoopAgent.generate() starts with whatever messages you give it. No automatic parent-context inheritance, no automatic redaction. Fully BYO behaviour.

Depends on mechanism: agent-tool returns last text event as {result: text} (schema-parsed if OutputSchema set, linked via FunctionResponse). Workflow agents stream events directly into parent iterator. Transfer relinquishes control entirely.

Each member produces a RunOutput re-injected as a tool result into the leader's loop. Four modes (coordinate synthesizes; route returns directly; broadcast concatenates; tasks decomposes a shared TaskList). Member runs linked via parent_run_id.

Sub-agent output reaches the parent only via Event::TaskComplete{sub_id, actor_name, result} on the runtime's event stream. No tool_use_id linkage because sub-agents are not modelled as tool calls. Parent must filter/assemble manually.
Parent LLM gets a single result string as ToolResultBlock on the next user message. Harness gets per-task TaskStarted/Progress/Notification messages with usage telemetry. Linked via tool_use_id.

Sub-agent result returns as tool_result block linked by tool_use_id, with a rich AgentOutput shape (totalTokens, durationMs, usage, toolStats, status). forwardSubagentText:true forwards nested assistant text with parent_tool_use_id linkage.

Crew delegation returns a single string ('the coworker's task output') wrapped as a tool-result message. Flow listeners receive Python values. No parent_tool_use_id linkage by default; A2A events carry parent IDs but only for A2A.

agentTool.InvokableRun returns the last assistant message content as a single string, linked via tool_call_id. Optional EmitInternalEvents:true streams sub-agent events up to parent iterator (UI-only, not in parent session).

Parent receives a single ToolResponse.Output (text or structured). Intermediate tool calls or token stream are not surfaced in parent's message stream — only as nested OTel spans. Linkage via ToolRequest.Ref/ToolResponse.Ref.

Pattern A: subgraph's final state becomes node's writes; reducer on parent's channels merges. Pattern B: ToolMessage.content string (sub-agent serializes), linked via tool_call_id. Flexible via state design.
agents-as-tools awaits .run() and returns result string linked via tool_id. AgentWorkflow handoff causes workflow to switch current_agent_name and continue; final result is an AgentOutput.

Synthesized agent-<name> tool returns structured {text, subAgentThreadId, subAgentResourceId, subAgentToolResults}. By default toolModelOutput strips to text, opt-in to includeSubAgentToolResultsInModelContext. Streams nested chunks via fullStream.

as_tool: parent receives a string as function_result content, linked via FunctionCallContent.call_id; intermediate observable via stream_callback. SubAgentsProvider: results pulled from SubAgents_GetTaskResults with status in SubAgentState.

as_tool returns nested agent's final_output as tool result string; custom_output_extractor lets you rewrite. Handoffs continue same RunResult. Linked via call_id; on_stream re-emits nested events as AgentToolStreamEvent.

asTool: nested agent's final output becomes function tool result (string by default, customizable via customOutputExtractor). Full nested RunResult exposed on FunctionToolResult.agentRunResult. Linked via tool_use_id.
Child returns AgentRunResult[OutputDataT]; parent tool returns .output or a string summary. Linkage to parent tool_use_id is implicit via ToolCallPart/ToolReturnPart pair.
Parent receives sub-agent's final String as a regular tool result, bound to the parent's tool_call_id. No streaming events bubble up; the parent only sees the sub-agent's terminal text.
_AgentAsTool.stream yields AgentAsToolStreamEvent for every intermediate event, then a ToolResultEvent with content=[{text:str}] or [{json: structured_output.model_dump()}]. Linked via tool_use_id.

asTool returns a ToolResultBlock containing either the sub-agent's structured output (JsonBlock) or a TextBlock of result.toString(). Linked via tool_use_id. Graph/Swarm aggregate into MultiAgentResult.

Whatever the tool returns. No automatic tool_use_id correlation between parent and child agents; you build that yourself. From the parent's perspective the child result is just the parent's tool's execute() return value.

BeforeAgentCallback/AfterAgentCallback fire and sub-agent events are forwarded into parent iterator. No dedicated 'sub-agent started/completed' event type — must infer from Author and Branch changes on consecutive events.
Dedicated TeamRunEvent enum emits MemberDelegationStarted, MemberDelegationCompleted, and propagates member RunStarted/ToolCallStarted/RunCompleted upward with parent_run_id set on each frame.

Parent sees TaskStarted, TurnStarted/Completed, ToolCallRequested/Completed, TaskComplete from child via the runtime's shared broadcast channel. Must filter by actor_id/actor_name/sub_id to attribute.

Dedicated TaskStartedMessage, TaskProgressMessage, TaskNotificationMessage with task_id, description, usage, status (added 0.1.46). Combined with SubagentStart/SubagentStop hooks, parent observes sub-agent lifecycle in flight.

SubagentStart/Stop hooks, TaskCreated/TaskCompleted hooks, plus SDKTaskStartedMessage/SDKTaskProgressMessage (with summary if agentProgressSummaries:true), SDKTaskUpdatedMessage, SDKTaskNotificationMessage on parent stream.
AgentExecutionStartedEvent/Completed/Error fire per agent execution. A2A delegation has ~30 events (A2ADelegationStartedEvent, A2AStreamingChunkEvent). Solid coverage.

callbacks.Handler.OnStart/OnEnd fire once per agent boundary; RunInfo.Component=ComponentOfAgent and Type distinguishes. Per-message sub-agent events not in parent iterator by default — opt in via ToolsConfig.EmitInternalEvents:true.

Sub-agent lifecycle observable via tracing only, not parent stream. OTel spans nest (parent generate → tool → sub-agent generate); parent's SSE stream shows just one toolResponse chunk for sub-agent's final answer.

stream_mode='tasks' emits TasksStreamPart start frame and TasksResultStreamPart finish frame per subgraph dispatch. With subgraphs=True parent stream sees (ns, mode, data) triples identifying the subgraph.
On handoff, AgentInput/AgentOutput/AgentStream events are emitted tagged with the new current_agent_name. Parent stream sees each sub-agent's tokens.

delegation.onDelegationStart/onDelegationComplete hooks (with bail to cancel siblings) and messageFilter for message routing. Sub-agent chunks streamed to parent fullStream as nested agent-execution-event-* chunks (network mode).
as_tool: stream_callback receives intermediate updates if provided. SubAgentsProvider: status retrievable via SubAgents_GetAllTasks but it's a pull API, not a streaming lifecycle.
as_tool(on_stream=callback) receives AgentToolStreamEvent for every inner event with the nested agent and tool_call reference. Parent stream can forward sub-agent progress events to its own consumer.
asTool({ onStream }) receives every RunStreamEvent from the nested run plus a reference to the toolCall that triggered it. Handoffs surface RunAgentUpdatedStreamEvent.
Parent stream does not auto-include child events. To bubble them, the parent's tool can iterate child.run_stream_events() and yield events back — custom code with no framework support.
No sub_agent_started/sub_agent_completed event. Parent loop sees only the eventual tool result. Tracing spans inside the sub-agent's prompt() are the only OTel-based observability path.

AgentAsToolStreamEvent forwards each child event to parent stream. Dedicated MultiAgent events for Graph/Swarm: MultiAgentNodeStartEvent, MultiAgentNodeStopEvent, MultiAgentHandoffEvent, MultiAgentNodeStreamEvent, etc.

Parent stream sees ToolStreamUpdateEvent carrying sub-agent's AgentStreamEvent (rewrapped at agent-as-tool.ts:171-175). Graph/Swarm have dedicated events: BeforeNodeCallEvent, AfterNodeCallEvent, NodeResultEvent, MultiAgentHandoffEvent.
Parent stream has no 'sub-agent started/progress/finished' event category. Child events live in its own streamText call and are not surfaced to the parent unless you explicitly writer.merge().
Each llmagent.New gets its own Model. Gemini Pro supervisor + Gemini Flash workers is the natural pattern. First-class.
Each Team.members[i] is an Agent with its own model. Supervisor Claude / worker Haiku is straightforward and well-supported.
Every AgentBuilder takes its own Arc<dyn LLMProvider>. Sonnet supervisor + Haiku workers wire naturally on the same runtime.
AgentDefinition.model='haiku' etc. — canonical pattern: Sonnet supervisor + Haiku workers. First-class.
AgentDefinition.model is exactly this knob (sdk.d.ts:56). Set to 'haiku' for cheap workers, leave parent on 'opus'. Required-but-trivial for tenant cost control.
Each Agent has its own llm. Building a Sonnet supervisor + Haiku workers crew is trivial via the manager_agent pattern.
Each ChatModelAgentConfig.Model is independent. Supervisor on claudeOpus + worker on claudeHaiku wired via SetSubAgents. First-class.
Trivial: since sub-agents are tools that internally call Generate, each can specify a different WithModelName. Supervisor on gemini-2.5-pro, persona workers on gemini-2.5-flash.
Each subgraph (sub-agent) built with its own model argument; Sonnet-supervisor + Haiku-worker is the standard pattern.
Each sub-agent in AgentWorkflow has its own llm (multi_agent_workflow.py:140). Orchestrator-on-Sonnet, workers-on-Haiku is straightforward.
Every sub-agent declares its own model. Supervisor Opus + workers on Sonnet/Haiku is the canonical pattern.
Each sub-agent can be constructed with its own ChatClient (Sonnet supervisor + Haiku workers via agent_as_tool composition). Implicit but well-supported.
Each Agent has its own model field, so a supervisor on gpt-5.1 can dispatch to a worker on gpt-5-mini via as_tool() or handoff.
Agent.asTool({ runConfig: { model: 'gpt-5.4-mini' } }) and handoff-target agents can each pin their own model. Example in examples/agent-patterns/agents-as-tools.ts:33-39.
Each Agent instance carries its own model; agent delegation can mix any models. The docs note USD computation may be limited when mixing providers.
Each sub-agent is a separate Agent<M> and can be on a different model than the parent (since the parent wraps the sub-agent via agent/tool.rs:16-50). Implicitly first-class.
Each sub-agent (whether as_tool(), Graph node, or Swarm node) carries its own model — Sonnet supervisor with Haiku workers is straightforward.
Each sub-agent has its own model config. Standard pattern: const supervisor = new Agent({ model: sonnet, tools: [haikuWorker] }).
Trivial: since sub-agents are BYO, you just instantiate each ToolLoopAgent with whatever model you want.

Ships a Source loader interface and a MergedSource for composition, but no registry, no publish/promote/retire lifecycle, no governance. Treats skills as the only resource and lets you BYO sources. Closest informal versioning is checking skills into git.

Has a Registry dataclass that catalogs tools, models, dbs, agents, teams (lookup helpers only, no register API) plus a separate Components subsystem with versioned configs (drafts + current + history) exposed via /components HTTP router. Real but partial — skills themselves are not managed by the Registry.

No Registry, no SkillSource, no plugin marketplace, no versioning, no publish workflow. Only an MCP TOML config loader for MCP servers exists, which is a local-filesystem loader for one resource type, not a general resource manager.

No registry, no source abstraction, no publishing workflow. The SDK's resource manager is the filesystem layout plus the setting_sources flag (user/project/local) and the SdkPluginConfig type=local plugin entries. options.skills/agents/plugins filter per request.

Filesystem-only discovery from .claude/skills/, .claude/agents/, .claude/commands/, plus plugins: SdkPluginConfig[] (only type='local'). Query.reloadPlugins() and Query.setMcpServers() are mid-session refresh APIs. No registry layer, no publishing workflow.

OSS ships local-only skill loader and BaseProvider/StorageBackend abstractions. Agent(from_repository='<slug>') fetches agent configs from CrewAI AMP (closed, paid). No unified registry for skills + sub-agents + prompts + tools in OSS.

Provides pluggable interfaces (skill.Backend, skill.AgentHub, skill.ModelHub) and ships only the filesystem Backend. No platform-level registry — you build a Resource Manager on top of these seams. None are layered, scoped, or versioned by default.

The only registry is the in-process *registry.Registry holding actions (tools, models, prompts, retrievers) for one running process — a runtime concept, not a publishing concept. Skills/prompts are loaded from local filesystem or embed.FS only.

OSS ships only BaseStore (put/get/search/list_namespaces/delete) as a 'resource as a row' abstraction — closest is namespace tuples like ('skills', tenant_id, ...). LangGraph Platform's Assistants API is the actual resource manager but sits behind paid hosting.

No registry, no source abstraction, no skill/resource concept. Tools are loaded from Python imports or via a tool_retriever. LlamaHub is a community directory of LlamaPacks but offers no draft/review/promote workflow.

Skills have a real resource-manager layer: VersionedSkillSource + CompositeVersionedSkillSource + blob storage, content-hashed refs, local>managed>external priority. Stored agents/skills track visibility (private/public), favoriteCount, and ownerId. Still no first-class draft to review to publish to promote pipeline.

Ships SkillsSource abstraction with Aggregating/Filtering/Deduplicating/Caching wrappers for both Python and .NET (FileSkillsSource, InMemorySkillsSource). Loader-level composition works, but no platform layer above — no draft/active/retired lifecycle, no publishing workflow, no RBAC.

No registry abstraction. Has LazySkillSource/LocalDirLazySkillSource for filesystem skills and MultiProviderMap for model routing, but no skills/agents/prompts registry. Agent and sandbox capability objects are constructed at boot.

Per-SandboxAgent manifest.entries supports localDir, localFile, dir, file, and gitRepo({repo, ref}) sources — including a real Git source. But it is per-agent only, no cross-agent registry, no versioning beyond git refs, no marketplace.

AgentSpec.from_file(path) and Agent.from_spec({...}) are single-source loaders for one agent at a time. No registry, no source composition, no publish workflow. MCP servers count as a runtime resource source.
The only "registry" is the ToolSet, a HashMap<String, ToolType> in process memory, plus ToolServerHandle::add_tool/remove_tool for runtime mutation. No skill, sub-agent, or prompt resource model.

AgentSkills(skills=[...]) is a thin loader with filesystem paths or HTTPS URLs and a ToolRegistry for tools. No registry abstraction over many skills/sub-agents/tools across teams. Closest to a resource model is the load_tools_from_directory hot-reload from ./tools/.
AgentSkills wraps a Map<string, Skill> with four loader sources (instance/dir/parent-dir/URL). No Registry, no ResourceManager, no versioning, no RBAC, no per-tenant scoping at registration time.
customProvider() and createProviderRegistry() are model registries (string-keyed lookup like registry.languageModel('openai:gpt-5')). No skills, sub-agents, prompts, or tools registry.

Filesystem source works over any fs.FS including embed.FS; preload wrappers (WithCompletePreloadSource, WithFrontmatterPreloadSource) cache in memory. Git, OCI, cloud blob, Postgres, HTTP, vendor registry are all BYO via implementing skill.Source.

LocalSkills(path) for skills (filesystem only). Knowledge content can live in Postgres via Knowledge(contents_db=...) and sessions/memories/traces/components are DB-backed. Git, OCI, cloud blob, vendor registry, HTTP are BYO.

The only first-party loader is the MCP TOML config (crates/autoagents-toolkit/src/mcp/config.rs:45), which reads MCP server definitions from a local TOML file. Everything else (filesystem skills, git, S3, Postgres, vendor registry, HTTP) is BYO.

Loads from cwd, .claude/, ~/.claude/ via setting_sources plus SdkPluginConfig type=local for plugin dirs. No git, OCI, cloud blob, DB, HTTP, or vendor registry sources for skills. SessionStore adapter touches S3/Postgres/Redis but only for transcripts.

Loads from ~/.claude/skills/, .claude/skills/, .claude/agents/, .claude/commands/, plus plugins (only type='local'). MCP HTTP/SSE/Stdio servers are dynamic tool sources via Options.mcpServers. SessionStore can use Postgres/Redis/S3 for sessions but not for skills.

Local filesystem for skills (skills=[Path(...)]), inline Python and agents.yaml for sub-agents, prompt_file for prompts. Agent(from_repository='<slug>') fetches from CrewAI AMP via HTTPS. No git, OCI, cloud blob, or Postgres source abstraction.

Ships only filesystemBackend via NewBackendFromFilesystem(ctx, &Config{BaseDir}). Git, OCI, cloud blob, Postgres, vendor registry, HTTP all require BYO implementations of skill.Backend. Agent and Model hubs are also BYO.

Skills: SkillPaths []string for local filesystem. Prompts: WithPromptDir(path) or WithPromptFS(embed.FS, path) — mutually exclusive. No git, OCI, cloud blob, Postgres, vendor registry, or HTTP sources for skills/prompts. Postgres works for embeddings via alloydb/postgresql plugins.

OSS supports local filesystem via Python imports and Postgres via BaseStore (the closest 'resource as a row' abstraction). LangGraph Platform's Assistants API is a vendor-managed registry but paid. No native git, OCI, cloud blob, or HTTP source.
Tools are loaded from Python imports or via a custom tool_retriever the user wires in. No first-class concept of 'load a skill from S3/GCS/Git'. Integration packages are versioned PyPI distributions.

Local filesystem for skills, VersionedSkillSource backed by BlobStore (S3/GCS/R2 adapters), Postgres via storage.getStore('agents'/'skills'/'favorites'), Mastra Cloud via deployers/cloud package. Git and HTTP are BYO.

FileSkillsSource and InMemorySkillsSource ship in both Python and .NET, plus AggregatingSkillsSource, FilteringSkillsSource, DeduplicatingSkillsSource, CachingSkillsSource wrappers. Git, S3/GCS/Azure Blob, OCI, vendor managed registry, and HTTP are all BYO via SkillsSource subclassing.

LocalDirLazySkillSource(source=LocalDir(...)) for filesystem skills. agents.sandbox.entries.GitRepo materializes a Git repo into the sandbox at run time, but it loads into the sandbox not into the SDK process. Cloud blob, Postgres, OCI, vendor registry, HTTP not provided.

Per manifest.entries supports localDir, localFile, dir/file (inline), and gitRepo({repo, ref, subpath}) — including a real first-class Git source that clones into the sandbox session. OCI, cloud object storage, Postgres, vendor registry, HTTP are not provided.

AgentSpec.from_file(path) and Agent.from_spec({...}) for filesystem/in-memory; MCPServerStdio, MCPServerSSE, MCPServerStreamableHTTP for tools via MCP. Git, OCI, S3/GCS/Blob, Postgres, vendor registry, HTTP fetch all BYO.

rig::loaders (crates/rig-core/src/loaders/file.rs) reads local files but not as a 'resource registry'. rig-s3vectors and rig-postgres are vector stores, not resource sources. Git, OCI, cloud blob (as resource source), vendor registry, HTTP all unsupported.

AgentSkills(skills=['./skills/']) for local filesystem; Skill.from_url('https://...') for arbitrary HTTPS skill loading; load_tools_from_directory=True for tool hot-reload from ./tools/. Git via clone-then-point; OCI, cloud blob, Postgres, vendor registry not provided.
AgentSkills has four sources: instance (programmatic), dir, parent-dir, and HTTPS URL via Skill.fromUrl (naive fetch, 30s timeout, no ETag). Git, OCI, S3/GCS, Postgres, vendor registry not provided.

No resource source loader for skills/sub-agents/prompts. createProviderRegistry and customProvider are model registries (string-keyed). Filesystem, git, OCI, cloud blob, Postgres, vendor managed registry, HTTP all BYO.

NewMergedSource queries sources in order; LoadFrontmatter/LoadInstructions/LoadResource return the first source that succeeds (earlier sources have priority). ListFrontmatters errors on duplicate skill names (ErrDuplicateSkill), so explicit 'tenant overrides global' requires a custom subtract/fallback wrapper.
Skills(loaders=[a, b, c]) loads all three; on name collision the later loader wins with a logged warning (agent_skills.py:42-44). No 'S3 source overrides Git source for tenant X' declarative pattern.
No source abstraction means no composition. Each MCP server is independent in the TOML config; no precedence/override semantics across sources.

Layered by setting_sources: user (~/.claude/) -> project (<cwd>/.claude/) -> local (settings.local.json), all three load by default. Plugins add another layer. The CLI defines conflict-resolution internally; the SDK does not expose precedence configuration.

Documented Settings cascade: --settings CLI > project local > project committed > user-global > managed. Resources from plugin-bundled + project + user + managed, project wins over user; same-name later-loaded wins. reloadPlugins() re-scans the disk after changes.

Loader iterates skill paths in order and de-duplicates by skill name (agent/core.py:451), so first occurrence wins. De facto composition but not declared; reverse the path order to override. No 'tenant overrides global' semantic.

Not provided as a primitive — you implement a layered Backend that merges multiple backends and applies your own priority logic (e.g. tenant wins over global by composing two skill.Backend instances).

For skills middleware: SkillPaths scanned in order, later entries with same name overwrite earlier ones via map mutation in scanSkills. For prompts: WithPromptFS and WithPromptDir are mutually exclusive (no composition).

BaseStore.search() takes a namespace tuple; you implement 'tenant > global' override by trying ('skills', tenant_id) first and falling back to ('skills', 'global'). No first-class layered source primitive.
Tools come from Python imports or a user-provided tool_retriever; no source-composition primitive at the framework level.

Explicit priority order local > managed > external (workspace-skills.ts:207). CompositeVersionedSkillSource mounts multiple versioned skill trees into a virtual filesystem with optional fallback to a live filesystem source for actively-edited skills.

AggregatingSkillsSource concatenates sources; DeduplicatingSkillsSource keeps first-occurrence when names clash; FilteringSkillsSource applies a predicate after aggregation. Priority is by ordering sources in the aggregator. No declarative priority/override (local > tenant > global) — you choose by order.
With no source abstraction, no composition primitive exists. All resources are Python objects constructed at boot.
A SandboxAgent has one defaultManifest; merging is cloneManifest + processManifest at capability level. No local > tenant > global cascading across manifests; per-manifest only.
Resource sources do not compose. Capabilities compose at the Agent level via CombinedCapability, but that is at the runtime composition layer rather than at a source-priority layer.
With no source abstraction, no composition exists. ToolSet has last-insert-wins by HashMap insertion but that is not a configured composition primitive.

_resolve_skills processes sources in order, later occurrences overwrite earlier ones with a logged warning on duplicate name (agent_skills.py:319-358). No declared priority order or override semantics.
Sources processed in order; a duplicate name overwrites the earlier one with a warning (agent-skills.ts:191-194). No priority/fallback/merge configuration.
No mechanism to stack sources for skills/sub-agents/prompts. You build any priority/override logic yourself.

No version field on Frontmatter. Compatibility is a free-text 500-char string with no enforcement. Versioning is whatever your filesystem/git provides; bake a version suffix into the directory name or use commit SHA.

Components have agno_components (definition) + agno_component_configs (versioned configs with drafts + current + history) and Schedules have agno_schedule_runs. Skills only have a descriptive metadata.version field; the framework does not pin or rollback skills by version.
No per-skill or per-tool versioning. Cargo handles crate versions but not artifact-level versioning.
No first-party versioning. The CLI version itself is pinned via _cli_version.py (e.g. 2.1.143); skill and agent versioning is the file mtime on disk.

Skills/sub-agents in plugins are versioned by the plugin's own git tag (the directory the plugin came from). No semver enforcement, no content-hash addressing, no immutable refs, no rollback API. To 'roll back' a skill: replace the file on disk and call Query.reloadPlugins().

No first-class versioning in OSS — no version field in SKILL.md frontmatter, no content-hash, no immutable refs, no rollback. AMP Agent Repositories support versioning in the dashboard but no API field for 'pin to version' in from_repository='...'.
Skills are mutable files or rows; no semver, no content-hash refs, no rollback. You build versioning in your backend.
Skills, prompts, tools are versioned by your source-control and deployment. No @semver, no content-hash, no immutable ref system in the framework.
OSS has no versioning model. LangGraph Platform's Assistants API ships versioned assistants but is paid hosted only.
Integration packages have their own PyPI semver in CHANGELOG.md, but agent resources (skills, sub-agents, tools) have no versioning — they live in your codebase.

Per-call versions via MASTRA_VERSIONS_KEY in request context for sub-agents and 'future primitives'. VersionedSkillSource uses SkillVersionTree manifest with content-hashed blob refs. No semver-based registry but immutable content-hash refs.
Skills have no version field beyond SkillFrontmatter.compatibility (free-form text). No semver, no content-hash, no immutable refs, no rollback.
Skill.compatibility: str | None is an opaque marker. The SDK does not enforce semver, content-hash, or immutable refs.
gitRepo({ ref }) lets you pin a Git ref (branch, tag, or SHA). No semver registry, no content-hash addressing beyond what Git provides, no rollback primitive shipped.
Capabilities are versioned per PyPI package (semver) and per-spec by your VCS. No content-hash, no immutable-ref system in-tree.
No versioning for skills, agents, or tools. ToolSet is mutated at runtime.
Skill metadata.version is a free-form field; the loader does not interpret it. Tools have no versioning at all.
Skills have no version field that the SDK reads. UUIDv7 snapshot IDs are used for session checkpoints, not for skills.
No semver, no content-hash, no immutable refs, no rollback for skills/sub-agents/prompts.

Source.ListFrontmatters(ctx) accepts a context so you can write a TenantAwareSource that dispatches per-tenant. Composition works via per-tenant Source + MergedSource(globalSrc, tenantSrc). No first-party TenantAwareSource and no publish-time tenant/scope field on Frontmatter — both layers are BYO.

Skills are constructed once at Agent construction; per-tenant catalogs require building a callable factory for agent.tools or constructing multiple agents per tenant. No publish-time scoping at the registry layer and no built-in Skills(filter=lambda run_context: ...) runtime hook. Components have JWT-based RBAC but no per-tenant publishing workflow visible.
No registry-side or runtime scoping primitive.

No registry-side scoping. Runtime per-tenant scoping requires materializing tenants/<tid>/.claude/skills/ and setting options.cwd + setting_sources=['project']. options.skills is acknowledged as a 'context filter, not a sandbox' (types.py:1826-1830) — files remain accessible to Read/Bash. Not safe for tenant isolation of sensitive logic.
