No publish-time scoping (no registry). Runtime scoping via Options.skills filter or per-tenant .claude/skills/ tree with cwd at the tenant root. No tenantId -> skills mapping API; same gap as Python SDK.

Scoping is by Agent construction with filesystem path (skills=[Path('./skills/acme')]) — different agents per tenant. No Agent.set_active_skills([...]) mid-run, no per-tenant filter, no publish-time tenant scoping. AMP RBAC is org/role granularity, not per-tenant-per-skill.

The Backend interface gets ctx context.Context on every List/Get so you can filter by tenant from ctx (filterByTenantPolicy). No first-class skill-scope field in FrontMatter — you add it in your backend metadata or sidecar file. Registry-side scoping is fully BYO.

Per-call runtime scoping via SkillPaths in ai.WithUse(&middleware.Skills{SkillPaths: [global, tenants/<id>]}). Different requests can attach middleware with different paths. No publish-time scoping — everything registered with genkit.DefineTool/DefinePrompt is global to that *genkit.Genkit instance.
BYO via BaseStore namespace tuples (e.g. ('skills', 'global', ...) vs ('skills', tenant_id, ...)). Convention only — no first-class scope or visibility primitive in OSS.
No registry-side or runtime scoping primitive. You write your own loader feeding tool_retriever or tools=[...].

Runtime scoping via SkillsResolver as a function reading requestContext (e.g. ctx.requestContext.get('userTier')). Stored agents/skills have visibility ('private' | 'public') and ownerId at the storage layer (since 1.35.0). RBAC + FGA under ee/ gate read/write/execute on stored entities. No explicit publish-time 'tenant X only' tag on skills.

Runtime scoping via FilteringSkillsSource(predicate=lambda s: tenant_id in s.frontmatter.metadata.get('tenants', '').split()). No publish-time tenant tag — you encode tenancy in metadata.tenants and filter against it. Requires constructing a SkillsProvider per tenant.
Per-agent, per-instance at construction time (or agent.clone(tools=[...])). No dynamic per-turn filtering of skills like there is for tools (is_enabled callable). No publish-time scoping.

Different defaultManifest per SandboxAgent or options.sandbox.manifestPatch override at run time. No built-in tenant-aware skill catalog and no registry-side scoping; you compose a manifest yourself based on runContext.context.tenantId.

Dynamic capabilities via factory reading RunContext: a callable user_skill(ctx: RunContext[str]) returns AbstractCapability or None per run (docs/capabilities.md:990-1024). Genuine runtime scoping primitive, with durable-execution caveats. No publish-time scoping.
No registry-side or runtime scoping primitive.

Per AgentSkills instance: one plugin per tenant, or mutate plugin.set_available_skills([...]) between invocations (affects all agents sharing the plugin instance). No publish-time scoping; all filtering is runtime.

Per-Agent: AgentSkills attaches to one agent and all invocations on that agent see the same catalog. Per-tenant requires creating one AgentSkills instance per tenant. Skill.allowedTools is parsed but explicitly not yet enforced (experimental).
BYO. You track skillId-tenant mapping in your DB and conditionally pass providerOptions.anthropic.skills per runtimeContext.tenantId.

No draft/active/deprecated/retired lifecycle states. Skills are either in the filesystem the Source reads or not. Multi-environment promotion is done via separate git branches or buckets per env — entirely operational.

Only for Components subsystem: POST /components to create, PATCH /components/{id} to update, POST /components/{id}/configs to add a new config version, POST /components/{id}/configs/{version}/set-current to promote — a draft to current model with version history. No separate staging environment baked in. Limited to components, not skills.
No publish/promote/retire workflow.
No publishing workflow. Multi-environment story is operational (separate git branches, separate buckets per env).
No draft -> review -> publish -> promote pipeline. You build it yourself with a Git repo per tenant for .claude/ trees, CI that publishes to per-tenant S3 buckets, and a sync agent on each pod.

AMP dashboard has a draft -> published flow for Agent Repositories. AMP Automations have dev/staging/prod separation via separate deployments + environment variables (docs/en/enterprise/features/automations.mdx). No formal approval gates documented. OSS has no publishing concept — git push your skill directories.
No draft/review/promote/multi-environment workflow. Build with git tags and your own CI.
No draft/active/deprecated states, no review/approval gates, no promotion across environments. Skills are source code shipped with your binary.
OSS has no publishing workflow. LangGraph Platform's Assistants API can be considered the publishing workflow but is paid hosted only.
LlamaHub site is a directory of community LlamaPacks; it offers no draft/review/promote workflow.

No first-class draft -> review -> publish -> promote workflow shipped. mastra deploy and the deployers (cloud/Vercel/etc.) handle env promotion at the application level, not at the per-skill/per-agent resource level.
There is no draft -> active -> retired model. No publishing workflow shipped.
No publishing workflow.
No draft/review/publish/promote stages, no multi-environment story.
Capabilities are published as PyPI packages by convention (docs/extensibility.md). No staged dev/staging/prod environments, no approval gates.
No publishing workflow.
No draft -> review -> publish -> promote pipeline. Git is the de-facto control plane.
No publishing workflow.
No draft/review/publish/promote, no multi-environment, no approval gates.
No lifecycle states, no RBAC, no approval workflow. Operational tooling only.

Component configs have versions and a 'current' pointer; old versions can be deleted via DELETE /components/{id}/configs/{version}. RBAC is scope-based via JWT (require_resource_access). No approval workflow, no publisher/reviewer roles, no automatic retirement.
No lifecycle states, no RBAC.
No lifecycle states, no RBAC on publish/scope/retire. Track in your own DB and enforce in your own UI.
No lifecycle states, no RBAC on publish/scope/retire.

OSS: none. AMP: RBAC with predefined Owner/Member roles plus custom roles (docs/en/enterprise/features/rbac.mdx). Entity-level permissions on automations, env vars, LLM connections, Git repos. No formal lifecycle states (draft/active/deprecated/retired) for skills or agents.
No lifecycle states (draft, active, deprecated, retired), no RBAC at the resource layer.
No RBAC, no audit log of who published what, no retirement workflow. Consistent with the 'skills are source code' philosophy.
OSS does not ship lifecycle states or RBAC at the resource layer. LangGraph Platform has organization-level access controls outside OSS.
No lifecycle, no RBAC.

Stored agents/skills have visibility (private/public) and favoriteCount fields (since 1.35.0). RBAC + FGA under ee/ gate who can read/write/execute stored entities. No explicit draft/active/deprecated/retired lifecycle state on skills themselves.
No RBAC, no lifecycle states.
No draft/active/deprecated/retired states, no RBAC.
No draft/active/deprecated/retired states, no RBAC.
None in-tree.
No lifecycle, no RBAC.
No RBAC, no lifecycle states.
No states (draft/active/deprecated), no RBAC.
No lifecycle states, no RBAC primitives.

row: Built-in tools (web search, file ops, exec)
note: thin shipped catalog, BYO,Ships only function-tool primitives, sub-agent-as-tool, skill/memory/artifact loaders, MCP toolset
details: exit-loop/example tools. No bash/Read/Write/Edit/WebFetch/Grep/Glob/Monitor. Gemini's native code execution is reachable via geminitool wrapper but lives server-side. Catalog is intentionally tiny; you BYO everything tool-shaped via functiontool.New.

row: Built-in tools (web search, file ops, exec)
details: Over 130 tool modules under libs/agno/agno/tools/ covering web search (DDG/Brave/Google/Exa/Perplexity/Serper), code/file ops, git/messaging/cloud/browser/data backends, plus E2B/Daytona/Docker code sandboxes. Most are thin SDK wrappers but a few (file tools, code-exec) encode line-numbered/sandboxed patterns. Catalog breadth is among the widest in the survey though depth (no anchor-matched Edit, no Monitor-style streaming process) is shallower than Claude Code's bundled toolkit.

row: Built-in tools (web search, file ops, exec)
details: autoagents-toolkit ships filesystem primitives (read/write/copy/move/delete/list/glob), brave_search, wolfram_alpha, document parsing, plus a WasmRuntime and a CodeAct executor that runs LLM-authored TypeScript in an embedded Deno/rquickjs JS runtime. No bash, no anchor-Edit, no Monitor, no WebFetch. Tools are thin stdlib wrappers; the WASM/JS sandbox layer is the differentiator rather than tool depth.

row: Built-in tools (web search, file ops, exec)
details: The CLI ships the full Claude Code catalog (Read/Write/Edit/MultiEdit/Bash/Glob/Grep/WebFetch/WebSearch/Task/Skill/TodoWrite/Monitor) plus server-executed tools (advisor, web_search, web_fetch, code_execution, bash_code_execution, text_editor_code_execution, tool search). Tools encode the best practices the benchmark cares about: line-numbered Read, anchor-matched Edit, sandboxed Bash, Monitor that streams stdout. Highest-depth catalog in the survey, tied with the TS SDK.

row: Built-in tools (web search, file ops, exec)
details: ToolInputSchemas enumerates 25+ built-ins: Bash with run_in_background and sandbox flag, Read with offset/limit/pages, anchor-based Edit with uniqueness validation, Glob, ripgrep-backed Grep with full flag set, WebFetch/WebSearch (Anthropic-managed), Agent sub-agent with worktree isolation, TaskCreate/Get/Update/List/Stop/Output, NotebookEdit, Skill (lazy fetch), AskUserQuestion, ListMcpResources/ReadMcpResource, EnterWorktree/ExitWorktree, ExitPlanMode. Same battle-tested catalog as Claude Code interactive mode; the report calls it the strongest built-in tool surface in the comparison.

row: Built-in tools (web search, file ops, exec)
details: Around 80 tools in crewai-tools covering web search (Serper/SerpAPI/Tavily/Brave/Exa), heavy web scraping (Firecrawl, Scrapfly, Brightdata, Stagehand, Apify, etc.), file/document/vector backends, E2B + Daytona code sandboxes, vision/image, GitHub/arxiv, AMP/Composio/Zapier bridges. Depth is shallow: no bash in OSS (deprecated CodeInterpreter), no anchor-matched Edit, no line-numbered Read, no Monitor. Breadth is excellent but agent-aware patterns are thin.

row: Built-in tools (web search, file ops, exec)
details: eino core ships zero tools, but the filesystem middleware bundles ls/read_file/write_file/edit_file/glob/grep/execute with line-numbered reads, anchor-style edits, and an oversize-result-stash pattern. eino-ext adds MCP clients, DuckDuckGo/Google/Bing/SearxNG/Wikipedia/HTTP, commandline shell, browser automation, sequential-thinking. Broader by name than Claude SDK but shallower per-tool (no Monitor, simpler Edit, no auto-line-numbered Read across all tools).

row: Built-in tools (web search, file ops, exec)
details: Few built-ins: use_skill, plus filesystem middleware (read_file/list_files/write_file/edit_file) backed by Go 1.25 os.Root with symlink-safe paths, bounded reads (256KB chunks, 10MB cap), line-numbered Read, mtime/size guard on writes. No first-party web search, bash, fetch, glob, grep, or monitor. The FS tools are well-engineered but the overall catalog is intentionally small.

row: Built-in tools (web search, file ops, exec)
details: LangGraph core ships zero general-purpose tools. The hundreds of tools live in langchain-community / langchain-experimental which are separate packages. No bash/Read/Edit/Glob/Grep/WebFetch/WebSearch/Monitor in this repo. Closest is a BaseStore-access convention pattern.

row: Built-in tools (web search, file ops, exec)
details: llama-index-core ships no general-purpose tools; integration packages (~40) cover code interpreters (Azure, local), web search (Bing/Brave/Google/Tavily), web scraping (BrightData/Desearch), SQL, Cassandra, Box/Airweave, artifact editor, MCP. Core adds RAG-oriented QueryEngineTool/RetrieverTool/OnDemandLoaderTool. No Claude-Code-style anchor Edit, line-numbered Read, or Monitor; depth is shallow per tool.

row: Built-in tools (web search, file ops, exec)
details: Built-ins are limited to skill tools (skill/skill_search/skill_read with line-range slicing and BM25/vector/hybrid search), a MastraBrowser, workspace filesystem primitives, plus @mastra/rag and channel/voice tools. No bash/Edit/Read/Grep/Glob/Monitor in core. Mastra's stance is intentional: tools are app-specific.

LocalShellExecutor/DockerShellExecutor with ShellPolicy, env sanitization, network mode, head-tail buffering. Hyperlight Wasm sandbox tool. details: webSearchTool, fileSearchTool, codeInterpreterTool, imageGenerationTool, toolSearchTool, hostedMcpTool, computerTool — all hosted thin wrappers that emit HostedTool descriptors. Sandbox shell capability (tool.ts:92-165) manages local/container shells with skill bundles and network policies — the only substantive locally-executed surface. No Read/Edit/Write/Grep/Glob/Monitor; file ops only inside SandboxAgent workspaces.

Local fallbacks under common_tools/: DuckDuckGo, Tavily, Exa, web_fetch, image_generation. Auto-switches to native when the model supports it. No anchor-Edit, line-numbered Read, or Monitor — Pydantic AI stays out of the coding-agent tool surface.

row: Built-in tools (web search, file ops, exec)
details: Sole in-tree tool is ThinkTool, a pass-through echo of LLM thoughts. No Read/Write/Edit/Bash/Grep/Glob/Monitor/WebFetch/WebSearch. "You bring the tools" is the explicit stance — the framework's value is the typed Tool trait and the proc-macro authoring story, not the catalog.

row: Built-in tools (web search, file ops, exec)
details: strands-agents-tools (Apache-2.0 companion package) ships ~40 tools: calculator (AST-validated), current_time, file_read/file_write/editor (intelligent diff modes), shell, python_repl (with confirmation prompts), http_request, Tavily/Exa/BrightData web search, image/video/audio I/O, slack, multiple memory backends, retrieve/RAG, environment, cron, journal, swarm/agent_graph/graph/use_agent/use_llm for nested agents, mcp_client, batch parallel calls, browser/use_computer/use_aws, code_interpreter, load_tool, think, stop, sleep, handoff_to_user, a2a_client. Strong breadth; editor is intelligent though not anchor-matched like Claude Code.

row: Built-in tools (web search, file ops, exec)
details: Vended-tools directory ships only bash, file-editor, http-request, and notebook. No web search, glob, grep, monitor, or MCP-bundled tools. File editor lacks anchor-matching and line-number patterns that Claude Code popularized. Significantly lighter than the Python companion.

row: Built-in tools (web search, file ops, exec)
details: SDK ships no first-party tools — its stance is "you bring the tools, we run the loop." Built-ins exist only via @ai-sdk/mcp passthrough, provider-side tools (Anthropic computer use/web_search/bash, OpenAI Assistants/code-interpreter), @ai-sdk/gateway tools, and Experimental_Sandbox-backed exec. No Read/Edit/Bash/Glob/Grep/WebFetch/Monitor shipped by the SDK itself.

functiontool.New[TArgs,TResults] takes a typed Go function and auto-infers JSON schema via jsonschema reflection on struct tags. Per-tool RequireConfirmation (or dynamic provider), IsLongRunning, OnToolErrorCallback, InputSchema/OutputSchema overrides. Concise smallest tool (~5 lines + handler) with typed args/results. Strong DX for Go.

@tool decorator inspects signature + type hints + docstring (docstring-parser) and builds a Function Pydantic model with JSON schema. Decorator options include name, description, strict, instructions, show_result, stop_after_tool_call, requires_confirmation, requires_user_input, user_input_fields, external_execution, pre_hook/post_hook/tool_hooks, cache_results/cache_dir/cache_ttl. First-class typed tool authoring.

#[tool(name, description, input)] proc macro on a struct + async-trait ToolRuntime::execute impl. ToolInput derive generates io_schema; schemars optionally backs JsonSchema. Smallest tool is ~20 lines of Rust ceremony (struct, derives, impl block, serde_json::from_value). Typed but verbose.

@tool(name, description, schema) decorator with schema being a {name: type} dict, TypedDict (fixed 0.1.51), raw JSON Schema, or Annotated[type, 'description'] (0.1.52). Wrapped via create_sdk_mcp_server and routed through the SDK MCP JSON-RPC bridge. Clean and typed; one small extra step to wrap into an MCP server vs. a direct function-tool API.

tool(name, description, zodSchema, handler) is the canonical API; schema is Zod v3 or v4 used for both LLM-facing JSON schema generation and runtime validation. Wrapped via createSdkMcpServer and namespaced as mcp__server__tool. First-class typed authoring.

Subclass BaseTool with name, description, args_schema: type[BaseModel], _run(...). Auto-derives args_schema from _run signature if omitted. Built-in result_as_answer (ends loop on tool return), cache_function, max_usage_count, _claim_usage. @tool decorator also available. Strongly typed and ergonomic.

utils.InferTool(name, desc, fn) generic helper auto-infers JSON schema from Go struct tags (jsonschema/description). utils.InferOptionableTool for options-aware tools, utils.NewTool for manual schema, or implement tool.InvokableTool directly. Runtime validation via sonic unmarshal; errors propagate to model. Clean typed API.

genkit.DefineTool(g, name, desc, fn) takes a typed Go function; schema inferred via core.InferSchemaMap (jsonschema reflection over struct tags + jsonschema/description/enum). Supports WithInputSchema override, WithStrictSchema for OpenAI strict mode, ToolContext as first arg. Smallest tool is ~3 lines.

@tool decorator from langchain_core.tools auto-generates JSON schema from signature + docstring. Pydantic/dataclass arg classes supported. async def is supported natively. Subclass BaseTool for richer control with name/description/_run. Mature, ergonomic — Pydantic v2 validation on each call.

Two methods: pass a typed Python callable directly (FunctionAgent wraps via FunctionTool.from_defaults) or build FunctionTool.from_defaults with explicit name/description/callback/partial_params overrides. Schema auto-generated via create_schema_from_function using Pydantic. Runtime validation raises ValidationError caught and wrapped in ToolOutput(is_error=True).

createTool({id, description, inputSchema, outputSchema, execute}) takes Zod schemas for both input and output; JSON schema auto-generated. Supports requestContextSchema for tenant-context validation. Tools receive a typed ctx with writer/agent/abortSignal. First-class typed authoring with output schema validation, a step beyond most peers.

Python: @tool decorator over a function or class, optional input_model: type[BaseModel] for strict schema; Pydantic-validated. .NET: AIFunctionFactory.Create infers schema from C# parameter metadata + DescriptionAttribute. approval_mode declarative. Both runtimes are typed and ergonomic.

@function_tool decorator parses signature and Griffe-style docstring (griffelib) to build a Pydantic params model + strict-mode JSON schema. RunContextWrapper/ToolContext as first arg, needs_approval boolean or callable. Output types: ToolOutputText/Image/FileContent. Strict-mode default produces guaranteed-JSON. Best-in-class typed authoring.

tool({name, description, parameters, execute}) accepts Zod or JSON schema, builds a FunctionTool<Context, TParameters, Result> with strict-by-default runtime validation. InvalidToolInputError routed through errorFunction so the LLM can self-correct. Generic over context, parameters, and result types — strongly typed and concise.

@agent.tool / @agent.tool_plain decorators on typed Python functions. Schema auto-derived from type hints + docstrings via _function_schema.FunctionSchema. RunContext[Deps] for typed dependency injection. ModelRetry mechanism turns Pydantic validation failures into structured retry prompts. Per-tool max_retries. Best-in-class Pydantic-native ergonomics.

Implement the Tool trait with NAME, Args: Deserialize, Output: Serialize, Error, definition(), and call() async methods. #[tool_macro] proc macro available via the derive feature. Static typing via generics but verbose: smallest example is ~30 lines of struct + impl. Typed but ceremonious.

@tool decorator extracts name, description, and JSON schema from signature + docstring + type hints (Pydantic-backed via create_model). tool_context: ToolContext parameter activates context-aware mode. Class-based tools implement AgentTool.stream returning a ToolGenerator. Pydantic-validated; invalid args yield ToolResult(status='error').

tool({name, description, inputSchema, callback}) accepts a Zod schema (runtime-validated) or a raw JSON schema (no validation; callback receives unknown). Subclass Tool for custom streaming. Concise and typed when Zod is used.

tool({description, inputSchema, execute}) with Zod 3 or 4 schema. Full surface includes contextSchema, onInputStart/Delta/Available, toModelOutput, needsApproval, outputSchema. Runtime validation via parseToolCall; experimental_repairToolCall can patch invalid calls before they surface to the LLM. First-class typed authoring.

Tool Run returns (map[string]any, error) — single-shot. IsLongRunning pauses the agent loop and emits LongRunningToolIDs but no mid-execution progress events back to the model. agent.LiveSession streams the LLM, not tool internals.

Tools can be Python generator functions; FunctionCall.execute detects isgenerator(result) and stores the generator (tools/function.py:1057-1064). The model adapter must consume it. There is no first-class "tool yields progress events to the LLM mid-execution" pattern — chunks are aggregated for the LLM.

ToolRuntime::execute returns a single Value, not a stream. A tool cannot yield progress events back to the model mid-execution. The execute signature has no Context access, so even out-of-band Event::SendMessage requires capturing a sender at tool construction time.

SDK MCP tool handlers must return a single {"content": [...]} dict — no streaming from third-party SDK MCP tools. The CLI itself streams tool output (e.g. Monitor) but that's only for built-in tools, not user-authored SDK MCP tools.

Partial support: Bash with run_in_background returns immediately and output is polled via TaskOutputInput.block:true. SDKToolProgressMessage emits elapsed_time_seconds heartbeats during long tool calls for UI rendering. Mid-execution partial results to the model itself are not supported — the LLM only sees the final tool_result block.

A tool's _run returns a single value (string or Any cast to string). No mechanism for a tool to yield partial results to the model mid-execution. Only option for long-running tools is to log progress to the event bus (or stdout) and return a single final string.

StreamableTool returns *schema.StreamReader[string] (components/tool/interface.go:53-57); the tool yields chunks the framework concatenates and forwards. EnhancedStreamableTool extends the same shape to multimodal results. First-class streaming.

Tool functions return (Out, error) after fully executing — no yield-style API for emitting partial results mid-execution. MultipartToolResponse can return multiple parts at the end, but not during. Long-running operations require a BackgroundModel pattern or polling on an Operation ID.

A tool that takes runtime: ToolRuntime can call runtime.stream_writer({"progress": 0.5}) to emit CustomStreamPart frames mid-execution (tool_node.py:1663-1730). Visible to clients on stream_mode='custom'. First-class progress streaming through the LangGraph event bus.

Tools receive the live Context and can call ctx.write_event_to_stream(...) inside the tool body to emit custom events to consumers mid-execution. Tools do not yield partial results back to the LLM mid-call though — the tool still returns a single value to the model.

Tools yield mid-execution progress via ctx.writer: ToolStream (packages/core/src/tools/types.ts:417), producing tool-output chunks in fullStream. Tools can also suspend(payload) via ctx.agent.suspend for HITL pauses with custom payloads. First-class streaming.

Tools cannot yield partial results to the model mid-execution (the LLM expects a single function_result content). The .NET FunctionInvocationDelegatingAgent exposes progress events to the surrounding agent stream so a UI can render in-flight progress, but this is UI-only and .NET-specific. Python has no equivalent.

Function-tool API returns when the async function returns — no yield-based incremental output to the model. Hosted ShellTool streams stdout deltas and ApplyPatchTool streams patch progress, but those are special-cased hosted-tool flows, not a generic API. Pattern for long-running tools: return a job_id and poll, or use a sub-agent.

execute returns a Promise<Result> — no yield-based incremental output to the model. Tools must buffer and return a single final string. For long-running tools the recommendation is to use HITL approval pause as a poor substitute.

Tools return a single value (sync or async). For "tool yields progress mid-execution", the recommended pattern is to call back into the parent agent loop via additional ToolCallPart/ToolReturnPart messages, or use deferred external execution (CallDeferred). No first-class yield API.
A tool's call returns one Output; there is no incremental yield mechanism for a tool to emit progress while running.

Tools return an AsyncGenerator; yielded values are wrapped as ToolStreamEvents (tools/executors/_executor.py:227-256) and surface to the agent stream. The final yield must be a ToolResult which the executor extracts. First-class streaming tools.

Tool callbacks can be async generators yielding ToolStreamEvent or arbitrary values (strands-ts/src/tools/tool.ts:93). Yielded values become ToolStreamUpdateEvents; the final return becomes the ToolResultBlock. First-class streaming tools.

Tool execute can return AsyncIterable<OUTPUT> (packages/provider-utils/src/types/tool-execute-function.ts:38). Each yielded chunk becomes a tool-output-available chunk with preliminary: true, then a final non-preliminary chunk. Useful for tools that progressively reveal output. First-class streaming.

No allow/deny list, no canUseTool, no sandbox. tool.FilterToolset only hides tools from the LLM. functiontool.Config.RequireConfirmation provides HITL approval but that's user-in-the-loop, not policy. No E2B/Daytona/Modal/Docker integration. Default-allow for everything registered.

@tool(requires_confirmation=True) HITL gate, tool_hooks can deny server-side, skill frontmatter allowed-tools, is_safe_path traversal protection, JWT scopes for RBAC at HTTP layer. E2B/Daytona/Docker tools all execute code in remote/isolated sandboxes. Default-allow for tools, default-deny for HTTP when JWT is configured. Multi-layered.

AgentHooks::on_tool_call returning Abort is the per-call allow/deny primitive — no per-tool allowlist data structure. WasmRuntime executes tools in a wasmtime sandbox. CodeActAgent runs sandboxed TypeScript via Deno AST + rquickjs. No E2B/Daytona/Modal integration. Default-allow. BYO sandbox is strong, ACL surface is thin.

SandboxSettings (types.py:873-916) controls macOS sandbox-exec / Linux seccomp bash sandboxing, with autoAllowBashIfSandboxed, excludedCommands, allowUnsandboxedCommands, SandboxNetworkConfig (allowedDomains/deniedDomains/allowManagedDomainsOnly/allowMachLookup). permission_mode ∈ {default, acceptEdits, plan, bypassPermissions, dontAsk, auto} where auto uses a model classifier and dontAsk denies anything not pre-approved. can_use_tool per-call interception. No E2B/Daytona/Modal adapters.

Full permission stack: canUseTool callback, PreToolUse hook with allow/deny/defer, PermissionMode (default/acceptEdits/bypassPermissions/plan/dontAsk/auto), PermissionRequest hook, declarative PermissionUpdate rules (addRules/replaceRules/removeRules/setMode/addDirectories) persisted to user/project/local/session/cliArg settings, per-MCP-server McpServerToolPolicy, disallowedTools hard removal, Options.tools:[] disables all built-ins. Built-in Linux bubblewrap sandbox via Options.sandbox with FS/network restriction. allowDangerouslySkipPermissions guard belt. The most complete sandbox + permission surface in the survey.

Allow/deny via Agent(tools=[...]) construction-time. max_usage_count cap per tool. before_tool_call hook returning False blocks execution. MCP ToolFilter restricts server-exposed tools. AMP RBAC scopes per-org-role. E2B and Daytona are first-party in crewai-tools with persistent/one-shot/attach lifecycle modes. Default-deny for tools (only what you pass via tools=[...]). Strong sandbox integrations, allow/deny is construction-time-only in OSS.

Allow/deny lists are BYO via BeforeAgent middleware filtering runCtx.Tools. canUseTool equivalent is WrapInvokableToolCall returning an error to deny. No per-tool ACL primitive, no built-in tool-execution sandbox (tools run with same OS perms as the Go process). eino-ext ships a filesystem-only Docker-Python sandbox for the filesystem middleware (adk/backend/agentkit) and a local backend with PDF/image rendering, but no E2B/Daytona/Modal. Default-allow.

ToolApproval middleware with AllowedTools list — any tool not on the allowlist triggers an interrupt and requires explicit RestartWith({toolApproved:true}) approval. Filesystem middleware uses os.Root sandbox (no .., absolute paths, or symlinks) with strict size caps (256KB chunks, 10MB files). Default-allow globally; ToolApproval flips to default-deny + allowlist. No E2B/Daytona/Modal sandbox adapters.

wrap_tool_call is the sole per-tool ACL hook; engineers wire the policy in the wrapper. No declarative allow_tools=[...] list. No sandbox provider integrations in this repo — engineers wire E2B/Daytona/Modal as @tool wrappers around their SDKs. Default-allow; wrap_tool_call is opt-in for tightening.

No canUseTool-style hook. Permission is enforced by what tools you put in tools=[...] at agent construction. Inside a tool you can raise to refuse, but no declarative ACL. Sandbox integrations: llama-index-tools-code-interpreter (local, not sandboxed by default), Azure code interpreter, AWS Bedrock AgentCore. No E2B/Daytona/Modal first-party packages. Default-allow.

activeTools per-call whitelist (Q6.5), requireApproval boolean or needsApprovalFn(args) per tool, RBAC+FGA at HTTP layer (agents:execute, agents:read, requiresPermission overrides). processInputStep returning {activeTools} is functionally equivalent to canUseTool. No canUseTool callback. Sandbox provider integrations are BYO — wrap E2B/Daytona/Modal in createTool. Default-deny for HTTP routes when server.auth is configured, default-allow for tools unless requireApproval/activeTools is set.

approval_mode ('always_require' / 'never_require') on FunctionTool and @tool. .NET ToolApprovalAgent with standing-approval rules (ToolApprovalRule + ToolApprovalState — 'always allow X for the rest of session'). Allow/deny lists via ContextProvider tool filtering (skills' allowed_tools frontmatter, or runtime filter middleware). canUseTool-style via FunctionMiddleware raising MiddlewareTermination. Hyperlight hardware-isolated Wasm sandbox, DockerShellExecutor with ContainerUser/DockerNetworkMode/ShellPolicy. Tools default-allow; shell tools default to deny-unless-allowed ShellPolicy.

Best-in-class sandbox catalog: 7 first-party providers under extensions/sandbox/ (blaxel, cloudflare, daytona, e2b, modal, runloop, vercel) plus core agents.sandbox with UnixLocalSandboxClient and 30+ files (capabilities, entries, manifest, materialization, session, snapshot). agents.computer.AsyncComputer for Computer Use / Operator. Permission stack: function_tool(needs_approval=True|callable) with ToolApprovalItem and RunState.approve/reject; MCP-server require_approval; the 4 guardrail decorators (input/output/tool_input/tool_output) with allow/reject_content/raise_exception tri-state; is_enabled per tool/handoff. ShellTool NetworkPolicyAllowlist/Disabled/DomainSecret. Default-allow but the building blocks compose to deny-by-policy.

tool({needsApproval: true|predicate}) runtime approval gate, tool({isEnabled}) visibility filter, tool({inputGuardrails, outputGuardrails}) per-tool block/mutate, agent.toolUseBehavior tool-loop limit. UnixLocalSandboxClient + OpenAI-hosted shell with container_auto; third-party Docker/Blaxel/E2B-like providers referenced in CHANGELOG. Default-allow (isEnabled: true, needsApproval: false). Strong overall but lighter than the Python sibling.

@agent.tool(requires_approval=True) + HandleDeferredToolCalls capability for HITL approval. before_tool_execute hook returning SkipToolExecution(result) or raising to deny is the canUseTool equivalent. PrepareTools capability for per-step ACL. ApprovalRequiredToolset (toolsets/approval_required.py:16) provides per-tool ACL. Third-party pydantic-ai-backend (Docker) for sandboxed execution; no first-party E2B/Daytona/Modal. Default-allow for declared tools.

on_tool_call hook returning Skip{reason} or Terminate is the entire permission model — no per-tool ACL, no canUseTool returning structured permission verdicts, no default-deny mode. No E2B/Daytona/Modal integration, no built-in sandbox. Default-allow-all-registered; filtering is opt-in via hook logic.

BeforeToolCallEvent.cancel_tool (set to True or a custom string) is the per-call cancel primitive. Interrupt mechanism for HITL approval. strands-agents-tools/code_interpreter ships sandbox bindings. Default-allow; python_repl and shell ship with confirmation prompts, otherwise caller is responsible. No declarative allowlist or first-party E2B/Daytona/Modal integration.

BeforeToolCallEvent.cancel (hooks/events.ts:255) or InterventionHandler.beforeToolCall() returning deny(reason) (interventions/actions.ts:60) is the cancel primitive. No declarative allowed_tools at agent config; engineers write the policy. No sandbox provider integrations — bash tool runs in-process and sandboxing is OS/container-level. Default-allow.

toolApproval per-tool or global function returns 'approved' | 'denied' | 'user-approval' (tool-approval-configuration.ts:111); denied tools surface tool-output-denied, user-approval pauses for HITL. activeTools allowlist filter. tool.needsApproval per-tool flag. Experimental_Sandbox interface (@ai-sdk/provider-utils) abstracts the runtime hosting tool execution; concrete E2B/Daytona/Modal adapters are not first-party. Default-allow; setting global toolApproval flips to default-deny-pending-human.

`tool/mcptoolset/` wraps the official `modelcontextprotocol/go-sdk` (`set.go:49-56`); session is created lazily on first list-tools, tool filtering via `tool.AllowedToolsPredicate`, and HITL via `RequireConfirmation` are built in. Directly drop-in to an `Agent`'s tools.

`agno.tools.mcp.MCPTools` (`tools/mcp/mcp.py:29`) is a `Toolkit` that connects to an external MCP server and exposes tools to the agent with one line, with header injection and dynamic header providers.

`McpToolsManager` (`autoagents-toolkit/src/mcp/client.rs:23`) connects to one or many MCP servers and wraps each tool as `McpToolAdapter` implementing `ToolT`. Built on `rmcp` but the config only wires stdio (`TokioChildProcess`), so external HTTP/SSE servers require host-built code.
`mcp_servers` field on the options object (`types.py:1615-1620`) is consumed by the Claude CLI which is the actual MCP client; full transport set including in-process SDK servers is supported.

`Options.mcpServers` (`sdk.d.ts:1498`) takes a record of stdio/SSE/HTTP/in-process server configs, plus mid-session `setMcpServers`, runtime toggle and reconnect APIs. The CLI handles the actual MCP client work.

`mcp/config.py` ships `MCPServerStdio`, `MCPServerHTTP`, `MCPServerSSE`; `Agent(mcps=[...])` accepts bare slugs (resolved via AMP integrations), URLs, or fully-typed configs (`agents/agent_builder/base_agent.py:325`), with per-server tool filtering.

`components/tool/mcp/` (mark3labs SDK) and `components/tool/mcp/officialmcp/` (modelcontextprotocol SDK) both expose `mcp.GetTools(...)` returning `[]tool.BaseTool` with auto schema translation, plus `components/prompt/mcp/` for MCP prompts.
`go/plugins/mcp/` is an entire plugin: `GenkitMCPClient` for one server and `MCPHost` (`mcp/host.go`) for orchestrating multiple servers, all built on `mark3labs/mcp-go`.

MCP client support is provided by the separately-versioned `langchain-mcp-adapters` package which exposes MCP server tools as standard LangChain `BaseTool` instances. Works inside any `ToolNode` / `create_react_agent`, but not bundled in `langgraph` core.

`llama-index-tools-mcp` ships `McpToolSpec` (`base.py:19`) that consumes any `mcp.ClientSession` and turns its tools into `FunctionTool`s, with helpers for stdio/SSE/streamable HTTP picked automatically by URL.
`packages/mcp/src/client/` wires external MCP servers in via the Mastra `mcpServers: { ... }` config and exposes management routes under `/api/mcp-clients/*`.

Python `MCPTool` base (`_mcp.py:188`) with concrete `MCPStdioTool`, `MCPStreamableHTTPTool`, `MCPWebsocketTool` subclasses; .NET has `Microsoft.Agents.AI.Workflows.Declarative.Mcp` plus Microsoft.Extensions.AI MCP support.

Companion repo `strands-agents/mcp-server` ships an MCP server that exposes Strands agents, but the SDK itself does not directly run an MCP server. Out-of-band component rather than first-class SDK feature.

`McpStdioServerConfig`, `McpSSEServerConfig`, `McpHttpServerConfig` (`types.py:602-624`) plus `McpSdkServerConfig` for in-process bridged tools (`types.py:627-633`).

note: stdio SSE streamable HTTP in-process plus WS

Inherits from underlying SDKs: `mark3labs/mcp-go` provides stdio, SSE, HTTP and the official `go-sdk` adds streamable HTTP. In-process clients are trivial since `client.MCPClient` can bridge directly.
`StdioConfig`, `SSEConfig`, `StreamableHTTPConfig` are all first-class (`mcp/client.go:31-72`); no in-process transport — local Go functions cannot be turned into MCP tools without a subprocess.

note: client stdio plus HTTP server HTTP only
details: Client side covers stdio + HTTP via `langchain-mcp-adapters`; server side (the `/mcp` route on `langgraph_api`) is HTTP only. No SSE on the server, no in-process transport advertised.

note: stdio SSE streamable HTTP plus in-process
details: `BasicMCPClient` (`client.py:22-24`) auto-picks among stdio, SSE, and streamable HTTP based on the URL/command (`client.py:54-66`); `workflow_as_mcp` covers the in-process server case.
Three transports plus an explicit in-process transport for SDK-defined MCP servers (no subprocess), covering both client and server use cases.

Python ships stdio, streamable HTTP, and WebSocket (`MCPWebsocketTool`); .NET ships HTTP/SSE via Microsoft.Extensions.AI + ModelContextProtocol SDK. Also supports registering an in-process function as MCP tool.

`MCPServerStdio`, `MCPServerSse`, `MCPServerStreamableHttp` cover the three wire transports. No first-party `InProcessMCPServer`; recommended pattern is `@function_tool` directly when you want in-process.
`MCPServerStdio`, `MCPServerStreamableHttp` (recommended), `MCPServerSSE` (legacy), plus `hostedMcpTool({...})` (`tool.ts:918`) for OpenAI-hosted MCP via the Responses API.

note: stdio SSE streamable HTTP plus FastMCP
details: `MCPServerStdio` (`:1069`), `MCPServerSSE` (`:1402`), `MCPServerStreamableHTTP` (`:1515`) plus FastMCP toolset for in-process / SDK transport.

Inherits stdio, SSE, HTTP from the `rmcp` crate depending on how you construct the `rmcp::service::ServerSink` (see `examples/rmcp.rs`). For in-process Rig-only setups, just register a regular `Tool`.

`mcp>=1.23.0` dependency covers stdio, SSE, and streamable HTTP; primary advertised pattern is subprocess (stdio) or remote (SSE/HTTP). In-process via `mcp.client.session` is possible but not the recommended path.

`StdioClientTransport` and `StreamableHTTPClientTransport` are first-class (`mcp.ts:83`); any transport conforming to the upstream MCP TS SDK `Transport` interface plugs in too. In-process is hand-rolled with `StdioServerTransport`.
`packages/mcp/src/tool/` ships stdio, SSE, and streamable HTTP transports plus a `mock-mcp-transport.ts` for tests. No first-class function→MCP wrapper since native `tool({...})` already covers that.

Lazy-connect on first `ListTools` (`set.go:31`); `connectionRefresher` (`tool/mcptoolset/client.go`) reconnects after errors. Credentials are whatever the underlying transport accepts (headers, env vars) — no built-in OAuth/JWT.

`MCPTools(headers=...)` and `header_provider: Callable[..., dict]` allow per-request JWT injection. `connect()` / `close()` are managed by `mcp_lifespan` (`os/app.py:77-86`) tied to AgentOS startup/shutdown.

details: Auth tokens passed via `env: HashMap<String, String>` on the server config (`config.rs:18`); `timeout: u64` (default 30s, `config.rs:25`). No automatic reconnection on failure documented in the code.

`ClaudeSDKClient.reconnect_mcp_server`, `get_mcp_status`, `toggle_mcp_server` (`client.py:402-448`); `McpServerStatus` per server (`types.py:712-737`); `strict_mcp_config: bool` (0.1.74) blocks project/user/global MCP configs — critical for multi-tenant isolation.

`Query.reconnectMcpServer`, `mcpServerStatus()` returning `{status, error?, tools?, serverInfo?}` (`sdk.d.ts:986, 2214`), background-connect by default (with `alwaysLoad` opt-out), `setMcpServers` mid-session swap, `toggleMcpServer`, OAuth (clientId/callbackPort/scopes), and `onElicitation` for server-prompt UX.

Headers (`Authorization: Bearer ...`) for HTTP/SSE, env for stdio. `MCP_MAX_RETRIES = 3` (`mcp/client.py:47`) with 30s timeouts for connection / discovery / tool execution; `_mcp_schema_cache` with 5-minute TTL; static/dynamic `ToolFilter`.

note: headers and meta delegate to SDK
details: `Config.CustomHeaders` (`components/tool/mcp/mcp.go:46-47`) injects Bearer tokens or any headers on every MCP call; `Config.Meta` for custom metadata. Reconnection, health, and version negotiation are delegated to the underlying SDK with no framework wrapping.

Credentials via `Headers` map for SSE/StreamableHTTP, env vars for stdio. `client.connect` (`mcp/client.go:110+`) supports re-establishing; `MCPHost` tracks `*GenkitMCPClient` per server name. No built-in healthcheck endpoint — transport errors surface on tool call.

`MakeRuntimeContext` initializes per-run MCP connections in `ert.context` lifecycle-bound to each run. External-server auth defers to standard `langchain-mcp-adapters` (env vars, OAuth flows). No explicit framework-level health/reconnect API.

`OAuthClientProvider` and `TokenStorage` interface (`client.py:25-26, 69+`) for OAuth flows; `DefaultInMemoryTokenStorage` is the default. Production multi-tenant deployments are expected to implement their own `TokenStorage` to persist tokens.

Credentials passed via `mcpClients` config at boot or `requestContext.get(MASTRA_AUTH_TOKEN_KEY)` for runtime forwarding (`packages/core/src/request-context/index.ts:46-51`). Reconnection and health left to the client implementation.

`MCPStreamableHTTPTool` accepts custom HTTP transport with auth headers (`_mcp.py:1472`); tools use lazy initialization (DevUI README:64-66 documents the gotcha). Health and version negotiation delegated to the underlying `mcp` SDK.

Headers / env credentials, explicit `connect()` / `cleanup()` and an `MCPServerManager`; `_InitializedNotificationTolerantStreamableHTTPTransport` (`server.py:112`) handles ordering edge case; 0.13.0 added `session_id` so streamable-HTTP sessions resume across reconnects or stateless workers; `require_approval` parameter (`server.py:55-91`).
