`McpClientHandler` reacts to `tools/list_changed` notifications and updates the `ToolServer` accordingly (`tool/rmcp.rs:5-7`), but auth is opaque — credentials wired solely via the `rmcp` transport setup; no framework-level health/OAuth/reconnect helpers.

Background-thread session with cleanup via `cleanup()` and finalizer (`tools/mcp/mcp_client.py`); registry calls cleanup on agent destruction (`agent/agent.py:699-709`); `_NON_FATAL_ERROR_PATTERNS` (`mcp_client.py:96-100`) keeps transient errors from tearing down the session; OTel via `mcp_instrumentation`.

`McpClientConfig` (`mcp.ts:78`) supports OAuth client credentials (`auth: {clientId, clientSecret, scopes}`), custom `authProvider: OAuthClientProvider`, `headers`, `failOpen`, OTel toggle, experimental `tasksConfig`, server-initiated `elicitationCallback`, and forwards the agent cancel signal to MCP tool calls (PR #1069).

OAuth support lives in `packages/mcp/src/tool/oauth.ts`; standard HTTP auth headers via the HTTP/SSE transports; `DefaultMCPClient` has reconnection logic (`mcp-client.ts:226+`) and capability/version negotiation occurs during handshake.
No first-party PII redaction, prompt-injection detection, or hallucination scoring. Report 18.1 explicitly says "Not provided — BYO" via BeforeModelCallback / AfterModelCallback.

First-class BaseGuardrail (libs/agno/agno/guardrails/base.py:8) with PromptInjectionGuardrail, PIIDetectionGuardrail, and OpenAIModerationGuardrail bundled. Wired declaratively via pre_hooks / post_hooks raising InputCheckError / OutputCheckError. Covers all three benchmark detectors (PII, injection, moderation) out of the box.

Dedicated autoagents-guardrails crate ships prompt_injection.rs, regex_pii_redaction.rs, and toxicity.rs guards. Integrated as an LLMLayer with Block / Sanitize / Audit policies so guards plug into the LLM pipeline alongside cache/retry/fallback. Block raises LLMError::GuardrailBlocked and propagates through the executor.

Report 18.1 flags no PII redaction, no prompt-injection detection, no hallucination detection. Engineers must roll their own via UserPromptSubmit / PostToolUse hooks. The SDK's strength is sandbox/permissions (18.2), not content guardrails.

No first-party PII redaction, prompt-injection detection, or hallucination detection. Report 18.1 says BYO via PreToolUse / PostToolUse hooks (e.g. regex redaction step). Same posture as the Python SDK.

Agent.guardrail / Task.guardrail callable hooks exist for output validation with retry-on-fail (max retries: 3). HallucinationGuardrail and pii-trace-redactions ship only in AMP (the paid enterprise tier), not OSS. No first-party PII redaction in open source.

Report explicitly states "Not first-party" — PII redaction, prompt-injection detection, and hallucination detection are all BYO via a ChatModelAgentMiddleware running regex/classifier/LLM-judge over messages.

Report 18.1 says guardrails are "Not provided as a first-party primitive" in go/. No PII redaction, prompt-injection detection, or hallucination detection. Engineers BYO via WrapGenerate / WrapTool middleware.

Report 18.1 states "Not provided — BYO". PII redaction / prompt-injection / hallucination detection live outside the OSS runtime. Common patterns use pre_model_hook for input scrubbing and LangChain integrations (Lakera, Presidio, OpenAI moderation) wired as callbacks — none ship with langgraph itself.

Not first-party in core. The llama-index-integrations ecosystem includes llama-index-guardrails (PyPI) and adapters for Guardrails AI / NeMo Guardrails, but nothing bundled in the core agent runtime. Score reflects ecosystem availability without in-tree primitives.

Comprehensive processors under packages/core/src/processors/: moderation.ts (LLM-based), pii-detector.ts, prompt-injection-detector.ts, plus cost-guard, regex-filter, language-detector, unicode-normalizer, system-prompt-scrubber. Each can ctx.abort('reason') to halt or auto-retry with feedback. Covers all three benchmark detectors plus extras.

Prompt-injection defense via information-flow control: IntegrityLabel, ConfidentialityLabel, ContentLabel, LabeledMessage, LabelTrackingFunctionMiddleware, PolicyEnforcementFunctionMiddleware (security.py). Backed by ADR 0024. Microsoft Purview integration for compliance/sensitivity labels. PII redaction is BYO via middleware, so not a full sweep of the three detectors.

The strongest guardrail framework in the benchmark: 4 decorator types (@input_guardrail, @output_guardrail, @tool_input_guardrail, @tool_output_guardrail) with tripwire mechanism and a unique allow/reject_content/raise_exception tri-state at tool-input AND tool-output layers. Parallel execution support. But no first-party PII / prompt-injection / hallucination detectors ship — BYO content classifier. Score reflects framework strength without bundled detectors.

First-class framework with five surfaces: InputGuardrail, OutputGuardrail, ToolInputGuardrail, ToolOutputGuardrail, HandoffEnabledPredicate, all returning tripwireTriggered. Strong policy plumbing, but no first-party PII / prompt-injection detectors — engineers wrap LlmGuard or Lakera. Score reflects the framework strength without bundled detectors.

First-party hooks (before_model_request, after_tool_execute, wrap_output_validate) let you plug in PII redaction / injection detection, but no bundled detector ships. Third-party pydantic-ai-backend with DockerSandbox handles isolated execution, not content filtering.

Report 18.1 states "Not provided" — no built-in PII redaction, prompt-injection detection, or hallucination check. The on_tool_call hook is the only policy surface and it operates on tool calls, not message content.

Bedrock Guardrails are first-class for that provider: GuardrailConfig in types/guardrails.py plumbs guardrail identifier/version/trace into the Bedrock API and the agent loop detects redactContent chunks and rewrites the user message (agent.py:927-938). For non-Bedrock providers, BYO via hooks. Provider-scoped rather than framework-agnostic.

BedrockGuardrailConfig attaches AWS Bedrock Guardrails per call with ModelRedactionEvent rewriting (agent.ts:1982). Generic interventions subsystem (proceed/deny/guide/confirm/transform) is the closest framework-agnostic surface. PII / prompt-injection detection itself is BYO via interventions — only the Bedrock-bound case has bundled detectors.

Report 18.1 says "Not provided — BYO". No PII redaction, prompt-injection detection, or hallucination detection. Engineers use LanguageModelMiddleware.transformParams or prepareStep to do pre-call redaction themselves.

internal/telemetry/telemetry.go wires OTel with GenAI semconv (`gcp.vertex.agent`) and emits invoke_agent / generate_content / execute_tool spans automatically. Setup via telemetry.New(ctx, opts) returns TracerProvider + LoggerProvider with OTLP HTTP out of the box plus WithOtelToCloud for GCP Cloud Trace. The REST server also ships an in-memory DebugTelemetry capturing the last 10k traces accessible via /debug/trace. No first-party LangSmith/LangFuse adapter but any OTel backend (incl. LangSmith via OTel ingest) works.

setup_tracing(db=db) wires a TracerProvider, an AgnoInstrumentor (auto-traces agent runs, model calls, tool executions, team coordination, workflow steps), and a DatabaseSpanExporter that persists spans/traces to agno_traces/agno_spans for in-app inspection. Standard OTLP exporters (Datadog, Honeycomb, Jaeger) plug into the same provider, and weave / openlit extras wire alternative backends. First-class out of the box.

autoagents-telemetry ships a TelemetryProvider trait with bundled OTLP and Langfuse (feature-flagged) implementations, plus a Tracer that subscribes to the event stream and converts events to spans. OtlpConfig supports HTTP/gRPC and a RedactionConfig. Solid OTel coverage but requires the extra crate and you have to subscribe before running to avoid missing usage events.

Since 0.1.60 the SDK auto-injects TRACEPARENT/TRACESTATE env vars into the CLI subprocess (subprocess_cli.py:441) so spans emitted by the CLI parent under the caller's distributed trace. Install with claude-agent-sdk[otel]. No first-party LangSmith/LangFuse/Datadog adapters and the spans themselves come from the CLI binary rather than Python code, which limits how much the SDK can customize them.

Caller's active OTel context is forwarded to the CLI subprocess so the CLI's LLM/tool spans parent under the host's distributed trace. No first-party LangSmith/LangFuse exporter shipped; users instrument host code around query() with @opentelemetry/api. Same caveat as Python — spans originate in the CLI, not the SDK.

Built-in OTLP HTTP exporter in telemetry/telemetry.py plus a 151-event bus you can subscribe to with a BaseEventListener. Documented first-party integrations include Datadog, Langfuse, Langtrace, Arize Phoenix, Braintrust, MLflow, Opik, Portkey, Weave, LangDB, plus more, and CrewAI AMP ships its own Prompt Tracing dashboard. One of the broadest tracing ecosystems in the comparison.

Three first-party tracing exporters in eino-ext (Langfuse with batching + redaction + sampling, LangSmith with hierarchical dotted_order, APMPlus on OTel) plus CozeLoop for ByteDance internal tracing. Wired via callbacks.AppendGlobalHandlers, after which every Graph/ChatModel/Tool/Retriever/Embedding/Lambda invocation is automatically traced.

go/core/tracing/tracing.go emits OTel spans (generate, tool, plus custom flow steps via genkit.Run) with GenAI-style attributes; tracing is on by default. The googlecloud plugin ships Cloud Trace / Metrics / Logging exporters. No first-party LangSmith integration on the Go side, but any OTel collector works.

LangSmith is the first-party hosted tracer and auto-traces every Runnable when LANGSMITH_API_KEY is set. No native OTel emitter; OTel and integrations (Langfuse, Arize Phoenix, W&B, Opik) come through the LangChain callback ecosystem, which is broad but not OTel-first. Strong if LangSmith is acceptable; otherwise you go via callbacks.

llama-index-instrumentation provides a dispatcher tree with async/thread-safe event and span handlers that preserves trace trees across coroutines. llama-index-observability-otel bridges spans to any OTel backend, and the callbacks ecosystem includes Arize Phoenix, Langfuse, Opik, OpenInference, W&B, HoneyHive, AgentOps and more (~20+).

ObservabilityEntrypoint runs three pipelines: stream-chunk usage on step-finish/finish, a MetricsContext bus with cost-aware emission, and span/trace tracking via IModelSpanTracker. Exporters: Langfuse, OpenTelemetry, custom storage. MODEL_GENERATION spans are re-stamped on model fallback so cost attribution stays correct, and metrics have cardinality protection (UUID values blocked, high-card labels blocked by default).

enable_instrumentation() (observability.py:83) wires tracer/meter/logger and emits invoke_agent / chat / execute_tool spans following GenAI semconv. CompactionTelemetry adds spans for context compaction. Compatible with Azure Monitor, Application Insights, Jaeger, and any OTel collector — clean first-class OTel story.

Built-in TracingProcessor interface with a default BackendSpanExporter that ships to OpenAI's hosted Traces dashboard. add_trace_processor / set_trace_processors swap or extend exporters; documented partners include Weights & Biases, Arize Phoenix, MLflow, Braintrust, Logfire, AgentOps, LangSmith, Maxim, Opik, Langfuse, Galileo, Portkey, and more. Rich span-data type coverage (Agent, Generation, Function, Guardrail, Handoff, MCPListTools, Response, Speech, Task, Transcription, Turn).

Custom tracing in packages/agents-core/src/tracing with AgentSpan, GenerationSpan, FunctionSpan, HandoffSpan, GuardrailSpan, MCPListToolsSpan, TranscriptionSpan, SpeechSpan. Default exporter goes to OpenAI Traces. AgentOps, Respan, PromptLayer are listed as external integrations but there is no first-party OTel adapter — third parties bridge via the TracingProcessor interface — which limits parity with the Python version.

The Instrumentation capability (capabilities/instrumentation.py) installs spans for the agent run, model requests, and tool calls using OTel-spec attribute names (_otel_messages.py). Logfire is a first-party partner backend and any other OTel collector works. Clean and minimal.

note: OTel GenAI semconv via tracing crate
details: Both non-streaming and streaming loops emit info_span! with full GenAI semconv fields (gen_ai.operation.name, gen_ai.agent.name, gen_ai.usage.input_tokens, gen_ai.usage.cache_read.input_tokens, gen_ai.usage.reasoning_tokens, etc.) plus execute_tool spans with arguments/result. crates/rig-core/src/telemetry exposes ProviderRequestExt/ProviderResponseExt/SpanCombinator traits for providers to fill spans with native request/response data. OTel export via tracing-opentelemetry.

Tracer (telemetry/tracer.py:77) creates agent, event-loop-cycle, model-invoke, and tool-call spans using gen_ai.* semconv attributes. Exports via OTLP when OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT is set (otel extra installs opentelemetry-exporter-otlp-proto-http).

setupTracer() configures a global OTel TracerProvider; the agent auto-emits spans for agent.invoke, agent.loop.cycle.<N>, agent.model.invoke, agent.tool.<name>. Exporters: OTLP HTTP, console, plus anything else on the global SDK. A lightweight in-memory AgentTrace tree is always collected regardless of OTel config and exposed on AgentResult.traces.

Telemetry interface exposes 12 lifecycle callbacks (onStart, onLanguageModelCallStart/End, onToolExecutionStart/End, onStepStart/Finish, onObjectStepStart/Finish, onEmbedStart/End, onRerankStart/End, onEnd, onError) plus executeTool wrapping for nested-span propagation. @ai-sdk/otel provides an OpenTelemetry implementation so spans land in Datadog / Honeycomb / Tempo / Signoz. No first-party LangSmith / LangFuse exporter — community plugs in via OTel.

Every session.Event carries Author + Timestamp + Content + Actions, persisted to DB and append-only by design (no UPDATE paths in session/database/service.go). The plugin.OnEventCallback hook lets you ship every event to Datadog logs, BigQuery, or another sink. Not tamper-evident (no hash chain or signing) but the event stream effectively IS the audit log and is suitable for forensic review.

No dedicated audit-event stream, but the combination is audit-friendly: JWT auth fills request.state.user_id, require_resource_access enforces per-resource RBAC, traces/spans land in agno_traces/agno_spans, runs persist with user_id/agent_id/timestamps, and the agno_approvals table records HITL decisions. No tamper-evidence, but compliance-grade footprint is present out of the box.

Events carry sub_id, actor_id, actor_name and timestamps you stamp on receive. No tamper-evident or sequence-numbered audit log primitive; engineers subscribe to the event stream and ship to their own sink.

The SessionStore mirror is your audit log — every transcript line (tool calls, results, prompts, mode changes) flows through SessionStore.append(). With include_hook_events=True (0.1.74) you also get a hook-execution audit stream via HookEventMessage (hook_event_name, subtype, exit codes, outcomes). No tamper-evident chain, but the framework gives you a first-class audit substrate without writing one yourself.

The on-disk JSONL transcript contains every loop action (tool calls, decisions, permission denials, model responses) and is append-only on local disk; a SessionStore mirror gives you a tamper-resistant copy. For a true audit log hook PostToolUse / PermissionDenied / PermissionRequest and push to your audit sink. Not first-class tamper-evident, but the substrate is built-in.

Event bus emits structured events with timestamps, emission_sequence, and parent IDs; event_record is part of every checkpoint so post-hoc reconstruction is straightforward. Persistence requires a custom listener and there is no hash chain or signature for tamper-evidence.

No dedicated audit primitive distinct from tracing. Engineers register a callbacks.Handler (or use WithCallbacks at the agent level) and emit structured audit events to their sink. Tamper-evident logging (hash chain, signed events) is not provided.

Tracing is the only built-in observability primitive. There is no audit-log interface you can swap to a separate tamper-evident sink — engineers wrap tools and flows manually to log to a write-once store.
Not provided as a tamper-evident audit stream. Engineers hook on_chain_start / on_chain_end / on_tool_start / on_tool_end and ship to an immutable log sink (S3, BigQuery, ClickHouse) themselves.
The instrumentation event stream plus your own Postgres / S3 sink is the recommended path. Not tamper-evident out of the box and not framed as an audit-log primitive.

Spans and metrics are the primary audit signal and storage/domains/observability persists them for query. RBAC + FGA route guards log denials at the middleware layer. No first-party tamper-evident audit log — you'd mirror spans to an append-only sink — but the storage and access-control footprint is more audit-aware than most peers.

Trace data is the audit substrate; no separate tamper-evident audit log. security.py's LabelTrackingFunctionMiddleware records which labelled content flowed through which tools — useful for prompt-injection forensics but not a general-purpose audit log.
Not first-class. Tracing serves a similar role but is not tamper-evident. For audit, hook into RunHooks.on_tool_start/on_tool_end and ship to your own append-only log.

Tracing spans capture LLM inputs/outputs and tool inputs/outputs when traceIncludeSensitiveData=true. For tamper-evident logging you build your own append-only sink and use addTraceProcessor to mirror traces into it.
Logfire treats every agent/model/tool span as an audit record. No tamper-evident store in-tree; for that you ship spans to a write-once backend yourself.
Not provided as a distinct facility. Tracing spans contain message-level data (gen_ai.input.messages, gen_ai.output.messages) and you route them to your exporter of choice as the audit trail.
Not first-class. Tracing serves double duty; for tamper-evident audit, BYO sink subscribing to MessageAddedEvent + BeforeToolCallEvent + AfterToolCallEvent.

Hook event stream is the natural audit-log source — every relevant event has a toJSON() designed for wire transport, so piping to a sink is a few lines. The new interventions subsystem (interventions/registry.ts) is closer to a tamper-evident policy log, though no signed/append-only ledger ships. More audit-aware than most peers.
Not provided. The Telemetry callback surface plus your structured logger is the natural sink point. No tamper-evident audit log primitives ship.

Tokens land on every session.Event via Gemini's UsageMetadata (prompt/candidates/total/cached/thoughts) and persist to the DB row, but ADK provides no per-turn/session/tenant rollup helpers — you sum events yourself by InvocationID or sessionID.

MessageMetrics on each assistant message, RunMetrics on RunOutput, SessionMetrics aggregated in agno_sessions, plus ModelMetrics per (provider, model_id) within a run; reasoning, cache-read and cache-write tokens are all tracked and accumulated via ModelMetrics.accumulate.

Usage is emitted only as a per-call StreamChunk::Usage with prompt/completion/total tokens — no per-turn, per-session, or per-tenant aggregation in the framework; the telemetry crate forwards to OTel where you must build the rollups.

AssistantMessage.usage per LLM call, ResultMessage.usage and model_usage per turn (including model fallback breakdown), TaskUsage for sub-agent tasks, plus get_context_usage() for live context categorisation — only per-session and per-tenant rollups are BYO.

SDKAssistantMessage.message.usage per call, SDKResultMessage.usage per turn, SDKResultMessage.modelUsage broken out by model when fallback or sub-agents differ, AgentOutput.usage per sub-agent, plus Query.getContextUsage() for the current state.

TokenCalcHandler accumulates LiteLLM callbacks into UsageMetrics with prompt/completion/cached/reasoning/cache-creation fields, exposed on LLMCallCompletedEvent, TaskOutput.token_usage, CrewOutput.token_usage and Crew.usage_metrics — per-tenant rollup is BYO since CrewAI has no tenant primitive.

ResponseMeta.Usage on each assistant message carries PromptTokens, CompletionTokens, TotalTokens plus cached and reasoning sub-details, but Eino provides no first-party rollup; per-turn and per-session aggregation is done via your own callbacks.Handler.OnEnd.

ModelResponse.Usage carries a very rich GenerationUsage (tokens plus characters, images, audio, video, cached, thoughts), but resp.Usage only reflects the last LLM call of the tool loop — multi-turn aggregation requires the addAutomaticTelemetry middleware or walking trace spans, and per-session/tenant rollups are BYO.

LangChain UsageMetadata on every AIMessage with input/output/total tokens, audio details, cache_creation, cache_read and reasoning sub-fields; per-call and per-turn are first-class, but per-session and per-tenant rollups require summing usage_metadata across thread state or installing a BaseCallbackHandler.

ChatResponse.raw exposes provider-shape usage per call and the TokenCountingHandler callback accumulates prompt_llm_token_count and completion_llm_token_count across the run, but everything beyond per-handler-instance aggregation (per-session, per-tenant) is BYO via instrument_tags spans.

LanguageModelUsage flows through three places — MastraModelOutput.totalUsage at run end, onStepFinish callback per LLM step, onFinish with cumulative totalUsage and per-step usage — covering input, output, reasoning, cachedInput and cacheCreationInput tokens, and persisted on conversation messages by the storage backend.

AgentResponse.usage_details and ChatResponse.usage_details report input/output/total token counts, INNER_ACCUMULATED_USAGE accumulates usage across inner chat-client calls inside one agent run, and gen_ai.usage.input_tokens/output_tokens are emitted as OTel attributes and a token-usage histogram — per-session is observable in the trace backend.

Usage on result.context_wrapper.usage (with request_usage_entries preserving per-call breakdown), per-call usage on result.raw_responses, per-turn aggregated via usage_delta in turn_span and per-session via task_span, plus on_llm_end hook access — only per-tenant requires BYO trace_metadata.

Usage class on RunContext.usage accumulates inputTokens, outputTokens, totalTokens, requests and requestUsageEntries across every model call in a run, plus per-call usage on ModelResponse.usage and on GenerationSpan; per-session and per-tenant are BYO.

ModelResponse.usage exposes RequestUsage per call and AgentRunResult.usage exposes the summed RunUsage across the whole run (requests, tool_calls, input/output/cache_read/cache_write tokens plus a details dict), and gen_ai.usage.* attributes are emitted as OTel.

CompletionResponse.usage per LLM call and PromptResponse.usage aggregated across all turns of one prompt() call (with input/output/total, cached_input, cache_creation_input and reasoning tokens), plus tracing spans recording gen_ai.usage.* attributes — per-conversation requires summing across prompt() calls yourself.

Usage lives in message metadata per assistant turn, agent.event_loop_metrics.accumulated_usage gives a running total across the agent session (inputTokens, outputTokens, totalTokens, cacheReadInputTokens, cacheWriteInputTokens), and BeforeModelCallEvent exposes projected_input_tokens; per-tenant is BYO.

Message.metadata.usage per assistant message, AgentResult.metrics.accumulatedUsage across all invocations, plus an AgentMetrics object that exposes cycleCount, agentInvocations[], toolMetrics per-tool callCount/successCount/errorCount/totalTime and latestContextSize/projectedContextSize — rich first-party rollup short of per-tenant.

LanguageModelUsage on every call, StepResult.usage per step and GenerateTextResult.totalUsage per run, with unusually thorough sub-token detail — noCacheTokens, cacheReadTokens, cacheWriteTokens, textTokens and reasoningTokens — that supports fine-grained prompt-cache cost analysis.
ADK Go reports tokens via Gemini's UsageMetadata but does not compute USD anywhere; you maintain your own per-model price table and multiply tokens by $/Mtoken yourself.

BaseMetrics.cost (USD) is computed by the model adapter using agno/models/defaults.py pricing tables and accumulated via ModelMetrics.accumulate, so RunMetrics.cost and SessionMetrics.cost are available out of the box without a host-side pricing table.
AutoAgents has no price-per-1k-token table and no USD conversion; cost in dollars is computed entirely by your own code from the StreamChunk::Usage events.

ResultMessage.total_cost_usd is computed by the Claude Code CLI on every turn — including across model fallback — giving the Python SDK an authoritative USD figure for free; explicitly called out in the report as the only stack in the comparison with first-party USD cost on the result object.

SDKResultMessage.total_cost_usd is computed by the CLI's bundled pricing tables on every result, and Options.maxBudgetUsd enforces a server-side dollar ceiling that surfaces an error_max_budget_usd subtype on overrun — unique combination of native cost reporting and native cost capping.

LLM.completion_cost exists as an Optional[float] field on the LLM class but no code path actually populates it from LiteLLM's cost_per_token or completion_cost helpers, so effectively no first-party USD computation is available — external vendors like Langfuse or AMP do their own pricing on top.
Eino reports tokens via TokenUsage and that is it — no pricing table, no cost field, no helper; USD is computed by your code from a price table you maintain (lookup by RunInfo.Type).

Genkit Go has no pricing.json, no cost_usd field and no getSpendReport helper; USD is computed either by your own pricing table or by an external observability platform like LangSmith on top of the OTel traces.

LangGraph OSS has no built-in price table, no total_cost_usd field and no max_budget_usd cap — the report flags this as materially different from Claude Agent SDK; cost computation is offloaded to the paid LangSmith platform which extends UsageMetadata with cost fields server-side.

A search of llama-index-core for cost_usd, cost_in_dollars or usd returns no results; USD is computed yourself from token counts and an external pricing table, or via callback integrations like Langfuse/Phoenix.

CostContext.estimatedCost is exposed on the metrics bus but it is just a field for the caller (host app or an exporter) to fill in — there is no pricing.ts inside @mastra/core that maps provider+model to USD-per-1k-tokens, so practical USD computation is fully BYO.

UsageDetails only carries input/output/total token counts; there is no first-party USD computation in Agent Framework — you compute cost in a downstream OTel processor or evaluator using your own per-model price table.

Only tokens are reported (Usage dataclass with input_tokens, output_tokens, cached_tokens, reasoning_tokens, request_usage_entries); you compute USD in a RunHooks.on_llm_end or in a TracingProcessor using a model→$/Mtok table you maintain.
The TS SDK only reports tokens via the Usage class — no pricing table, no cost field; USD is computed from your own pricing table against the per-call RequestUsage entries.

Pydantic-AI ships first-party USD computation via the genai-prices package (Pydantic-maintained) which RequestUsage.extract uses, so per-call and per-run USD is computable directly from RunUsage plus model name and provider without a host-side price table.

Rig surfaces a rich Usage struct (input/output/total, cached_input, cache_creation_input, reasoning) but does not compute USD — you multiply by your own price table after reading PromptResponse.usage or CompletionResponse.usage.
Strands Python has no per-model price table and no cost_usd field anywhere; USD is computed in an AfterModelCallEvent hook by multiplying message metadata usage by your own price table.
Strands TS only counts tokens — the example in the report explicitly shows computing costUsd as inputTokens * 0.000003 + outputTokens * 0.000015 in the host, since the SDK does not provide it.

The ai package itself does not compute cost in USD — no pricing tables, no costUSD field, no tokenCost helper; the only USD figures come from the Vercel AI Gateway's GatewaySpendReportRow REST API (totalCost, marketCost) and only for calls that go through the Gateway, so direct provider calls leave you to compute cost yourself.

No first-party tenant or per-conversation cost rollup; the suggested pattern is to tag OTel spans with tenant_id (e.g. via plugin.OnEventCallback that reads app:tenant_id from session state) and query in your tracing backend.

RunOutput.metrics.cost gives you a per-run USD figure, but per-tenant or per-conversation rollups require tagging the session with tenant_id in metadata and aggregating yourself via a DB query against agno_sessions or agno_metrics — no first-party helper.
No tenant primitive in the framework; per-tenant cost is computed entirely by your own code on top of the Usage events, optionally tagged via the autoagents-telemetry provider's attribute support.

total_cost_usd is per-turn, so per-tenant or per-conversation aggregation requires accumulating it yourself keyed by SessionKey.project_key (the natural tagging key); there is no SDK rollup but the building block — authoritative USD per turn — is unusually strong.

total_cost_usd is per-SDKResultMessage; for per-tenant or per-conversation you aggregate by session_id and your own tenantId mapping yourself — the SessionStore is opaque pass-through, not an aggregation point, so the SDK does not roll cost up for you despite native USD reporting.

BYO via a BaseEventListener on LLMCallCompletedEvent tagging by tenant, but listeners attach to a global bus so they fire for every crew in the process — to filter you must check source.id inside the handler, which the report calls awkward but workable for batch use cases.
First-party rollup is absent; the pattern is callbacks.Handler.OnEnd that reads tenantId from the ctx (set via WithSessionValues) and emits metrics tagged by tenant against an OTel/Datadog meter.
Not provided in the SDK; you add tenant_id as an OTel resource attribute or via a WrapGenerate middleware that calls span.SetAttributes, then query downstream in Cloud Trace, Datadog or Grafana.

Not provided in OSS LangGraph; the pattern is stamping metadata['tenant_id'] on every run and installing a BaseCallbackHandler that joins tenant_id with model_name and usage_metadata to emit OTel metrics — LangSmith does this server-side if you pay for it.

Per-tenant cost is BYO; the recommended primitive is the instrument_tags context manager which tags spans with arbitrary key/value pairs (e.g. tenant_id, user_id) that your OTel or callback exporter then groups on.

Mastra exposes a metrics bus (MetricsContext.emit) with a dedicated CostContext payload and re-stamps MODEL_GENERATION spans when fallback models serve a request so cost attribution stays correct — but actual tenant aggregation is still BYO via onStepFinish hooks that compute tokens × your pricing table, and several high-cardinality labels including tenant_id-style ids are blocked by default.

No first-party tenant rollup; the pattern shown in the report is a custom ChatMiddleware (e.g. TenantTagger) that stamps dm.tenant_id on the current OTel span from ctx.kwargs, then a downstream OTel exporter aggregates.

Per-tenant is still BYO but the SDK provides explicit propagation hooks: RunConfig.trace_metadata={'tenant_id': 'acme'} and RunConfig.group_id flow through the trace pipeline, plus on_llm_end hooks expose response.usage so a custom TracingProcessor or hook can ship USD-tagged metrics — stronger primitives than most OSS stacks even though the rollup itself is host-built.

Per-tenant cost is BYO — attach tenantId to runContext.context and use RunConfig.groupId to bind related runs into a trace group; aggregation happens in your downstream tracing backend rather than in the SDK.

Pydantic AI Gateway adds per-project, per-user and per-key USD caps with daily, weekly and monthly windows — the only framework in the set with a managed multi-tenant cost-cap surface; in-process is still BYO via a before_run/after_run hook that folds result.usage into a billing store keyed by metadata['tenant_id'].

Not provided — Rig surfaces Usage on every response and gen_ai.usage.* attributes on every span, but per-conversation or per-tenant aggregation is built entirely on top of either tracing or the Usage values.

BYO; the recommended pattern is an AfterModelCallEvent hook that reads invocation_state['tenant_id'] and emits a per-tenant cost gauge to Datadog/OTel after multiplying message metadata usage by a host-side price table.

BYO; per-tenant is done by setting agent.traceAttributes = { tenantId } so every span carries it, then aggregating downstream in the OTel collector — the SDK does not roll up cost or even tokens per tenant itself.

Through the Vercel AI Gateway, getSpendReport supports groupBy: 'user' | 'tag' | model | provider with totalCost and marketCost in USD; you tag each call with runtimeContext.tenantId via providerOptions.gateway.tags and group by tag. Without the Gateway, both tenant rollup and USD are BYO from LanguageModelUsage × your pricing table.

First-class `userID`, `appName`, and `sessionID` are dedicated `Run` arguments, and `WithStateDelta` lets you stuff `app:`/`user:`-prefixed keys (tenant_id, locale, strategy) into Session.State. There is no first-class `tenant_id` argument — that has to go through the state delta convention — but the existing primitives are typed and well-routed.

`Agent.run(...)` accepts a `dependencies: Dict[str, Any]` and `metadata` bag plus typed `user_id`/`session_id`, all carried on a `RunContext` that flows through the run. Strong, well-named carrier; still untyped at the schema level (no `tenant_id` field).

`Task` carries only `prompt`/`image`/`system_prompt`/`submission_id` and there is no `tenant_id`, `user_id`, `metadata`, or arbitrary context field anywhere. Tenant identity can only enter by stuffing it into the prompt or capturing it as a tool struct field at construction.

`ClaudeAgentOptions` has ~50 fields but no arbitrary user-context channel into tool handlers; tenant must be threaded via `cwd`, `env`, closures inside hooks/`can_use_tool`, and `SessionKey.project_key` (which scopes the store only). Not a typed run-loop input.

Same shape as the Python SDK — ~80-field `Options` with no typed `tenantId`. Tenants are modeled via `cwd`, `SessionKey.projectKey`, `env`, and closure capture inside `canUseTool`/hooks. Recommended workaround documented but not first-class.

No `tenant_id`/`user_id` field on Crew/Agent/Task/Flow. The only channels are `Crew.config`, `Agent.config`, `execution_context` (free-form), or OTel baggage carrying `crew.id`/`crew.key`. Documented as a real gap and CrewAI itself states it is not architected for multi-tenant in-process serving.

Inputs are `context.Context` plus `WithSessionValues(map[string]any)` — both flow through the entire run but neither is typed. No `Spec T` / `Context T` field like LangGraph's `Runtime[ContextT]`; the idiomatic Go-style ctx-value plumbing works but is untyped.

`ContextProvider` is a designed entry point that extracts `tenantId`/`userId` from request headers into `core.ActionContext` on `context.Context`. Strong first-party plumbing, though `ActionContext` is `map[string]any` (not a typed struct).

`StateGraph(context_schema=Context)` declares a typed dataclass/TypedDict for tenant deps that is resolved into `Runtime.context` and frozen for the run. This is the canonical first-class typed run-loop input among the surveyed stacks.

`AgentWorkflowStartEvent` has no first-class `tenant_id`/`user_id`/`metadata`. Tenant info enters via `initial_state` (lands in `ctx.store['state']`) or via arbitrary `**kwargs`. Functional but untyped and convention-bound.

`RequestContext<TRequestContext>` is a typed Map with four reserved keys (resourceId, threadId, versions, authToken) that explicitly take precedence over client-supplied values for security. Supported by `requestContextSchema` validation in tool definitions.

Python `agent.run()` accepts a `function_invocation_kwargs` mapping forwarded into `FunctionInvocationContext`; .NET uses `AdditionalProperties` on `AgentRunOptions`. Neither is a typed `tenant_id` field — callers stuff tenant data into a free-form dict.

`Runner.run(starting_agent, input, context=TContext, ...)` carries a user-typed `TContext` wrapped in `RunContextWrapper` and threaded through the whole run. First-class typed context with strong propagation guarantees.
`run(agent, input, { context: TContext })` produces a typed `RunContext<TContext>` that flows to every tool, hook, and handoff. Same first-class typed model as the Python SDK.

`Agent.run(..., deps=AgentDepsT, metadata=AgentMetadata)` exposes both a typed `deps` channel (compile-time-checked) and a free-form `metadata` channel for OTel tagging. The deps generic is part of the agent's type and is enforced at the type level.

`PromptRequest` has no `tenant_id`/`user_id`/metadata field — the only carriers are the LLM-visible `preamble`/`prompt`, the `conversation_id` string (parseable but stringly typed), or per-tool closure capture at build time.
`Agent.stream_async(prompt, *, invocation_state=...)` accepts a free-form `dict[str, Any]` propagated to tools and hooks. Working channel but untyped and undocumented as a typed tenant slot.
`stream(args, { invocationState })` accepts a `Record<string, unknown>` per-call bag threaded by reference into every hook and `ToolContext`. Functional but not typed at the framework level.

`ToolLoopAgent<CALL_OPTIONS, TOOLS, RUNTIME_CONTEXT, OUTPUT>` is generic over the runtime context type, and per-tool `contextSchema` validates `toolsContext[toolName]` at runtime. Strongest typing of the surveyed stacks alongside LangGraph and Pydantic-AI.

row: Tenant identity propagation into tool calls
details: Every tool's `Run(ctx tool.Context, args any)` receives a context exposing `UserID()`, `AppName()`, `SessionID()`, `State()` (with `app:`/`user:` prefixes), `Branch()`, `UserContent()`, etc. Auto-propagated by the framework; tenant ID is fetched from state by convention rather than a first-class field.

row: Tenant identity propagation into tool calls
details: If the tool function signature includes `run_context: RunContext`, the framework injects it automatically and the tool reads `run_context.dependencies['tenant_id']`/`run_context.user_id`. Clean idiomatic propagation, just not typed at the dependencies layer.

row: Tenant identity propagation into tool calls
details: `ToolRuntime::execute(&self, args: serde_json::Value)` receives only the LLM-generated JSON args — no context parameter exists, so tenant identity literally cannot reach a tool except by being captured on the tool struct at construction.

row: Tenant identity propagation into tool calls
details: SDK MCP tool handlers receive only `dict[str, Any]` LLM args — no `RunContext`/`ToolContext`. Tenant identity must be captured in a Python closure at server construction (`make_tools(tenant_id='acme')`) or forced via the `PreToolUse`/`can_use_tool` callbacks rather than reaching the tool directly.

row: Tenant identity propagation into tool calls
details: Same as the Python SDK: handler is `(args, extra) => ...` with no harness-injected context; tenant flows via closure-captured factory functions, AsyncLocalStorage, or `PreToolUse`/`canUseTool` `updatedInput`.

row: Tenant identity propagation into tool calls
details: Tool `_run(self, **kwargs)` receives only LLM-validated args; there is no `context: ToolContext` parameter. Workarounds (global `before_tool_call` hook, closure on a `BaseTool` subclass, walking `self.agent.execution_context`) all have correctness or scoping problems.

row: Tenant identity propagation into tool calls
details: `InvokableRun(ctx context.Context, argumentsInJSON, opts...)` receives the same `context.Context` you set values on plus per-tool typed options via `tool.GetImplSpecificOptions[T]`. Untyped Go-style propagation, but reaches every tool automatically.

row: Tenant identity propagation into tool calls
details: `*ai.ToolContext` embeds `context.Context`, and `core.FromContext(ctx)` returns the `ActionContext` populated by your `ContextProvider`. Auto-propagated with a designed extraction API.

row: Tenant identity propagation into tool calls
details: Tools declare a `runtime: ToolRuntime[ContextT, StateT]` parameter and read `runtime.context.tenant_id` directly. The parameter is excluded from the LLM-visible JSON schema, so identity reaches the tool but never appears in the model-facing surface.

row: Tenant identity propagation into tool calls
details: Tools that declare `ctx: Context` get the live workflow context injected automatically; tenant is read as `state = await ctx.store.get('state'); state['tenant_id']`. Context params are excluded from the LLM-facing JSON schema. Works, but key-by-string lookup.

row: Tenant identity propagation into tool calls
details: Every tool's `execute(args, ctx)` receives a typed `ToolExecutionContext` whose `requestContext` is the same typed Map passed by the caller. `requestContextSchema` lets tools validate the keys they need. First-class auto-propagation.

row: Tenant identity propagation into tool calls
details: Tools declare a `ctx: FunctionInvocationContext` parameter and the framework auto-discovers it (`_discover_injected_parameters`). `ctx.kwargs` carries `function_invocation_kwargs`. .NET uses `FunctionInvokingChatClient.CurrentContext`. Auto-injected but still untyped.

row: Tenant identity propagation into tool calls
details: Tools whose signature declares `ctx: RunContextWrapper[TContext]` get the same wrapper threaded through the whole run (with cumulative usage and approvals), and `ToolContext` extends it with per-call metadata. Schema-extraction skips the ctx parameter, so the LLM never sees it.

row: Tenant identity propagation into tool calls
details: Every `tool({ execute })` callback receives `(parsedInput, runContext, details)` automatically, with `runContext.context` typed as the caller-supplied `TContext`. Documented contract that every agent/tool/hook in a run shares the same `RunContext` type.

row: Tenant identity propagation into tool calls
details: `@agent.tool` functions whose first arg is `ctx: RunContext[DepsT]` get the typed deps plus rich call metadata (`tool_call_id`, `usage`, `retries`, `metadata`, etc.). One of the cleanest typed-deps stories in the survey.

row: Tenant identity propagation into tool calls
details: `Tool::call(&self, args)` receives no context object — the trait is stateless from the harness's perspective. Tenant identity reaches the tool only if you make it a field on the tool struct at construction time.

row: Tenant identity propagation into tool calls
details: Tools receive `invocation_state` via the executor's update of the dict, and decorated tools can request a `ToolContext` parameter that wraps it. Auto-propagated but untyped.

row: Tenant identity propagation into tool calls
details: `ToolContext` always exposes `invocationState`, `toolUse`, and `agent`, threaded by reference so writes in a hook are visible to later tools. Auto-injected to every tool callback.

row: Tenant identity propagation into tool calls
details: Each tool's `execute(input, { context })` receives a typed `CONTEXT` validated against the tool's `contextSchema`. `validateToolContext` rejects mismatches at runtime. Type-checked end-to-end.

`BeforeToolCallback(ctx, tool, args map[string]any) (map[string]any, error)` lets the host mutate args in-place before dispatch; returning `(nil, nil)` runs with the mutated args. Functional, but the LLM still sees the field in the tool schema unless you scrub it manually — no declarative `InjectedToolArg` equivalent.

`tool_hooks` middleware can mutate `args` before calling `next_func(**args)` and the hook can receive `run_context` automatically. This is the recommended mechanism, but there is no per-tool typed `spec T` / `inputSchema` override and no built-in schema scrubbing.

Hooks receive `&ToolCall` by shared (immutable) reference and cannot mutate args. The only workaround is capturing tenant as a struct field on the tool at construction time and ignoring whatever the LLM passes — which means one agent per tenant and the LLM still sees the field in the schema.

`PreToolUse` hooks return `{hookSpecificOutput: {updatedInput: ...}}` and `can_use_tool` callbacks return `PermissionResultAllow(updated_input=...)`. Both run out-of-band in your Python process via the control protocol, so the LLM cannot bypass them. `PreToolUse` fires on every call regardless of permission state.

Identical first-class mechanism to the Python SDK: `canUseTool` returns `{ behavior: 'allow', updatedInput }` and `PreToolUse` hooks return `updatedInput`. CLI dispatches with the harness-supplied input, not the LLM's, so the LLM cannot bypass.

Only mechanism is a process-global `before_tool_call` hook that mutates `ctx.tool_input` in place. Documented gotchas: hook is global across all crews in the process, tenant must be threaded via `ContextVar`, LLM still sees the field in the schema, multiple tenants concurrently fire the same hook.

`ToolsNodeConfig.ToolArgumentsHandler` and `compose.ToolMiddleware.Invokable` / `WrapInvokableToolCall` middleware can rewrite the raw arguments JSON before dispatch. Report explicitly contrasts this with LangGraph's declarative `InjectedToolArg` as strictly worse — you write middleware and remember to scrub the JSON schema yourself.

`Hooks.WrapTool` middleware can mutate `params.Request.Input` before calling `next(ctx, params)`. The pattern works but doesn't ship as a built-in, the report calls this BYO, and the field stays in the LLM-visible schema unless scrubbed.

Tools annotated with `InjectedToolArg`/`InjectedState` have those keys stripped from the LLM-visible JSON schema and overwritten in `ToolNode._inject_tool_args` — an LLM that supplies `tenant_id` has it silently replaced with the harness value. Report describes this as the cleanest forced-arg mechanism in the benchmark.

`FunctionTool(partial_params={...})` is a default-filler — LLM-provided kwargs win over `partial_params` because of merge order. Real forcing requires either closure-wrapping the tool (ignore the LLM-supplied field) or reading from `ctx.store` inside the tool; both are conventions, not enforced.

Mastra explicitly has no `PreToolUse → updatedInput` hook. The recommended pattern is to keep tenant fields out of the tool's `inputSchema` entirely and read them from `requestContext` (with `requestContextSchema` validation). `prepareStep`/`processInputStep` can also rebuild tools with closures, but a true argument-override hook is missing.

`FunctionMiddleware.process(context, call_next)` can mutate `context.arguments` before dispatch — recommended pattern in the report. Not first-class as a declarative `pinned_args` decorator; BYO middleware per agent.

No `PreToolUse → updatedInput` hook and no `experimental_refineToolInput` equivalent. Recommended pattern is to not expose tenant in the tool schema and read from `ctx.context` inside `execute`; for richer cases, build `FunctionTool` instances with custom `on_invoke_tool` that rewrites JSON. Tool input guardrails can only reject, not rewrite.

No mid-loop tool-arg mutation hook. `callModelInputFilter` operates on messages, not on pending tool args. Standard pattern is to ignore the LLM's arg in `execute` and pull from `runContext.context`, optionally hiding the field via `isEnabled`. Effective but convention-bound.

`@hooks.on.before_tool_validate(tools=['topic_search'])` can return a new `RawToolArgs` dict that takes precedence over the LLM's, and per-tool `args_validator` is even more type-safe. Plus the idiomatic ignore-from-deps pattern is documented. Not quite the declarative `InjectedToolArg` of LangGraph but very close.

`on_tool_call` hook gets `&str` args (immutable) and can only `Continue`/`Skip`/`Terminate`. Forcing requires building tool structs that own `tenant_id` per request and ignore the LLM-provided field — works only for static per-tenant agent construction, not per-call override.

`BeforeToolCallEvent.tool_use` is explicitly writable (`_can_write` allows `tool_use` along with `cancel_tool`/`selected_tool`) and the executor re-reads the mutated `tool_use` after the hook returns. Report calls this equivalent to Claude Agent SDK's `PreToolUse → updatedInput`.

`BeforeToolCallEvent.toolUse.input` is documented as mutable for hooks that need to rewrite tool input, id, or name before execution. Same pattern as the Python SDK; plus a typed `interventions.transform({apply})` API.

`experimental_refineToolInput` is a first-class per-tool function applied inside `parseToolCall` before dispatch, so the refined input is what tools, callbacks, and telemetry see. Caveat: must keep the same JSON shape — for true forcing, the report recommends combining with `contextSchema`/`toolsContext` to keep tenantId out of the LLM-visible schema entirely.

`Toolset.Tools(ctx ReadonlyContext)` is called per request and `FilterToolset(toolset, predicate)` supports reading `ctx.ReadonlyState()` for tenant-conditional inclusion. Caveat: static `agent.Tools []tool.Tool` slices are NOT filtered per request — only Toolsets are. You must wrap static tools as a Toolset to get tenant filtering.

`agent.tools` accepts a `Callable[..., List]` factory that receives `agent`, `run_context`, `session_state` by name and returns the filtered tool list. `cache_callables=False` disables caching so the filter re-runs per request. Same pattern works for `knowledge`/`members`/`instructions`.

`AgentDeriveT::tools()` returns a fixed `Vec<Box<dyn ToolT>>` at agent build time and the `#[agent]` derive macro lists tools statically. No `activeTools`/`allowed_tools`/`prepareStep` mechanism. Per-tenant filtering means constructing a different agent per tenant.

Three layered mechanisms (`tools`/`allowed_tools`/`disallowed_tools`) at construction, plus `set_permission_mode` and `toggle_mcp_server` for mid-session changes, and `PreToolUse` denial as a per-turn veto. No first-party `set_tools()` control request, but multiple knobs cover the use case.

Same construction-time mechanisms as the Python SDK plus mid-session `Query.setMcpServers(...)` to replace MCP servers and `applyFlagSettings({ permissions })` for per-turn permission changes. `AgentDefinition.tools`/`disallowedTools` provide per-sub-agent scoping.

`Agent(tools=[...])` is set at construction and there is no `prepareStep`/`activeTools` mid-run equivalent. Only mid-run dynamism is `BaseTool.max_usage_count` (returns an error string when exceeded). MCP `tool_filter` is connection-level, not per-turn.

`ChatModelAgentMiddleware.BeforeAgent` gives a mutable `runCtx.Tools []tool.BaseTool` slice for once-per-run filtering, and the `dynamictool` middleware shows how to wrap the chat model so `model.WithTools(filteredToolInfos)` runs per turn. Two-tier story; per-turn requires a custom wrapper.

Tool set is declared per `Generate(...)` call via `ai.WithTools(...)`; per-tenant filtering branches before the call. No per-turn `activeTools` analogue — once the call is in flight the tool set is fixed. Middleware can add but not remove tools.

Per-turn filtering is first-class: pass a callable for `model` taking `(state, runtime)` that returns a different `bind_tools([...])` per turn, plus `wrap_tool_call` can short-circuit forbidden tools. `bind_tools` and prebuilt registry filter combine cleanly with the typed runtime context.

Filtering at construction is trivial; per-turn dynamism comes from `tool_retriever: ObjectRetriever` which the framework calls each turn with the current `user_msg_str` (`get_tools` merges static `tools` plus retrieved). Not a tenant-aware filter primitive specifically, but the retriever can branch on tenant from state.

Three first-class layers: dynamic `tools` callable receiving `requestContext`, per-call `activeTools` whitelist, and `prepareStep` returning `{ activeTools }` per step. `toolCallStep` rejects non-active tools by name. Strongest per-tenant tool-filtering surface in the survey.

`agent.run(messages, options={'tools': [...]})` lets a per-run tools list override the agent default, and `ContextProvider`s can contribute tools via `SessionContext.tools` (used by `SkillsProvider`). Plus `FilteringSkillsSource` filters skills. No per-turn `activeTools` callable based on request context.

`Tool.is_enabled` accepts `(RunContextWrapper, AgentBase) -> bool | Awaitable[bool]` and `Agent.get_all_tools` evaluates it per-turn via `_check_tool_enabled` with `asyncio.gather`. Handoffs have the same `is_enabled`. Per-turn, context-aware, no agent reconstruction needed.

Per-tool `isEnabled?: boolean | ((args: { runContext, agent }) => boolean | Promise<boolean>)` is evaluated in `Agent.getAllTools(runContext)` at turn-prep time. Handoffs support the same predicate. MCP tools have a separate `MCPServer.toolFilter` knob.

Multiple first-class options: `@agent.toolset` decorator from `RunContext`, `prepare_tools` callable per step returning a filtered `list[ToolDefinition]`, plus `.filtered(predicate)`/`.prepared(prepare_func)` wrappers on any `AbstractToolset`, plus per-run `toolsets=[...]`. Comprehensive coverage.

Tools visible to the LLM come from `tool_server_handle.get_tool_defs(...)`. Per-request filtering requires building a fresh `Agent` with only the desired tools, or mutating a shared `ToolServerHandle` (which leaks across concurrent users). No `activeTools`/`allowedTools`/`prepareStep`.

`Agent(tools=[...])` is the primary surface; no per-turn `activeTools`/`prepareStep` is exposed. Workarounds include mutating `agent.tool_registry.registry` between turns, MCP `ToolFilters` at load time, or vetoing in `BeforeToolCallEvent.selected_tool = None`. Per-turn LLM-visible filtering is not first-class.

`ToolRegistry` is mutable and the visible tools are read once per model call via `_toolRegistry.list()`. Per-turn filtering is BYO: build a per-tenant Agent, mutate the registry between cycles, or cancel-in-Before. No `prepareStep`-style filter.

Three coexisting layers: agent-level `activeTools`, per-step `prepareStep(...) → { activeTools }` via `filterActiveTools`, and per-call `prepareCall(...) → { tools }` for templating one `ToolLoopAgent` to emit different toolsets per request based on typed `CALL_OPTIONS`.

`tool.Context` exposes `UserID()` and `AppName()` (auto-routed) and `context.Context` carries whatever you put on it. No first-class principal/claims type; the framework provides identity hooks (`authPreprocessor`) for OAuth-flow tools but not for per-call caller identity.

AgentOS authentication propagates the JWT `sub` claim to `RunContext.user_id` automatically, and `RemoteAgent` calls forward the token via `auth_token`. Tools needing caller permissions read `run_context.user_id`. First-class auth plumbing at the HTTP layer.
No identity reaches the tool — the runtime has no notion of a principal or auth context. Identity must be captured as a struct field at tool construction.
No SDK primitive automatically threads caller JWT to every tool call. Tenant/auth identity is captured via Python closures into hook/tool callbacks. BYO.

Same as the Python SDK — caller identity does not flow into tool calls automatically. SDK-MCP tools run in your Node process so identity can be pulled from your own request context via AsyncLocalStorage; CLI built-in tools execute under the subprocess OS user.

Caller's identity does not propagate. External-API tools (gmail, slack, salesforce) are configured per-tool-instance with their own credentials; no 'use the caller's bearer token' notion. AMP's Connected Apps binds at user-org level, not per-request.

Caller identity reaches the tool only because the host puts it on `context.Context`. Pattern is documented (extract identity in `BeforeAgent`, set on tool's BQ client) but not built-in — no automatic per-tool-call STS or impersonation.

If a `ContextProvider` loads auth credentials into `ActionContext`, tools that read `core.FromContext(ctx)` see them; there is no automatic IAM/RBAC layer at the tool boundary. Firebase plugin ships an auth helper for one provider.

`runtime.context` carries caller identity into every tool; engineers wire tenant-scoped DB connections/JWTs into `runtime.context` and tools run under that scope. Plus LangGraph Server's `@auth.on.*` decorators are first-class for HTTP-layer filtering on threads/runs/store.
Auth identity is whatever you stash in `ctx.store` and read inside the tool. No built-in identity propagation from an outer HTTP handler.

`MASTRA_AUTH_TOKEN_KEY` is a reserved key on `RequestContext` for forwarding caller auth tokens into tool execution, and the editor uses it to forward auth to MCP servers requiring same auth as the Mastra server. First-class plumbing.

Caller identity is not automatically propagated. Must be injected via `function_invocation_kwargs` (Python) or `AdditionalProperties` (.NET), or via a custom `FunctionMiddleware`/`ContextProvider`. Tool approval flow is orthogonal to identity propagation.

Typed `TContext` reaches every tool call automatically, so tokens, RLS predicates, and tenant rules flow without thread-locals. `ToolContext` adds `tool_call_id`/`tool_arguments`/etc. for correlation. Report calls this one of the cleanest models alongside Mastra.

Whatever you put in `runContext.context` is automatically reachable from every tool, lifecycle hook, guardrail, and handoff — documented contract that they share the same context type. Tools enforce auth in `execute`.
`ctx.deps` flows to every tool by construction, and the host code constructing deps (from an incoming HTTP request) is the natural auth termination point. Strong typed plumbing.
No principal, no auth_token, no per-call identity. Tools execute with whatever permissions you wired into their `call` body; identity is captured as a struct field at tool construction.
Whatever you stash in `invocation_state`/`agent.state` is forwarded to every tool. No first-class JWT/OAuth identity object — you build it.

Caller identity propagates via `invocationState` only. No built-in auth principal type; tools execute under the host process credentials, with per-call auth passed via `invocationState.userId`/`.scopes`/`.jwt`.

Caller identity reaches tools via `runtimeContext`/`toolsContext` with per-tool `contextSchema` validation. Typed and clean, but the report notes no automatic plumbing — engineers must place identity into the context bag.

No `MaxTokens`/USD/rate-limit middleware per tenant. Trigger controllers have a `MaxConcurrentRuns` cap but it is global to the trigger, not per-tenant. Token usage exposed via `Event.UsageMetadata` for the host to roll up.

`tool_call_limit` per agent caps tool-call count. `Metrics.cost` is computed in USD but reported after the fact — nothing enforces a per-tenant monthly cap. A DB-backed tenant counter with a pre-hook is required.
Only `ExecutorConfig { max_turns }` (default 10) — a turn cap. No USD budget, no per-tenant cost tracking. `Usage` extracted from stream chunks but enforcement is BYO.

`max_budget_usd: float | None` is wired through to the CLI as `--max-budget-usd`; overrun ends the run with `error_max_budget_usd`. Real per-run USD cap (rare in the survey) but no per-tenant aggregation — sum `total_cost_usd` across runs yourself. `RateLimitEvent` surfaces Anthropic rate-limit transitions for back-off.

Same `Options.maxBudgetUsd` as the Python SDK (per-run USD ceiling enforced server-side), plus `maxTurns` and an alpha `taskBudget.total` (token budget exposed to the model). No per-tenant cumulative cap — you aggregate `total_cost_usd` in your store.

`Agent.max_rpm`/`Crew.max_rpm` enforce requests-per-minute via `RPMController` but the counter is process-local, not per-tenant. No USD budget cap; `UsageMetrics` tracks token counts only, no `cost_usd` field is populated.
No USD budget enforcement, no per-tenant token ceiling. Token counts come off `ResponseMeta.Usage` and the host enforces caps via a `callbacks.Handler.OnEnd` that aborts.
Only per-call cap is `MaxTurns` (turn count). Token usage exposed on `resp.Usage` after the call; per-tenant enforcement (e.g. Redis counter in `WrapGenerate` middleware) is BYO.
No token-budget cap, no USD-cost cap in OSS. LangGraph Platform exposes per-deployment rate limits but not per-tenant USD ceilings.
`TokenCountingHandler.token_budget` raises `ValueError` when exceeded — but per handler instance, not per tenant, and counts tokens not USD. No USD budget cap.

`stopWhen` supports `tokenLimit`/`maxSteps`/custom predicates. `CostGuardProcessor` fires a tripwire when cost exceeds a threshold but depends on caller-provided pricing (`CostContext.estimatedCost`) with no built-in pricing tables. Real per-tenant dollar ceilings require composing both with your own pricing.
Tokens are observable via OTel histograms and `UsageDetails` but no built-in USD cap or per-tenant ceiling.

`Usage` reports tokens (input/output/total/cached/reasoning) and request counts. No dollar-cost field, no per-tenant budget cap, no 'stop run if usage > $X' mechanism. Enforcement happens in `on_llm_end` hooks against your billing store.

SDK surfaces token usage on `RunContext.usage`/`RunResult.state._context.usage` but does not enforce caps. Ceilings via custom `Model` wrapper or `agent_tool_start` listener that throws. No USD budget cap.

`UsageLimits` caps per-run tokens, requests, and tool calls (`request_limit=50` default). No in-tree USD cap; Pydantic AI Gateway adds project/user/key-level daily/weekly/monthly USD caps. Per-tenant rate limiting is BYO inside a `before_run` hook.
Only `max_turns` (turn cap) and `max_tokens` (per-completion cap). No USD budget, no per-tenant rate limit.
`EventLoopMetrics.update_usage` tracks tokens at the agent-instance level; per-tenant aggregation and cap enforcement must be implemented in hooks.

`AgentMetrics.accumulatedUsage` reports tokens but no USD computation and no enforcement. Caps via `BeforeModelCallEvent.projectedInputTokens` or polling `agent.metrics?.accumulatedUsage` from a host-level budget tracker.
`stopWhen` accepts step-count and tool-name stop conditions but no USD-cost or token-count budget cap. AI Gateway's spend report is observational, not enforcing.

REST eval routes exist (`server/adkrest/internal/routers/eval.go:30-46`) but all return HTTP 501 via `controllers.Unimplemented`. The Python ADK ships eval; adk-go users run a sister adk-python process or write their own harness.

note: first-class eval suite, no dataset format
details: `AccuracyEval`, `PerformanceEval`, `ReliabilityEval`, `AgentAsJudge` (`libs/agno/agno/eval/`) with results persisted in `agno_evals` table via `db.create_eval_run`. Each eval class is the unit of regression rather than a dedicated golden-dataset type, so multi-case suites are composed by hand around the eval objects.

Standard `cargo test --features full --workspace` runs SDK unit tests; the `crates/autoagents-llm/src/evaluator/parallel.rs` is unrelated to agent-output evaluation. No dataset format, no regression harness.
Report explicitly marks golden datasets, LLM-judge, and CI gates as 'not provided'. Users compose evals around `query()` themselves.

No golden-dataset format, no regression harness. The only test-shaped artifact is the `SessionStore` adapter conformance suite (`examples/session-stores/shared/conformance.ts`) — that tests adapters, not agent behaviour.

`crewai test [-n N]` invokes `CrewEvaluator` (`utilities/evaluators/crew_evaluator_handler.py`) which spawns a `Task Execution Evaluator` agent and prints a quality score table. There is no dataset format — you re-run the crew with hard-coded or `kickoff_for_each` inputs and the CLI never fails the build on low scores.
No `Dataset`, `Evaluator`, or `EvalRun` primitives. Recommended pattern is Go's `testing` package + recorded `model.BaseChatModel` mocks.

`go/ai/evaluator.go:38-94` defines `Example` (test-case-id, input, output, reference, traceIds) and `EvaluatorRequest{Dataset: []*Example, EvaluationId}`. Datasets are managed via the Genkit JS CLI (`genkit-tools/cli/src/commands/eval-*`). Built-in evaluators (`plugins/evaluators/evaluators.go`) are deterministic (`DeepEqual`, `Regex`, `Jsonata`); LLM-as-judge is BYO in Go.
No dataset or evaluator primitives in this OSS repo. Dataset management and evaluators live in the paid LangSmith product; local-only users wire `pytest` around `graph.invoke(...)`.

`llama-index-core/llama_index/core/evaluation/` ships `RetrieverEvaluator`, `RelevancyEvaluator`, `FaithfulnessEvaluator`, `CorrectnessEvaluator`, `AnswerRelevancyEvaluator`, `GuidelineEvaluator`, `SemanticSimilarityEvaluator`, `BatchEvalRunner`, plus `RagDatasetGenerator`/`LabelledRagDataset`. Coverage skews RAG; agent-behavior regression requires composing primitives yourself or piping to Phoenix/Langfuse/Opik.

`packages/core/src/datasets/` defines `Dataset` types persisted via `storage/domains/datasets/`; `runEvals(...)` (`packages/core/src/evals/run/index.ts:57-119`) accepts `{agent, dataset, scorers, concurrency}` and returns an `EvalRunResult`. Scorers wire into the agent loop via `isTaskComplete: { scorers, strategy: 'all' }`, a unique closed-loop feature in this benchmark, with results persisted to `storage/domains/scores/`.

`_evaluation.py` (1941 lines, gated by `@experimental(feature_id=ExperimentalFeature.EVALS)`) ships `EvalItem`, `LocalEvaluator`, and helpers `evaluate_agent`, `evaluate_workflow`, `evaluate_traces`, `evaluate_foundry_target` (per `docs/decisions/0023-foundry-evals-integration.md`). Experimental tag and Foundry-centred design mean production use today needs caution.
No first-party dataset/eval primitives — community pattern is to use Braintrust, Phoenix, Langfuse, or LangSmith which all consume the SDK's tracing.
No agent-eval primitives ship in the SDK. The repo's own tests use vitest. Users adopt Braintrust/Phoenix/Langfuse/LangSmith which consume the SDK's traces.

`pydantic_evals/` ships `Dataset`/`Case` (JSON/YAML serialisable, `dataset.py`), built-in plus custom plus LLM-judge evaluators (`evaluators/`), production traffic sampling (`online.py`), and reports + OTel emission (`reporting/`, `otel/`). The most complete first-party golden-dataset + regression toolkit in the benchmark, including snapshot/VCR support for replay.

`crates/rig-core/src/evals.rs` (feature-gated `experimental`) exposes `EvalOutcome<Output>` (`Pass`/`Fail`/`Invalid`) and an `Eval` trait with `eval`/`eval_batch(input, concurrency_limit)`. It is a primitive, not a dataset+harness; there is no first-party golden-dataset format.
Standard `pytest` (see `tests/`, `tests_integ/`) is used internally for the SDK; no built-in eval harness or dataset type for agent regression.
Repo has its own unit/integration tests (`strands-ts/test/integ/`, `strands-ts/src/**/__tests__/`) but ships no dataset format or runner for agent-behaviour regression.

`@ai-sdk/test-server` (`packages/test-server/`) mocks providers for unit tests; there is no SDK-shipped dataset format. Eval/regression harnesses are explicitly external (Braintrust, LangSmith, your own).
Report flags 'no first-party rubric / scorer / judge classifier'. You wire an LLM-judge from scratch on top of the Go runtime.

`AccuracyEval` (`eval/accuracy.py:24-58`) drives an LLM (defaults to the agent's own model) to grade outputs 1–10 against `expected_output` with reasoning; `AgentAsJudge` (`eval/agent_as_judge.py`) generalises the pattern. Results persist in `agno_evals` for trend analysis.
No LLM-judge ships. The `evaluator/parallel.rs` in `autoagents-llm` is for parallel execution, not output rubric scoring.
Report marks LLM-as-judge explicitly 'not provided'. Users compose a second `query()` call as judge themselves.
Report explicitly marks it 'BYO'. Compose with another `query()` call against a rubric prompt yourself.

`crewai test` spins up an `Agent(role='Task Execution Evaluator', ...)` to grade each task on a 1–10 `quality` scale via `TaskEvaluationPydanticOutput` (`utilities/evaluators/crew_evaluator_handler.py`). The rubric is hardcoded to 'completion, quality, overall performance' with no first-party knob beyond `task.expected_output`; richer judging needs Patronus or AMP integrations.
Eino ships no judge framework. Recommended pattern is to write a function that calls an LLM with a rubric prompt over the agent's output.

Go side ships only deterministic evaluators (`DeepEqual`, `Regex`, `Jsonata`); LLM-as-judge is a documented pattern of defining your own `ai.DefineEvaluator` that calls `genkit.GenerateText` with a judge prompt and returns the `Score` type (which supports numeric/string/categorical). First-class LLM judges live on the JS side, not Go.
Hosted LLM-judges are in LangSmith (paid); `langchain` has `load_evaluator(...)` but is separately packaged. Local LangGraph users compose judges themselves.

`RelevancyEvaluator`, `FaithfulnessEvaluator`, `CorrectnessEvaluator`, `AnswerRelevancyEvaluator`, `GuidelineEvaluator`, `SemanticSimilarityEvaluator` all use an LLM-against-rubric pattern out of the box. RAG-focused defaults, but the breadth and ergonomics are top of the benchmark.

`createScorer({ id, description }).generateScore(async ({ run }) => { ... })` supports both code-based predicates and LLM rubrics, and scorers can be wired back into the agent loop (`isTaskComplete: { scorers, strategy: 'all' }`) so the agent retries on judge failure. Built-in scorer types ship under `packages/core/src/evals/`.

`Evaluator` protocol (`_evaluation.py:507`) ships pre-built checks (`keyword_check`, `tool_calls_present`, `tool_call_args_match`, ...) and accepts custom LLM-judge callables. Still under the `@experimental(EVALS)` flag, which knocks it just below pydantic-evals/agno/mastra.
`examples/agent_patterns/llm_as_a_judge.py` is a usage example, not a built-in scorer; rubric, parsing, and aggregation are user-built.
`examples/agent-patterns/llm-as-a-judge.ts` shows the pattern (one agent grades another) but no judge primitive ships in the SDK.

First-party `llm_judge` evaluator under `pydantic_evals.evaluators` (`docs/evals/evaluators/llm-judge.md`), integrated with the rest of the `pydantic-evals` Dataset/Case pipeline and OTel reporting. Strongest combination of built-in LLM judging plus surrounding regression harness.

Pattern is to implement the `Eval` trait around an `Extractor<M, YourRubric>` (`extractor.rs:31-80`) and return `Pass`/`Fail`/`Invalid`. It works but is bare metal — no rubric prompt templates, no judge presets.
No LLM-judge primitive. Users implement rubric prompting themselves.
Report explicitly: 'Not provided'.

No first-party rubric primitive; the report notes you can trivially compose a judge with `generateObject({ model: judgeModel, schema, prompt })`. Everything else (rubric, threshold, aggregation) is host code.

Closest primitive is the internal `replayplugin` (`internal/configurable/conformance/replayplugin/`) that records and replays LLM-driven traces deterministically; it is internal-only and you would fork it. No turnkey pre-merge gate ships.

No first-party 'pre-merge gate' CLI. Documented pattern is to run `eval.run()` / `eval.arun()` inside pytest and assert `result.score >= threshold`. Persistence to `agno_evals` gives you trend data once the gate is wired.
Only `cargo test --features full --workspace` ships (README.md:173). No agent-behaviour CI gates.
Report flags 'not provided'. Users wire pytest around `query()` themselves.
Report explicit: build a gate with your own eval harness over `query()`.

`crewai test` prints a quality table but its exit code is 0 unless an exception is raised — there is no `--min-score` threshold or JUnit output. AMP markets 'Crew Testing' in the dashboard but no documented PR gate integration.
No first-party gate. Recommended pattern is to run agent against fixtures in CI, assert outputs match expected or judge-score above a threshold, and block PR.
Pattern is to invoke `genkit eval:run` (JS CLI) in CI against a JSON dataset and assert on scores yourself. No first-party gate or JUnit output ships.
OSS repo ships nothing. Typical pattern is a pytest job running a sample of `graph.invoke(...)` against golden datasets and blocking merge on regression.
No first-party gate. Report says wire `BatchEvalRunner` into your CI and assert on scores; primitives are rich but the gate plumbing is yours.

`runEvals` runs cleanly inside Vitest `it()` blocks and is the documented pattern; eval results persist in the configured storage backend for trend dashboards. No dedicated 'ScoredTest' macro or JUnit gate, so threshold logic is host-written.
Not packaged as a turnkey gate — run `evaluate_agent` in CI and fail on score yourself. `FoundryEvals` is offered as a managed alternative.
Report explicit: 'BYO'. Gating relies on partner products.
Report explicit: 'Not provided'.

Datasets run under `pytest`; the framework's own suite uses `inline-snapshot` + `pytest-recording` + `vcrpy` for replay-based LLM testing (`AGENTS.md:107-115`) and is the recommended template for users' CI. No dedicated gate CLI, but the surrounding toolchain is the most CI-friendly in the benchmark.
Pattern is a `cargo test` that calls `eval_batch(...)` and asserts; no turnkey CI gate or threshold reporter.
Report explicit: 'Not provided — BYO'.
Report explicit: 'Not provided'.
Report explicit: 'Eval is your CI's responsibility'. The SDK provides nothing beyond `@ai-sdk/test-server` for unit-test mocking.

The `adkgo` binary walks for `root_agent.yaml` and launches the full stack (Web UI, REST, A2A, agent-engine emulator). Sub-launchers cover `web`, `webui`, `api`, `a2a`, `console` (TUI/REPL), and `agentengine`. Programmatic launcher and library mode also supported.

`python run.py` starts AgentOS on port 7777 and pairs with the hosted UI at os.agno.com. `agno` CLI scaffolds infra and `Agent.cli_app()` / `print_response()` provide rich terminal REPLs for quick experimentation.

No first-party playground. Run via `cargo run --example <name>` against the 20+ examples directory. A separate `AutoAgents-CLI` repo provides a YAML-driven HTTP runner but is out of scope for the SDK itself.
The `claude` CLI binary is itself a TUI you can run locally. The Python SDK ships `examples/quick_start.py` for headless runs but there is no separate dev UI for the SDK consumer.

Same underlying `claude` CLI works as an interactive REPL, but the TS SDK ships no playground/TUI/web dev UI. SDK consumers run scripts with `bun run` / `tsx` and inherit the CLI only via the subprocess transport.

Comprehensive CLI: `crewai chat` terminal REPL, `crewai run` (uv-based), `crewai checkpoint` and `crewai memory` TUIs, plus `crewai create crew|flow` scaffolders. No first-party web playground in OSS — AMP Crew Studio is cloud-hosted only.

No `eino dev` CLI, no TUI, no playground. CloudWeGo ships IntelliJ/JetBrains plugins (orchestration + debug) but they are Chinese-documented and not equivalent to Mastra/LangGraph Studio. No web-based equivalent.
`genkit start -- go run .` spawns the process, opens a browser Dev UI with action runner, trace viewer, prompt playground (`.prompt` live preview), and dataset/eval runner. First-class local sandbox.

`langgraph dev` boots a local HTTP server with `InMemorySaver` plus the LangGraph Studio web UI for graph visualization, state stepping, message sending, and interrupt triggering. Studio is closed-source but bundled in the CLI dev workflow.
Not provided in `llama-index-core`. The `llama-index-cli` package is for document indexing, not agent chatting. Users typically run agents in Jupyter notebooks or plain scripts.
`mastra dev` boots a local server with Mastra Studio (Playground) at localhost:3000 — run agents, inspect traces, run evals, iterate on skills, view memory. React-based and first-class.

`agent-framework-devui` (`devui ./agents --port 8080`) auto-discovers agents/workflows, exposes OpenAI-compatible API, and provides a debug web UI. Marked as sample app, not for production, but covers the dev sandbox use case.
`run_demo_loop` (`src/agents/repl.py`) provides a terminal REPL for quick manual smoke tests with streaming and tool-call surfacing. No web playground, TUI, or Mastra-style dev UI.
No CLI playground shipped. Closest is `examples/sandbox/basic.ts` run with `tsx`. SDK consumers wire their own runner with `tsx`/`node`/`deno`/`bun`.
Strong CLI surface: `clai` (uvx), `Agent.to_web()` exposes a Starlette + HTML chat UI at localhost:7932, and `to_cli_sync()`/`to_cli()` drop the agent into an interactive REPL.

`agent_os.serve(reload=True)` enables uvicorn auto-reload on `.py` and `.yaml` changes (`os/app.py:1518-1521`). Process-level reload rather than in-flight skill swap, but first-class flag.

Skills/agents/plugins are loaded on each subprocess spawn — change a SKILL.md on disk and the next `query()` picks it up. No long-lived caching daemon to flush, so iteration is instant.

`Query.reloadPlugins()`, `Query.applyFlagSettings()`, and `Query.setMcpServers()` swap plugin/setting/MCP state mid-session. Skills, sub-agents, system prompts, and tool list (outside plugins/MCP) need a `query()` restart. No source-watch for skills.
No hot reload. Changing a `SKILL.md`, YAML config, or Python code requires restarting your process. `crewai run` uses uv subprocess so changes wait for the next run. No watch-mode.
